Result: CAT outperforms baselines on ranking metrics (AUROC +11.0% on physical trajectories; AUPRC +15.8% on human traces). Ablations show the benefit of spatial conditioning and per-robot prototypes. Demonstrations achieve embodiment-aware obstacle avoidance on legged and wheeled platforms at 4.8 Hz on embedded hardware.

Conclusion: Embedding embodiment into the learned representation yields superior, morphology-aware traversability predictions, enabling safe, real-time navigation across diverse robot morphologies and settings.

Abstract: Estimating traversability in unstructured environments requires conditioning on robot embodiment, as the same terrain can be traversable for one platform and unsafe for another. Existing methods often transfer predictions across morphologies through late-stage trajectory filtering rather than encoding platform constraints in the learned representation. We propose Capability-Aware Traversability (CAT), a framework that embeds physical limits directly into the spatial feature space. CAT grounds dense supervision masks in physical trajectories through an interactive annotation pipeline and modulates semantic terrain maps with robot-specific traversability vectors through Spatially-Adaptive Denormalization (SPADE) blocks. Across human-annotated and trajectory-aligned datasets, CAT leads all ranking-based metrics, improving AUROC by 11.0% on physically executed trajectories and AUPRC by 15.8% on human traces over the strongest baseline. Ablations show that spatial conditioning and per-robot prototypes produce capability sensitivity beyond generic path prediction. Deployments on a legged quadruped and a wheeled skid-steer demonstrate embodiment-aware obstacle avoidance on embedded hardware at 4.8 Hz.

</details>


### [102] [FELT: Generating Tactile Signals from Vision for Visuo-Tactile Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20683)
*Zinan Li,Yiyang Ling,Yuming Gu,Binghao Huang,Chenhao Liang,Sharfin Islam,Hisham Bedri,John Chirikjian,Yunzhu Li,Stefanos Nikolaidis,Daniel Seita*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FELT synthesizes tactile signals from RGB to enable visuo-tactile control with minimal tactile data, using a frozen visual encoder and separate decoders for left/right tactile panels; it can produce tactile images or latent features at inference, improving manipulation policies over vision-only baselines across four tasks, with latent features not requiring real tactile sensors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tactile data are scarce and fragile, hindering robust visuo-tactile learning; generating tactile signals from RGB reduces the need for tactile-equipped data while maintaining performance.

Method: A large frozen visual encoder is paired with a lightweight query decoder to predict per-finger tactile signals in a single forward pass. Separate branches for left and right tactile panels respect their physical topology and asymmetry. At deployment, only RGB is needed; outputs can be tactile images or latent tactile features.

Result: Experiments on four contact-rich manipulation tasks show that both generated tactile images and latent tactile features improve policy success over vision-only baselines; latent features achieve this without using any real tactile sensor during training or deployment.

Conclusion: FELT offers data-efficient visuo-tactile policy learning by enabling tactile information to be obtained from RGB, with latent tactile features providing a tactile-sensor-free deployment path and potentially easier data collection.

Abstract: The sense of touch is central to manipulation, especially when vision is occluded or ambiguous. Although combining vision and touch improves manipulation, learning robust visuo-tactile policies requires substantial tactile data. Such data remains scarcer than visual data, because tactile sensors are fragile, specialized, and hard to standardize. To address this, we present Feature-Extracted Latent Tactile (FELT), a learning-based framework that synthesizes per-finger pressure tactile images from RGB observations, reducing the need for tactile-equipped data collection. FELT uses a large frozen visual encoder and a lightweight query decoder to predict tactile signals in a single feed-forward pass. To respect the physical topology of dual-finger tactile sensors, FELT decodes the left and right tactile sensor panels through separate branches, capturing the asymmetric contact patterns during interactions such as wiping, insertion, and in-hand rotation. At inference time, FELT only requires RGB data, allowing us to augment existing vision-only data with tactile observations, either as generated tactile images or as latent tactile features. Experiments on four contact-rich manipulation tasks demonstrate that both generated tactile images and latent tactile features improve policy success over vision-only baselines, with latent feature requiring no real tactile sensor during policy training or deployment. Supplementary material is available on our anonymous website: https://felt-tactile.github.io/.

</details>


### [103] [Decentralized UAV Swarms for Ground Target Protection in GPS- and Communication-Denied Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20710)
*Dimitria Silveria,Paulo Ricardo Marques de Araujo,Tiago Nascimento,Sidney Givigi*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GPS-denied, sensor-only autonomous UAV swarm for ground-target defense; uses relative-position Kalman filters and decentralized encirclement to detect, encircle, and intercept hostile UAVs; validated on real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rising UAV threats and the limitations of GPS/comm-based defenses in modern conflicts demand autonomous, GPS-denied swarms capable of protecting ground targets.

Method: Proposes a complete pipeline where onboard sensors estimate target and swarm states using relative measurements via Kalman filters; a decentralized encirclement strategy adapts to target motion; coordination relies on swarm autonomy without GPS or global positioning.

Result: Experimental validation with real robots demonstrates effective detection, encirclement, and interception of hostile UAVs in GPS-denied scenarios.

Conclusion: Sensor-centric, GPS-denied swarm defense is viable; decentralized encirclement combined with relative-state estimation provides robust target protection in contested environments.

Abstract: The presence of UAVs in military operations has recently increased, also increasing the demand for defense systems against UAV attacks. UAVs can also be used as countermeasures. Most available methods rely on UAV-to-UAV communication and global positioning. However, such resources may not be available in modern warfare scenarios. To address these limitations, we propose a pipeline for ground-target protection against UAV attacks that employs autonomous swarms of UAVs. We assume a communication- and GPS-denied environment in which the UAVs use onboard sensors to track the target and coordinate as a swarm. We developed Kalman filters to estimate the states of unknown targets and the positions of UAVs in the swarm using only relative measurements. Also, our strategy is to encircle the target of interest to maximize coverage. To achieve that, we propose a decentralized swarm encirclement technique that adapts to the target's motion. Our approach was extensively validated using real robots, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting, encircling, and intercepting hostile UAVs.

</details>


### [104] [Self-Supervised Bio-Inspired Robotic Trajectory Planning with Obstacle Avoidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20743)
*Miroslav Krupa,Miroslav Cibula,Kristína Malinovská*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Neuro-inspired self-supervised trajectory planning using forward and inverse models; feasible in obstacle environments but planner tends to exploit supervisory signals; proposes additional training regimes and mitigation strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the high computational cost and limited generalization of sampling-based planners in high-dimensional, obstacle-rich spaces by leveraging model-based, self-supervised learning for efficient trajectory planning.

Method: A self-supervised framework where forward and inverse models provide internal supervision for trajectory planning. Experiments are conducted in environments with obstacles to test feasibility. The work also investigates failure modes (signal exploitation) and evaluates mitigation strategies through additional training regimes.

Result: Feasibility of the approach demonstrated; planner shows a tendency to exploit the forward/inverse supervisory signals, revealing a learning signal leakage. Mitigation strategies and extra training regimes are proposed and evaluated.

Conclusion: The neuro-inspired self-supervised framework is promising for efficient trajectory planning in obstacle-rich environments, but requires careful design of training regimes to prevent exploitation of the supervisory signal and to improve generalization.

Abstract: Trajectory planning is a fundamental problem in robotics, requiring the generation of collision-free and efficient trajectories in a potentially complex environment. While sampling-based planners remain the dominant approach, they are often computationally expensive, particularly in high-dimensional spaces and obstacle-rich environments. Methods based on model learning offer a promising alternative, enabling efficient planning through a bounded number of forward passes through a neural trajectory planner, but commonly suffer from low sample efficiency or limited generalisation due to their reliance on exploration or expert demonstrations. This follow-up work tests our neuro-inspired self-supervised learning framework for trajectory planning that leverages forward and inverse models as the internal supervisory mechanism in an environment that contains an obstacle. Experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the approach while revealing a tendency of our planner to exploit the learning signal provided by the forward and inverse models. To address this issue, additional training regimes and mitigation strategies are proposed and evaluated.

</details>


### [105] [A real-time RGB-D perception pipeline for autonomous impact hammers in mining: self-filtering, rock segmentation and rock-breaking poses generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20748)
*Martín Gallegos,Francisco Leiva,Patricio Loncomilla,Michelle Cortés,Javier Ruiz-del-Solar*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time RGB-D perception pipeline integrating instance segmentation and geometric processing to autonomously operate hydraulic impact hammers in mining, achieving ~10 Hz on embedded hardware with ~675 ms latency and enabling closed-loop control in a scaled test environment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Underground impact hammers require teleoperation, limiting efficiency and safety. An autonomous perception-and-pose-estimation pipeline could enable autonomous rock-breaking, reduce operator workload, and improve throughput.

Method: Fuse image-based instance segmentation with geometric point-cloud processing to generate operationally feasible rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D workspace representation. Implemented on embedded hardware at about 10 Hz with total latency ~675 ms. Designed to integrate with a control system for closed-loop operation.

Result: Experimental evaluation in a representative scaled scenario demonstrates real-time feasibility for autonomous hammer operation and the generation of usable rock-breaking poses and workspace maps.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates viability of real-time autonomous operation for hydraulic impact hammers and provides a foundation for further development toward deployment in underground mining; future work should address more diverse environments, robustness, safety, and full field trials.

Abstract: Impact hammers, also known as rock-breakers, are essential machines in mining operations, where they perform secondary reduction. In underground mining, these machines are typically teleoperated, limiting operational efficiency. This paper presents a real-time RGB-D perception pipeline as a step towards automating the operation of hydraulic impact hammers used in mining. The proposed system simultaneously generates operationally feasible rock-breaking poses and a robot-free 3D representation of the workspace. The proposed approach combines image-based instance segmentation with geometric point cloud processing, and operates on embedded hardware at approximately 10 Hz with a total latency of around 675 ms, enabling responsive closed-loop behavior when integrated with a control system. Experimental results in a representative scaled scenario demonstrate that the proposed system is suitable for real-time autonomous impact hammer operation.

</details>


### [106] [Emergent Compositional Skills in Mixture-of-Experts VLAs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20771)
*Shlok Shah,Rhiaan Jhaveri,Tharun Kumar Tiruppali Kalidoss,Chirayu Nimonkar,Ishaan Javali*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A VLA with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) head learns emergent, reusable primitives and high-level sequencing from demonstrations, matching a monolithic baseline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether end-to-end learning with an MoE action head can yield modular, interpretable task decomposition without explicit hierarchy, i.e., do experts emerge as reusable primitives and does the router induce high-level sequencing.

Method: Train a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model with a simplified MoE action head on expert demonstrations; analyze cross-task expert reuse, interpretability of low-level behaviors, and task performance versus a monolithic baseline.

Result: Learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and correspond to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors; the router appears to perform high-level sequencing; MoE matches the task performance of the monolithic baseline while showing meaningful expert specialization.

Conclusion: End-to-end data-driven MoE-based policies can emergently produce modular, interpretable robot primitives, a step toward scalable, interpretable robotic control without predefined task decompositions.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning compositional robot policies end-to-end from expert demonstrations, without any pre-specified notion of task decomposition or hierarchy. We ask whether a VLA trained with a simplified Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) action head can emergently learn to decompose tasks into reusable, interpretable primitives. We find that learned experts are heavily reused across tasks and consistently correspond to qualitatively distinct low-level behaviors, suggesting that the router implicitly learns to perform high-level sequencing while experts serve as compositional primitives. Our MoE matches the task performance of a monolithic baseline while demonstrating meaningful expert specialization, a step toward modular, interpretable robot policies that emerge from data alone.

</details>


### [107] [Socially Consistent Multi-Robot Navigation Using Decoupled Planning and Trajectory Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20772)
*Matthew M. Sato,Kincho H. Law*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A partially decentralized framework for socially aware multi-robot motion combines a social-norm aware A* path planner with a shared social path graph and a mixed-integer convex program for trajectory coordination, achieving predictable, socially consistent behavior across large fleets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon, socially compliant robot navigation is essential in human-centric settings. Existing methods focus on short-term, locally reactive planning and struggle with consistency and predictability over time, overburdening local planners.

Method: 1) Modify A* to penalize trajectories that violate macroscopic social norms and share planned paths to build a social graph of established routes. 2) Use the emergent structure of these paths to formulate multi-robot trajectory coordination as a mixed-integer convex program that ensures conflict-free trajectories and supports dynamic task assignment.

Result: Enforcing social consistency at the path planning stage yields predictable and socially compliant paths, and simplifies multi-robot coordination, enabling scalable coordination for large fleets.

Conclusion: Embedding social-consistent path planning reduces coordination complexity and enhances predictability of multi-robot motion in human-centered environments.

Abstract: The successful integration of mobile robots in human-centric environments requires navigation that is not only safe and efficient, but also predictable and aligned with social conventions, key precursors for human comfort and acceptance. While significant research addresses short-term human-aware planning, these methods often lack mechanisms for ensuring consistent and predictable behaviors across long horizons. Without socially aware long-term planners, local planners are overburdened, resulting in inefficient and locally reactive movements that undermine predictability. This paper introduces a partially decentralized framework that generates predictable and socially consistent multi-robot motion by decoupling global path planning from trajectory coordination. First, we propose a modified A* planner that embeds macroscopic social norms into the planner cost function. Planned paths are shared across mobile robots to collaboratively build a social graph of established routes, which enforces path consistency and reduces future planning effort. Second, we leverage the emergent structure of the socially constrained paths to formulate the multi-robot trajectory coordination problem as a mixed-integer convex program. The convex program enables efficient computation of conflict- free trajectories, scaling effectively to large fleets and supporting dynamic task assignment. Our results demonstrate that enforcing social consistency at the path planning stage produces predictable, socially compliant mobile robot paths and simplifies the otherwise complex problem of multi-robot coordination.

</details>


### [108] [Robostral Navigate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20785)
*Arjun Majumdar,Avinash Sooriyarachchi,Benjamin Tibi,Chris Bamford,Elliot Chane-Sane,Guillaume Lample,Khyathi Raghavi Chandu,Ludovic Ho Fuh,Mathieu Poiree,Olivier Duchenne,Rosalie Millner,Srijan Mishra,Theo Cachet,Thomas Chabal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A scalable monocular RGB navigation policy (8B VLM) that predicts image-space waypoints, trained on massive synthetic data with efficient training and attention masking, achieving SOTA on R2R-CE and RxR-CE with single RGB camera.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address hardware restrictions and data inefficiency in robotics navigation by eliminating depth/multi-camera prerequisites and enabling cross-embodiment generalization.

Method: 8B vision-language model; monocular RGB stream; image-space waypoint pointing; prefix-caching training to compress episodes; tree-based attention mask; reinforcement learning; 2.4M trajectories across 350k simulated scenes.

Result: State-of-the-art success rates on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE) at 77.4% and RxR-CE at 75.1%, surpassing monocular and depth/multicam baselines.

Conclusion: Demonstrates effective, scalable, hardware-agnostic navigation with efficient training; promising for deployment across diverse robots, but real-world validation and study of sim-to-real transfer needed.

Abstract: Deploying navigation systems at scale requires a recipe that minimizes sensor assumptions, generalizes across robot embodiments, and trains efficiently. Yet, today's best systems depend on depth sensors, multi-camera rigs, or pre-built maps, limiting the hardware they support and increasing deployment cost. We introduce Robostral Navigate, an 8B vision-language model built around this scalability objective. The model consumes only a stream of monocular RGB images - the most ubiquitous sensor across robotic platforms and predicts waypoints by pointing to the next target location in the current camera view. Operating purely in image space, rather than robot-specific coordinates, makes the policy naturally robust to changes in camera intrinsics and scene scale, enabling deployment across wheeled, legged, and aerial robots without recalibration. We generate 2.4 million trajectories across 350k simulated scenes to reduce the reliance on real-world data collection and scale easily. We further introduce a prefix-caching training recipe that packs entire episodes into single training sequences, reducing training tokens by 22x and cutting training time from months to days. A tree-based attention mask prevents conditioning on previous ground-truth actions, encouraging visually grounded action prediction, and reinforcement learning is used to further improve exploration and recovery capabilities. On the Room-to-Room and Room-Across-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE and RxR-CE) benchmarks, Robostral Navigate sets a new state of the art. On R2R-CE, it achieves a 77.4% success rate, surpassing the best monocular method by 10.5 points and the strongest depth- or multi-camera system by 5.3 points despite using only a single RGB camera. On RxR-CE, it reaches 75.1% success rate, outperforming all monocular baselines.

</details>


### [109] [URF: A Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework for Stable Contact Aware Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20912)
*Jiyou Shin,Youngjin Seo,Jaeseog Won,Sungwon Seo,Hyunjun Kim,Seokmin Yoon,Tuan Luong,Hyungpil Moon*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: URF unifies manipulation policy with controller-mode switching between admittance and impedance control, predicting a virtual target, a stiffness matrix, and an impedance-admittance switch ratio to improve contact stability and safety; switch labels are derived from contact-force measurements; shows higher success and fewer failure modes in box-flipping and line-pressing tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Rigid-contact manipulation suffers when learned actions are executed through a potentially mismatched low-level controller, leading to instability, tracking errors, excessive loading, or tool damage. A framework that jointly learns actions and execution mode can improve safety and robustness.

Method: URF takes multimodal sensor observations and predicts three outputs: a virtual target (desired pose/trajectory), a stiffness matrix (hence compliance), and an impedance-admittance switch ratio (controller mode). Ground-truth stiffness is unavailable, so switch labels are constructed from measured contact forces to supervise controller-mode prediction. The method is evaluated on box-flipping and line-pressing tasks, demonstrating improved performance and safer contact behavior.

Result: URF achieves higher task success rates and reduces failure modes associated with admittance-only execution, such as rapid force buildup, force oscillations, tool breakage, and robot safety stops.

Conclusion: Integrating controller behavior into learning-based policies yields more robust, contact-aware manipulation; predicting both compliant actions and the executing controller enables safer, more reliable performance in contact-rich tasks.

Abstract: Learning-based manipulation policies usually predict robot actions from sensory observations and leave their execution to a separate low-level controller. In rigid contact, this separation can be problematic: the same motion to a virtual target or compliant motion command can lead to unstable contact, tracking error, excessive loading, or tool damage, depending on the low-level controller. In this paper, we propose a \textit{Unified Robot Control-Policy Framework} (URF), which connects compliant action prediction with unified impedance-admittance control. Given multimodal observations, URF predicts a virtual target, a stiffness matrix, and an impedance-admittance switch ratio. The switch ratio determines when the controller should behave more like admittance control for accurate motion tracking and when it should move toward impedance control for safer rigid contact. Because demonstration data do not provide ground-truth environment stiffness, we construct switch-ratio labels from measured contact forces and use them to supervise controller-mode prediction. Across box-flipping and line-pressing tasks, URF achieves higher task success rates while reducing failure modes observed with admittance-only execution, including rapid force buildup, large force oscillations, tool breakage, and robot safety stops. These results suggest that contact-aware policies benefit from predicting not only compliant actions but also the controller behavior used to execute them. Project page: https://jiyou384.github.io/urf_project_page/

</details>


### [110] [Deep Reinforcement-Learning-Guided Model Predictive Control for Preventing Overtakes in Autonomous Racing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20973)
*Yufei Xi,Yijie Liao,Tulga Ersal*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A hierarchical RL-guided MPC is proposed for defensive blocking in autonomous racing to regulate spatial occupancy and delay opponents, using Soft Actor-Critic in the Frenet domain to produce geometry-aware references embedded as regularization within a nonlinear MPC under friction limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Defensive blocking in autonomous racing requires maintaining control near dynamic limits while preventing faster opponents from overtaking, challenging traditional lap-time optimization. The work reframes this as spatial occupancy regulation and seeks real-time, robust defense by leveraging learned strategic guidance within a model-based controller.

Method: A Soft Actor-Critic strategic layer operates in the Frenet domain to generate defensive references that encode geometry constraints. These references are embedded into a nonlinear MPC as spatial regularization under tire friction constraints. The framework is evaluated in simulation on Thunderhill West circuit.

Result: The method increases average overtaking time from 8.8 s to 14.6 s and reduces opponent progress; it allows the vehicle to utilize 83.4% of available tire force; mean solve time is 33.3 ms with 13.9 ms standard deviation, enabling real-time adversarial interaction.

Conclusion: A RL-guided MPC approach can effectively implement defensive blocking by shaping the vehicle’s spatial occupancy and exploiting tire-friction limits, delivering real-time performance gains and adversarial robustness in high-speed autonomous racing.

Abstract: This paper addresses defensive blocking in autonomous racing, where a vehicle must prevent a faster opponent from overtaking while operating near its dynamic limits. Different from lap-time minimization, we formulate defense as a spatial occupancy regulation problem via a hierarchical reinforcement-learning guided model predictive control framework. A Soft Actor-Critic strategic layer operates in the Frenet domain to generate geometry-aware defensive references, which are embedded into the nonlinear model predictive control formulation as spatial regularization under friction constraints. Evaluated on the Thunderhill West circuit in simulation, the framework increases average overtake time from 8.8 s to 14.6 s while significantly reducing opponent progress. Meanwhile, it allows the vehicle to utilize 83.4% of available tire force. The framework achieves a 33.3 ms mean solve time (13.9 ms std), supporting real-time high-speed adversarial interaction.

</details>


### [111] [Distributed Model-Based Diffusion For Scalable Multi-Robot Trajectory Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20992)
*Haejoon Lee,Xinyi Wang,Taekyung Kim,Dimitra Panagou*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Distributed Model-Based Diffusion (DMBD) enables scalable multi-robot trajectory optimization by decomposing the reverse diffusion into local conditional denoising with server-facilitated coordination; achieves sub-second performance and outperforms baselines across multiple coordination tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the curse of dimensionality and the need for global access to all robots' dynamics, constraints, and objectives in centralized model-based diffusion when scaling from single-robot to multi-robot systems; aims for a distributed, scalable, real-time capable framework in non-convex, non-differentiable environments.

Method: Decompose the reverse diffusion process into local conditional reverse diffusion steps. Each robot denoises within its own control subspace while conditioning on current trajectory estimates of other robots, which are aggregated and broadcast by a centralized server. This distributed server-robot architecture enables parallelism and reduces the need for global information.

Result: Extensive simulations across goal swapping, multi-floor coverage, parking, and rush-hour scenarios show that DMBD scales well, solves many challenging coordination tasks in sub-seconds, and significantly outperforms existing baselines.

Conclusion: DMBD provides a scalable, distributed diffusion-based solution for multi-robot trajectory optimization, enabling efficient coordination in complex environments and offering substantial performance gains over centralized approaches and existing baselines.

Abstract: Trajectory optimization for multi-robot systems remains a critical challenge, particularly when navigating highly non-convex, non-linear, and non-differentiable environments. While Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) has recently emerged as a promising sampling-based optimization paradigm for single-robot trajectory generation, extending it to multi-robot systems results in a centralized, high-dimensional inference problem that (i) suffers from poor sample efficiency due to the curse of dimensionality and (ii) requires global access to all robots' dynamics, constraints, and objectives. To address this, we propose Distributed Model-Based Diffusion (DMBD), a distributed server-robot framework that decomposes the reverse diffusion process into local conditional reverse diffusion processes. This decomposition enables each robot to iteratively perform denoising independently within its own control subspace while conditioning on the current trajectory estimates of the other robots that are aggregated and broadcast by the server. Extensive simulations in goal swapping, multi-floor coverage, parking, and rush-hour scenarios demonstrate that DMBD achieves strong scalability, solving many challenging coordination tasks in sub-seconds and significantly outperforming existing baselines.

</details>


### [112] [TableVerse: A Large-scale Tabletop Dataset with Real-world Grounded Layouts for Generalizable Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21017)
*Boyuan Wang,Yue Zhang,Xutao Xue,Xueyu Song,Yu Sun*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: TableVerse introduces a Real2Sim pipeline to reconstruct real-world tabletop scenes from unstructured internet imagery into high-fidelity, simulation-ready environments, with an automated trajectory generator and a 100k-strong TableVerse-100K dataset of physically consistent scenes and manipulation demos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalizable robotic manipulation is limited by the availability of large-scale, high-fidelity scene data. Existing synthetic methods often yield physically implausible layouts and fail to capture dense clutter of real human environments, hindering policy generalization.

Method: Propose TableVerse Real2Sim pipeline that deterministically reconstructs unstructured in-the-wild image data into high-fidelity tabletop environments with accurate metric scales, authentic topologies, and verified mechanical stability. Integrate automated task-conditioned trajectory generation to synthesize collision-free pick-and-place demonstrations. Compile TableVerse-100K dataset comprising 100,000 unique, physically consistent environments paired with interactive manipulation trajectories.

Result: A scalable, high-fidelity data foundation is created: TableVerse-100K contains 100,000 environments with realistic asset compositions, spatial distributions, and high-quality manipulation demonstrations, enabling robust training for generalizable robotic manipulation in cluttered real-world-like settings.

Conclusion: TableVerse-100K provides a scalable, high-fidelity data foundation for future research in generalizable robotic manipulation, advancing beyond imaginative layout generation by anchoring dataset creation in real-world data reconstruction and automated trajectory synthesis.

Abstract: The development of generalizable robotic manipulation policies is inherently bounded by the availability of large-scale, high-fidelity scene data. While recent automated synthesis methods attempt to bridge this gap via text-to-layout hallucination or simplified procedural generation, they frequently suffer from physical implausibility and fail to capture the complex, dense clutter of actual human environments. In this paper, we introduce TableVerse, a fully automated Real2Sim pipeline that shifts the paradigm from imaginative layout generation to deterministic reconstruction from unstructured, in-the-wild image data. Our framework seamlessly processes unscripted internet media into high-fidelity, simulation-ready tabletop environments with accurate metric scales, authentic topologies, and verified mechanical stability. Furthermore, an automated task-conditioned trajectory generation framework is integrated to synthesize high-quality, collision-free pick-and-place demonstrations. Leveraging this complete pipeline, we construct the TableVerse-100K Dataset, a large-scale corpus comprising 100,000 unique, physically consistent environments paired with interactive manipulation trajectories. By capturing diverse asset compositions, realistic spatial distributions, and high-quality demonstrations, TableVerse-100K establishes a highly scalable and high-fidelity data foundation, providing significant value to facilitate future research in generalizable robotic manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [113] [ZONDA: Zero-shot Object Navigation with Dynamic Avoidance in Multi-floor Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21025)
*Shaomin Liang,Xuanhong Liao,Shiyao Zhang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: ZONDA enables zero-shot object navigation across multi-floor, dynamic environments by integrating heuristic cross-floor planning, multi-view target verification, and dynamic pedestrian avoidance; it shows strong real-robot and simulation performance, including robustness in dynamic HM3D-DYNA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing object navigation methods are limited to static, single-floor settings and often neglect cross-floor topology and dynamic pedestrians; there is a need for zero-shot, platform-agnostic navigation without specialized controllers.

Method: Three components: (i) Heuristic multi-floor planning using height-difference traversable maps to enable stair traversal and cross-floor exploration without platform-specific learned controllers; (ii) Multi-view target verification by cross-checking multi-scale observations with a vision-language model to reduce false positives; (iii) Dynamic pedestrian avoidance by explicitly tracking and predicting moving pedestrians to generate anticipatory behaviors.

Result: Empirical evaluation on a real Direct Drive Tech TITA biped robot and extensive simulations on HM3D and MP3D shows significantly improved results; ZONDA maintains robust navigation on the dynamic HM3D-DYNA benchmark compared to existing baselines.

Conclusion: Integrating planning, perception verification, and dynamic avoidance yields zero-shot navigation capable in dynamic, multi-floor environments, supporting potential real-world deployment.

Abstract: In Object Goal Navigation task, existing methods are typically restricted to static and single-floor environments, ignoring cross-floor topologies and dynamic pedestrian, which limits their real-world deployment. To address these limitations, we propose ZONDA, a zero-shot object navigation with dynamic avoidance framework. In particular, ZONDA integrates three core components: (i) Heuristic multi-floor planning: from height-difference traversable maps, enables stair traversal and cross-floor exploration without a platform-specific learned controller; (ii) Multi-view target verification: cross-checks multi-scale observations with a vision-language model, significantly reducing false positives; and (iii) Dynamic pedestrian avoidance: explicitly tracks and predicts moving pedestrians to generate anticipatory behaviors. Evaluated on a real Direct Drive Tech TITA biped robot and extensive simulations on HM3D and MP3D, ZONDA achieves significantly improved results. Moreover, ZONDA can maintain robust navigation on the dynamic benchmark HM3D-DYNA compared to the existing baseline.

</details>


### [114] [A Real-Time Generalized Nash Equilibrium Framework for Interaction-Aware Autonomous Driving in Mixed Traffic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21043)
*Nouhed Naidja,Mohamed-Cherif Rahal,Steve Pechberti,Stéphane Font,Guillaume Sandou,Marc Revilloud*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A real-time, GNEP-based decision framework for AVs in mixed traffic, solved with a PSO-based solver, validated on hardware to produce safe, comfortable, human-like trajectories with convergence under 50 ms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the interdependent nature of AV decisions and human driver reactions in mixed traffic. Traditional decoupled optimization can be unsafe due to ignoring shared safety and geometric constraints; requires a joint, real-time approach that guarantees feasibility.

Method: Formulates driving interactions as a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem with shared safety and geometry constraints. Introduces a dedicated Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) solver to handle the non-convex, real-time requirements. Validated on a real Renault Zoe interacting with a human driver on a test track.

Result: Demonstrates the ability to generate comfortable, human-like trajectories in critical scenarios. The PSO-based solver converges in under 50 ms, showing practical real-time feasibility. Experimental benchmarks corroborate the solver’s performance and the method’s feasibility.

Conclusion: A feasible, real-time framework for joint AV-human interaction planning under shared constraints. The GNEP formulation with a PSO solver yields safe, smooth trajectories and real-time operation, with potential for broader multi-agent extensions and deployment considerations.

Abstract: Safe and efficient navigation in mixed-traffic environments remains a critical challenge for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs), primarily due to the complex interdependence between the AV's decisions and the unpredictable reactions of human drivers. This paper introduces a comprehensive decision-making framework that formulates the driving interaction as a Generalized Nash Equilibrium Problem (GNEP). Unlike decoupled optimization approaches, this framework explicitly models shared safety and geometric constraints, ensuring that the feasibility of the AV's strategy is dynamically linked to the opponent's actions. To solve this non-convex problem in real-time, we propose a dedicated solver based on Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). The complete architecture was validated on a test track using a real autonomous Renault Zoé interacting with a human driver. Experimental results demonstrate the system's ability to handle critical scenarios by generating comfortable, human-like trajectories. Benchmarks confirm the solver's operational feasibility, achieving convergence in under 50 ms.

</details>


### [115] [GuidedAttention: Interpretable and Correctable Visual Attention for OOD-Robust Robot Manipulation via Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21049)
*Masaki Murooka,Ryoichi Nakajo,Keisuke Shirai,Tomohiro Motoda,Hanbit Oh,Ryo Hanai,Yukiyasu Domae*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GuidedAttention introduces interpretable, fixable visual attention as an intermediate representation for visuomotor imitation, using task-relevant attention keypoints to condition a diffusion-based policy; users can inspect/edit keypoints at rollout setup, with a tracking module propagating corrections during execution, yielding improved manipulation especially under pose/appearance OOD.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end visuomotor policies often lack interpretability and robust generalization; providing human-understandable attention and a mechanism to correct it can improve robustness and transparency.

Method: Predicts task-relevant attention keypoints from camera images to condition a diffusion-based action policy; at rollout initialization, users may inspect and correct selected keypoints; a tracking module automatically propagates corrected attention throughout execution.

Result: In both simulation and real-world experiments, GuidedAttention consistently improves robot manipulation performance, with pronounced gains under positional and appearance out-of-distribution conditions.

Conclusion: Interpretable, correctable attention as an intermediate representation improves performance and robustness of visuomotor imitation; human-in-the-loop corrections can be effectively propagated during execution.

Abstract: End-to-end visuomotor policies provide little opportunity for humans to understand or correct the policy's visual attention. We propose GuidedAttention, a visuomotor imitation learning framework that introduces interpretable and correctable visual attention as an explicit intermediate representation. Task-relevant attention keypoints are predicted from camera images and condition a diffusion-based action policy. Users can inspect and optionally correct selected keypoints once at rollout initialization, after which the corrected attention is automatically propagated throughout execution by a tracking module. Experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that GuidedAttention consistently improves robot manipulation performance, particularly under positional and appearance out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions.

</details>


### [116] [Human-Inspired Framework for Robotic Craniotomy: Integrating Multimodal Fusion and Adaptive Trajectory Adjustment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21058)
*Renzhen Le,Xiao Zhang,Di Wu,Yuanyu Wei,Jiachen Zhu,Zhenzhi Ying,Pengfei Zhang,Liming Shu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A human-inspired closed-loop robotic craniotomy framework fuses preoperative planning with intraoperative perception to adapt tool trajectories in real time, achieving high detection accuracy and safe tissue isolation in ex vivo tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual craniotomy is high-risk and fatigue-prone; existing open-loop robotic systems rely on preoperative images and cannot correct intraoperative registration errors or tissue deformation, necessitating real-time sensing and adaptive control.

Method: Adaptive dual-contour fusion algorithm generates trajectories conforming to cranial geometry while maintaining tool-bone pose. Intraoperative perception uses a multimodal CMA-TCN-Transformer network with an adaptive Bayesian filter to fuse force and acoustic signals for robust breakthrough detection. Upon detection, an in-situ projection-based trajectory adjustment compensates depth deviations. Validation on bovine ribs yielded breakthrough prediction accuracy of 97%, latency 0.048 ± 0.097 s, and overshoot 0.29 mm. Four ex vivo cranial experiments completed without dural injury.

Result: Breakthrough prediction accuracy: 97%; detection latency: 0.048 ± 0.097 s; maximum overshoot: 0.29 mm; all four ex vivo cranial experiments completed without dural injury.

Conclusion: The proposed cybernetic closed-loop framework enables safe, autonomous craniotomy with highly effective closed-loop control.

Abstract: Manual craniotomy is a high-risk, skill-dependent procedure associated with surgeon fatigue and potential dural injury. While robotic approaches have improved safety, existing open-loop systems rely solely on preoperative images and cannot compensate for intraoperative registration errors or tissue deformation. To address this, we propose a human-inspired closed-loop robotic craniotomy framework that intelligently integrates preoperative planning with intraoperative execution. An adaptive dual-contour fusion algorithm is employed to generate trajectories that conform to complex cranial geometries while maintaining a consistent tool-bone relative pose. For intraoperative perception, a multimodal two-stage cross-modal attention block (CMA)-temporal convolutional network (TCN)-Transformer network combined with an adaptive Bayesian filter fuses force and acoustic signals to achieve robust breakthrough detection under varying bone conditions. Upon detection, an in-situ projection-based trajectory adjustment strategy dynamically compensates for depth deviations, enabling safe residual bone isolation. Experiments on bovine ribs show a breakthrough prediction accuracy of 97%, a detection latency of 0.048 +/- 0.097 s, and a maximum overshoot of 0.29 mm. All four ex vivo cranial experiments were successfully completed without dural injury. These results demonstrate that the proposed cybernetic framework enables safe and autonomous craniotomy with highly effective closed-loop control.

</details>


### [117] [RL-MACRO: A Cybernetic Closed-Loop Intelligence Framework for Multimodal Adaptive Robotic Craniotomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21113)
*Xiao Zhang,Jiaxuan Li,Renzhen Le,Di Wu,Chao Sun,Jiachen Zhu,Haoyuan Zhang,Xiang Li,Jian Liu,Zhenzhi Ying,Pengfei Zhang,Liming Shu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A data-driven cybernetic framework (RL-MACRO) for autonomous bone cutting that reconstructs hidden temperature via CNN-LSTM, uses offline IQL policy with a dual-head actor to coordinate cutting parameters, and executes via online trajectory planning; validated ex vivo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address partial observability in robotic craniotomy, particularly unknown tissue properties and inaccessible cutting temperatures, enabling safe and efficient autonomous operation.

Method: Multimodal perception: CNN-LSTM observer fuses force and sound to reconstruct temperature; offline IQL policy uses belief state; dual-head Actor coordinates feed rate, spindle speed, cutting depth; online trajectory re-planning and velocity servoing; experiments on bovine ribs and ex vivo goat skulls.

Result: Reconstruction accuracy: R^2=0.939, MAE=1.717°C; robust perception and adaptive recovery from excursions; smooth execution on irregular surfaces; validated on six ex vivo goat skulls and bovine ribs.

Conclusion: Introduces a data-driven cybernetic paradigm for safe, efficient autonomous bone cutting, demonstrating end-to-end perception, decision-making, and execution under partial observability.

Abstract: Autonomous robotic craniotomy requires continuous regulation of tool-tissue interactions to mitigate mechanical overload and thermal damage while maintaining surgical efficiency. However, this process is inherently partially observable due to unknown, time-varying tissue properties and the inability to directly measure cutting temperatures under physical occlusion. To address these challenges, we propose RL-MACRO, a cybernetic closed-loop intelligence framework that couples multimodal perception, adaptive decision-making, and robotic execution. This framework empowers the surgical robot to autonomously perceive inaccessible states from partial sensory feedback and dynamically optimize its behaviors under uncertain environment. A CNN-LSTM observer first fuses force and sound feedback to reconstruct the hidden temperature state (R^2=0.939, MAE = 1.717 deg C). This reconstructed temperature, alongside multi-sensor features, forms the belief state for an offline Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) policy. A novel dual-head Actor dynamically coordinates the feed rate, spindle speed, and cutting depth to optimize efficiency within strict safety bounds. These decisions are seamlessly translated into spatial motions via online trajectory re-planning and velocity servoing. Experiments on bovine ribs and six ex vivo goat skulls validate the system's robust perception, adaptive recovery from force/temperature excursions, and smooth execution on irregular surfaces, establishing a data-driven cybernetic paradigm for safe and efficient autonomous bone cutting.

</details>


### [118] [FORGE-plus: Force-Budgeted Recovery for Contact-Rich Assembly with a Frozen LLM Supervisor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21227)
*Kyupaeck Jeff Rah,Midum Oh*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A two-layer framework uses a frozen text-only LLM to assign per-object force ceilings and select recovery maneuvers for force-constrained reinforcement learning, with a low-level controller enforcing ceilings. Evaluation shows a single policy achieves perfect evaluation on fragile and robust objects in simulation, with meaningful force metrics and partial recovery under slip; PPO fails under strict force constraints. No sim-to-real claim; a fixed recovery menu and known break thresholds play key roles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the practical challenge of selecting appropriate force limits for force-constrained RL in tight-clearance assembly, and enable robust recovery from insertion failures without exceeding a safe force ceiling.

Method: A frozen text-only LLM assigns a per-object force ceiling before execution and chooses recovery maneuvers from a fixed textual force-signature menu; a low-level controller enforces the ceiling and a separate evaluator knows the break threshold. Evaluation uses two grippers on fragile bottle placement and 0.4 mm gear insertion in rigid-body simulation with hidden break thresholds.

Result: Policy passes 256/256 episodes on both fragile and robust objects without breakage, predicts release timing, and completes a table-pick-and-insert with mean peak force 5.4 N. Under in-grip slip, the recovery strategy resolves 40% (two-gripper) and 64%; baseline fits (press-harder) are ineffective or cause breakage. PPO fails under strict force constraints; learned release strategies fail. No sim-to-real claim; experiments confined to simulation with hidden threshold breakage.

Conclusion: The proposed LLM-assisted, two-layer framework demonstrates strong policy performance in simulation under force ceilings and offers a recovery mechanism, but its evaluation is limited to rigid-body sim with masked thresholds and lacks real-world validation; design enforces safety via ceilings and fixed recovery, yet generalization, real-world transfer, and dynamic release strategies remain open questions.

Abstract: Force-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) enables tight-clearance assembly under a commanded force ceiling, but practical deployment requires determining an appropriate force limit for each object and recovering from insertion failures without exceeding it. We present a two-layer framework in which a frozen, text-only large language model (LLM) assigns a per-object force ceiling before execution and selects recovery maneuvers from a fixed action menu using compact textual force signatures. The LLM never controls force directly: a low-level controller enforces the force ceiling, the recovery policy cannot increase it, and the hidden breaking-force threshold is known only to the evaluator.
  We evaluate the framework on fragile bottle placement and 0.4 mm diametral-clearance gear insertion using two grippers (Robotiq 2F-140 and Franka Panda hand). A single policy passes 256/256 evaluation episodes on both fragile and robust objects without breakage, correctly predicts release timing, and completes a full table-pick-and-insert pipeline with a mean peak force of 5.4 N. Under injected in-grip slip, the force-signature recovery strategy resolves 40% and 64% of failures on the two grippers, whereas a press-harder baseline is either ineffective or causes frequent breakage. We also report negative results, including the failure of PPO to solve the task under strict force constraints and unsuccessful learned release strategies. All experiments are conducted in rigid-body simulation with hidden force-threshold breakage; no sim-to-real claim is made.

</details>


### [119] [Factorized Spatio-Temporal Convolutions for Human Pose Estimation from Planar Lidar](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21309)
*Simone Arreghini,Mirko Nava,Nicholas Carlotti,Antonio Paolillo,Alessandro Giusti*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A lightweight 360° LiDAR-based framework for localizing nearby humans and estimating facing direction on service robots, using Space-Time Blocks and cross-modal self-supervision, achieving real-time CPU performance with notable error reductions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable robust human sensing and facing-direction estimation for service robots equipped only with omnidirectional planar LiDARs and modest processors, addressing the gap where pipelines rely on cameras/3D LiDAR or GPU compute.

Method: A lightweight network based on Space-Time Blocks that decouples spatial processing along scan rays from temporal aggregation across scans. Processes 360° LiDAR sequences to output per-ray human presence, distance, and relative orientation. Trained with cross-modal self-supervision from a narrow RGB-D body tracker in the sensor overlap region to avoid manual LiDAR labeling.

Result: Outperforms a parameter-matched baseline by reducing distance error by 38%, position error by 28%, and orientation error by 15%. Demonstrates real-time CPU inference on a service robot and provides Benchmarks on the FROG dataset with in-field demonstrations.

Conclusion: Shows viability of spatial perception for computation-constrained service robots; the Space-Time Block-based approach offers accurate 2D pose and direction estimation from omnidirectional LiDAR with efficient inference.

Abstract: Localizing nearby humans and estimating their facing direction are key capabilities for safe navigation and socially aware human-robot interaction. Many pose-estimation pipelines target cameras and 3D LiDAR or assume GPU-class compute, whereas service robots are often equipped only with omnidirectional planar LiDARs and modest onboard processors. We address omnidirectional human detection and relative 2D pose estimation from planar LiDAR sequences with a lightweight network based on Space-Time Blocks, which explicitly separate spatial processing along scan rays from temporal aggregation across scans. Our network processes 360° LiDAR sequences to output per-ray human presence, distance, and relative orientation. We train it via cross-modal self-supervision from a narrow RGB-D body tracker in the sensors' overlap region, removing the need for manual LiDAR labels. Quantitative experiments show that our approach consistently outperforms a parameter-matched baseline model, reducing errors in distance (-38%), position (-28%), and orientation (-15%). We further benchmark on the public FROG dataset, report real-time CPU inference on a service robot, and validate with in-field demonstrations, supporting its suitability for spatial perception on computationally constrained service robots.

</details>


### [120] [Grasp, Handover, Rotate: Bimanual Object Reorientation via Compositional Diffusion and Energy-Based Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21341)
*Wun Lam Yeung,Wenjun Liu,Yui Cheung Yu,Zhengyan Lambo Qin,Qijin She,Heng Li,Ziqi Wang,Ping Tan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: BiCompoDiff is a diffusion-and-energy-based framework that jointly optimizes grasping, handover, regrasp, and motion planning for bimanual object reorientation, using gradient guidance and annealed MCMC to satisfy collision, smoothness, handover-feasibility, and safety constraints; achieves higher success and smoother trajectories with sim-to-real validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bimanual object reorientation is valuable when direct placement from the initial grasp is infeasible due to collisions, kinematic constraints, or suboptimal final orientation, and multiple objectives must be balanced.

Method: A compositional framework combining a pretrained grasp diffusion model with bimanual planning energy-based models (EBMs). Gradient guidance is injected during reverse diffusion to enforce collision avoidance, trajectory smoothness via differentiable inverse kinematics, handover feasibility, and regrasp safety. Annealed MCMC sampling refines grasp poses on the energy landscape.

Result: In simulated household tasks, BiCompoDiff achieves >20% higher success rates and up to 37% smoother trajectories (joint displacement) than strong sampling baselines; real-world experiments demonstrate effective sim-to-real transfer and robustness in challenging scenes.

Conclusion: BiCompoDiff effectively enables robust, multi-objective bimanual reorientation by integrating diffusion-based grasp priors with energy-based planning, offering improved success and smoother motions with demonstrated sim-to-real transfer.

Abstract: Bimanual object reorientation - picking an object, handing it over between two arms, and placing it in a desired target pose - is valuable when direct placement from the initial grasp is infeasible due to collisions, kinematic constraints, or poor final orientation. However, achieving this under multiple competing objectives remains challenging. We introduce BiCompoDiff, a compositional diffusion and energy-based framework that jointly optimizes grasp selection, handover, regrasp, and motion planning under multiple constraints. By combining a pretrained grasp diffusion model with bimanual planning energy-based models (EBMs), our method injects gradient guidance during reverse diffusion to enforce collision avoidance, trajectory smoothness (via differentiable inverse kinematics), handover feasibility, and regrasp safety. Annealed MCMC sampling further refines grasp poses over the composite energy landscape. Experiments across diverse simulated household reorientation tasks demonstrate that BiCompoDiff achieves over 20% higher success rates and up to 37% smoother trajectories (measured by joint displacement) compared to strong sampling-based baselines. Real-world validation confirms effective sim-to-real transfer and robust performance on challenging scenes.

</details>


### [121] [VoLN: Vision-Only Long-Horizon Navigation---Paradigm, Benchmark, and Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21400)
*Jiabin Lou,Haopeng Wang,Yuanshuai Wang,Xinyu Liu,Xuxin Lv,Yuxin Guo,Lei Huang,Rongye Shi,Wenjun Wu*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: VoLN reframes Vision-Only Long-Horizon Navigation for UAVs by removing external route priors, relying on in-scene cues to reach a goal view. It introduces VoLN-UAV (7,210 episodes) and VoLN-MLLM baseline; initial results on unseen splits are low, highlighting challenges in long-horizon integration and stability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To align evaluating embodied navigation with deployment realities where route priors (orientation, distance, layout) are unavailable. By relying on locally observable cues, VoLN assesses true perception-action capabilities over long horizons in GPS-denied, 3D flight.

Method: Define VoLN framework with destination specified by goal views; use locally observable cues for route information; instantiate in UAV domain as VoLN-UAV (7,210 episodes) with long-horizon flight, continuous 3D motion, large viewpoint changes, beacon selection. Propose VoLN-MLLM baseline that aligns self-supervised visual features to a semantic space and predicts short-horizon waypoint segments from observation history, goal views, tokens, and proprioception.

Result: VoLN-MLLM achieves 7.4% Easy, 4.5% Normal, 1.8% Hard success on five-environment Test-Unseen split, indicating a promising but underperforming baseline; results expose substantial challenges in aggregating long-horizon evidence, cross-view alignment, and closed-loop stability.

Conclusion: VoLN offers a complementary, vision-centric paradigm for long-horizon navigation without external task priors. The initial results reveal considerable room for improvement in perception-to-action integration, cross-view goal matching, and stable long-horizon planning, warranting future research into stronger baselines, better representations, and scalable benchmarking.

Abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) enables embodied agents to follow natural-language instructions. However, route-level instructions commonly encode spatial priors, such as orientation, distance, and layout, that are not explicitly available from onboard sensing at deployment in open, GPS-denied environments. Benchmark performance under such interfaces therefore jointly reflects visual navigation ability and the use of route structure explicitly supplied by the task description. As a complementary formulation, we propose Vision-Only Long-Horizon Navigation (VoLN), which shifts route-relevant information from externally supplied instructions and global guidance to locally observable in-scene cues. In VoLN, goal views specify the destination, while route-relevant information is available only through locally observable in-scene cues that the agent must detect, interpret, and select online. We instantiate VoLN for aerial navigation through VoLN-UAV, a 7,210-episode benchmark that combines long-horizon goal-directed flight, continuous 3D motion, large viewpoint changes, and context-dependent beacon selection. We further provide VoLN-MLLM as an initial reference baseline. It aligns self-supervised visual features with a structured semantic space and predicts short-horizon waypoint segments from observation history, goal views, retrieved visual--semantic tokens, and proprioception. On the five-environment Test-Unseen split, it obtains success rates of 7.4%, 4.5%, and 1.8% on Easy, Normal, and Hard episodes, respectively. These results provide an initial evaluation of VoLN and reveal substantial remaining challenges in long-horizon evidence integration, cross-view goal matching, and closed-loop stability. Project page: https://admire-ljb.github.io/VoLN-UAV/

</details>


### [122] [GLAM-SLAM: Real-time Gaussian Large-scale Mapping via Flow Densification and Spatial Decomposition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21416)
*Panagiotis Mermigkas,Argyris Manetas,Petros Maragos*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Real-time, scalable Gaussian-splatting SLAM for long-horizon outdoor sequences using a decoupled frontend, sparse anchor-grid mapping, epipolar-based flow densification, and multi-scene MLP-initialized Gaussians; reports ~15% QoR gain on KITTI/Oxford/Málaga with real-time performance and long-sequence scalability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing monocular Gaussian-splatting SLAM methods struggle in real-time and long-horizon outdoor scenarios due to memory and speed constraints; there is a need for scalable, efficient, real-time SLAM leveraging Gaussian splatting.

Method: Frontend: lightweight, robust feature-based SLAM for tracking. Mapping: structured, sparse anchor-grid representation for scalable operation and coherence over long sequences. Dense initialization for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) via geometry-based flow-densification anchoring using epipolar constraints. Multi-scene mapping treated as a partitioned problem; scene-specific Gaussians initialized by MLPs to provide strong spatial priors for localized Gaussian generation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on KITTI Odometry, Oxford RobotCar, and M\'alaga datasets shows ~15% improvement in reconstruction quality over the second-best method, while preserving real-time performance and enabling longer-sequence scalability. Code released.

Conclusion: GLAM-SLAM demonstrates that decoupled frontend/mapping, a sparse anchor-grid, geometry-informed flow-densification, and multi-scene priors enable real-time, scalable Gaussian-splatting SLAM for large outdoor environments, with competitive reconstruction quality.

Abstract: Existing Gaussian-splatting-based monocular Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems are either tailored to short sequences, are not real-time, or suffer from prohibitive GPU memory requirements, limiting their applicability in realistic, long-horizon scenarios. To address this, we present GLAM-SLAM, a real-time, decoupled Gaussian-splatting SLAM system designed for large-scale outdoor scenes. We ensure lightweight tracking using a robust, feature-based SLAM frontend, while for mapping, we adopt a structured, sparse anchor grid representation that ensures scalable operation and maintains scene coherence across long-term sequences. To satisfy the dense initialization requirements of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), we introduce a geometry-based flow-densification anchoring strategy using epipolar constraints. Furthermore, by treating mapping as a multi-scene problem, we propose a scene-partitioning strategy that introduces a strong spatial inductive bias via MLP initializations to generate localized Gaussians. We evaluate our system on the challenging, long-sequence KITTI Odometry, Oxford RobotCar, and M'alaga datasets. Extensive ablations and comparisons demonstrate a 15% improvement in reconstruction quality over the second-best performer, while maintaining real-time performance and the ability to scale to longer sequences. Code is publicly available for the benefit of the community.

</details>


### [123] [GS-Agent: Creating 4D Physical Worlds With Generative Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21522)
*Hongxin Zhang,Chunru Lin,Junyan Li,Zhou Xian,Tsun-Hsuan Wang,Chuang Gan*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: GS-Agent is an end-to-end multi-agent system that generates controllable, physically plausible 4D worlds from natural language by integrating physics engines and decomposing tasks (asset curation, materials, placement, motion, rendering) among specialized agents who iteratively refine the scene with multimodal feedback.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce manual, labor-intensive creation of 4D worlds and to improve physical plausibility and controllability beyond what existing generative models offer.

Method: An agentic framework where multiple specialized agents interact with a physics engine via code, manage 3D assets, materials, placement and motion, and configure rendering (camera/lighting). They seek multimodal feedback and collaborate to iteratively construct scenes aligned with NL descriptions. The physics loop ensures realism.

Result: GS-Agent can produce diverse, physically plausible 4D worlds featuring interactions among liquids, deformables, and rigid bodies, with cinematic camera and lighting control.

Conclusion: GS-Agent represents a new paradigm for 4D world generation—an automated, agent-driven pipeline that integrates physics in the loop and enables scalable, controllable creative content and physical AI.

Abstract: Creating dynamic and physically realistic 4D worlds from natural language descriptions is both fascinating and challenging. Traditional computer graphics methods rely on manual creation, requiring extensive human effort to fine-tune materials, motions, and visual fidelity. Recent advances in generative foundation models have sparked interest in learning to generate such 4D worlds from large-scale data; however, existing methods still struggle to ensure physical plausibility and controllability. In this work, we take a different path by leveraging foundation models to construct an agentic system that emulates how humans traditionally create 4D worlds, yet automates the entire process. We present GS-Agent, an end-to-end multi-agent framework that integrates physics engines in the loop to generate realistic, dynamic, and controllable 4D physical worlds from natural language. Inspired by how humans build 4D worlds, GS-Agent decomposes the task into entity management, covering 3D asset curation, material tuning, placement, and motion control, and rendering configuration, including camera and lighting manipulation. Multiple agents with distinct expertise interact with the physics engine via code, seek multimodal feedback, and collaborate to iteratively construct 4D worlds that align with the given descriptions. Experimental results show that GS-Agent effectively converts natural language into diverse and physically plausible 4D worlds exhibiting rich interactions among liquids, deformable objects, and rigid bodies, while achieving cinematic camera and lighting control. We envision GS-Agent as a foundation for a new paradigm in 4D world generation, empowering creative content creation and physical AI. Project page at https://umass-embodied-agi.github.io/gs-agent/

</details>


### [124] [Beyond Episodic Evaluation: Memory Architectural Bottlenecks in Sequential Embodied Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21571)
*Zikui Cai,Kaushal Janga,Tan Dat Dao,Seungjae Lee,Shivin Dass,Mingyo Seo,Kaiyu Yue,Mintong Kang,Nandhu Pillai,Monte Hoover,Aadi Palnitkar,Ruchit Rawal,Ruijie Zheng,Bo Li,Yuke Zhu,Roberto Martín-Martín,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: Spatially grounded visual memory mapping to 3D geometry is necessary for effective sequential EQA; naive memory or short-horizon episodic training fail to retain visual-semantic evidence or reuse it across questions, harming performance. Structured, metric 3D memory improves accuracy and reduces navigation cost in both simulated and real robots.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EQA has typically been evaluated episodically, but real-world robots operate continuously and must accumulate, retain, and reuse prior information. There is a gap in understanding how memory architectures support sequential reasoning in EQA.

Method: Systematic evaluation of memory architectures for sequential EQA: compare 2D occupancy-map memory (traversability only) with spatially grounded 3D geometry memory. Test agents trained on episodic data and on continuous histories across multiple questions in the same scene. Evaluate in simulated environments and on a real mobile robot, measuring answer accuracy and navigation cost.

Result: 2D/traversability-only memory preserves explored areas but loses visual-semantic evidence; agents trained on short-horizon episodic data exhibit temporal mismatch when faced with continuous histories. In contrast, spatially grounded memory mapping persistent visual observations to metric 3D geometry preserves semantic evidence, yielding higher accuracy and lower navigation costs, breaking the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff.

Conclusion: Structured, spatially grounded visual memory is essential for continuous, intelligent operation in physical environments and improves EQA performance in both simulation and real-world robotics.

Abstract: Embodied question answering (EQA) is traditionally evaluated under an episodic formulation, where agents solve each task independently and reset internal state between episodes. However, real-world robots operate continuously and must accumulate, retain, and selectively reuse information acquired from prior interactions. Despite this practical requirement, the architectural mechanisms needed to support sequential memory in EQA remain underexplored. In this work, we investigate how different memory architectures behave when EQA agents are evaluated sequentially, with multiple questions answered in the same scene while memory is carried forward across queries. We find that simply preserving existing memory is often insufficient. Agents that retain only traversability information, such as 2D occupancy maps, remember where the robot has explored but not the visual-semantic evidence needed for later questions. Agents trained on short-horizon episodic data face a different challenge: when exposed to continuous, multi-query histories, their inherited context suffers from severe temporal mismatch, rather than forming a reusable scene representation. To overcome this architectural bottleneck, we highlight the necessity of structured, spatially grounded memory: architectures that map persistent visual observations onto metric 3D geometry preserve visual-semantic evidence in a coherent scene representation. Extensive experiments in simulated environments reveal that this form of memory breaks the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in sequential settings, simultaneously achieving higher answer accuracy and lower navigation costs. We further validate these findings on a real-world mobile robot, demonstrating that spatially grounded visual memory is critical for enabling continuous, intelligent operation in physical environments.

</details>


### [125] [Scale Up Strategically: Learning Compositional Generalization via Bias-Aware Evaluation and Data Collection for Robotic Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21582)
*Yu Qi,Zhang Ye,Xinyi Xu,Yuxuan Lu,Amitoj Sandhu,Boce Hu,Haojie Huang,Jonathan Tremblay,Lawson L. S. Wong*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A diagnostic framework identifies and quantifies instruction-factor biases in language-conditioned policies to diagnose compositional generalization failures; introduces Factor Dominance Rate (FDR) and Factor Dominance Hierarchy (FDH); shows a consistent factor ordering (color ≥ object ≥ spatial ≥ verb ≥ size) with color most dominant and verb/size most under-grounded; demonstrates a bias-aware data collection strategy that reallocates a fixed budget toward under-grounded factors, achieving better sample efficiency in simulation and on a real robot with half the demonstrations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretrained, language-conditioned policies often shortcut by exploiting salient cues rather than grounding language, leading to poor compositional generalization. There is a need to diagnose errors at the level of instruction factors (e.g., color, verb, object, size, spatial attribute) and to translate that diagnosis into actionable improvements in data collection and training.

Method: Define instruction factors as reusable semantic components. Formalize instruction factor bias as a tendency to over-rely on dominant factors. Propose two metrics: Factor Dominance Rate (FDR) to capture pairwise factor bias, and Factor Dominance Hierarchy (FDH) to aggregate pairwise biases into a global ranking. Evaluate across six foundation policies to derive a factor ordering. Propose a bias-aware data collection strategy that allocates a fixed labeling or demonstration budget toward under-grounded factors to improve learning.

Result: Across six foundation policies, the framework yields a broadly consistent factor ordering: color ≥ object ≥ spatial ≥ verb ≥ size, with color most dominant and verb and size most under-grounded. The diagnosis enables a bias-aware data collection approach that outperforms baselines, achieving more sample-efficient policy learning and improved generalization. This strategy is validated in both simulation and on a real robot using half the demonstrations.

Conclusion: The proposed diagnostic framework provides actionable insight into how instruction factors bias language-grounded policies and offers a practical data-acquisition strategy to mitigate reliance on shortcuts. By quantifying factor bias with FDR and FDH and reallocating data collection toward under-grounded factors, policies become more robustly grounded and sample-efficient, with demonstrated gains in both simulated and real-robot settings.

Abstract: Compositional generalization is essential for robot to follow diverse instructions. However, pretrained policies are known to take shortcuts, deferring to salient cues rather than grounding language. We introduce a diagnostic framework that localizes this failure to individual \textit{instruction factors}, \textit{e.g.,} reusable semantic components such as color, verb, object, size, and spatial attribute. Our framework formalizes instruction factor bias, the tendency of fine-tuned policies to over-rely on dominant factors as shortcuts, and quantifies it through two metrics: Factor Dominance Rate (FDR), capturing pairwise bias between factors, and Factor Dominance Hierarchy (FDH), aggregating these into a global ranking. Evaluation on six foundation policies reveals broadly consistent ordering, \textit{i.e.}, color $\geq$ object $\geq$ spatial $\geq$ verb $\geq$ size, with color dominant, and verb and size most under-grounded. We further show the diagnosis is actionable: a bias-aware data collection strategy that reallocates a fixed budget toward under-grounded factors outperforms baselines in simulation and on a real robot using half the demonstrations, thereby enabling more sample-efficient and generalizable policy learning.

</details>


### [126] [AXIS: A Growable Community-Driven Data Engine for Scalable Robot Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21588)
*Mengfei Zhao,Dihong Huang,Yikai Tang,Peihao Li,Mingxuan Yan,Ruiqi Zhuang,Yanjia Huang,Jie Wang,Hai Zhai,Tony Zhou,Rui Zhang,Zhexi Luo,Yuchen Huang,Jianfei Yang,Jiachen Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: AXIS is a browser-based, scalable data engine and benchmark for robot manipulation that collects diverse demonstrations at scale and provides automated data curation and evaluation; results show strong scaling and improved continual pretraining against RoboCasa365.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome data collection bottlenecks in robot learning due to specialized hardware, centralized operators, and fixed task suites; need scalable, quality, diverse demonstrations and automatic validation.

Method: Browser-based teleoperation for demonstrations; automatic generation/validation of tasks; automated success checking, quality filtering, trajectory smoothing; visual and physics-based augmentation; data organized into task snapshots; unified evaluation suite; continual pretraining experiments; comparison against RoboCasa365; perturbation tests.

Result: AXIS includes 207 tasks and 50k+ trajectories; continual pretraining on AXIS improves pi_0.5 by 5.8%; outperforms RoboCasa365 by 37.3%; data-volume scaling shows consistent gains, largest under layout, sensor-noise, camera perturbations.

Conclusion: AXIS enables scalable data collection and robust evaluation for scalable robot learning; supports continual pretraining benefits and resilience to perturbations; sets a foundation for large-scale, community-driven benchmarks.

Abstract: Learning effective robot manipulation policies requires diverse, high-quality demonstrations, yet existing data pipelines are often difficult to scale because they rely on specialized hardware, centralized operators, or fixed task suites. We present AXIS, a growable community-driven data engine and benchmark for scalable robot learning, which enables browser-based teleoperation for large-scale demonstration collection, automatically generates and validates new manipulation tasks, and transforms community-collected demonstrations into training-ready data through automated success checking, quality filtering, trajectory smoothing, and visual and physics-based augmentation.
