The AXIS dataset currently contains 207 diverse tasks and 50K+ trajectories. Meanwhile, AXIS organizes data into task snapshots and evaluates policies with a systematic held-out protocol. We compare vision-language-action (VLA) policies under a unified AXIS evaluation suite and analyze scaling behavior across different data volumes. Continual pretraining on AXIS substantially improves the overall success rate of $π_{0.5}$ by 5.8%, outperforms the model pretrained on RoboCasa365 by 37.3%, and exhibits consistent scaling with increasing data volume, with the largest gains observed under layout, sensor-noise, and camera perturbations.

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [127] [DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20465)
*Hao Liang,Qifeng Cai,Yibo Lin,Jianzhuo Du,Qifeng Xia,Sizhe Qiu,Linzhuang Sun,Meiyi Qiang,Zhaoyang Han,Xiaochen Ma,Bohan Zeng,Ruichuan An,Conghui He,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DataPrep-Bench is a unified benchmark for end-to-end LLM-driven data preparation, jointly evaluating data construction and data quality evaluation across six domains; introduces Data-Construction-Skill and the DAS metric, achieving strong gains and correlations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is no unified, downstream-grounded benchmark to assess how well LLM-driven data preparation improves downstream training, combining both data construction and quality evaluation.

Method: A two-track benchmark: (1) data construction, where raw sources are transformed into supervised data and evaluated by fine-tuning base models (with Dolly-15k); includes Data-Construction-Skill agent that improves Dolly baselines. (2) data quality evaluation, where scoring functions are correlated with downstream performance using a shared candidate pool; introduces DAS, a distribution-based measure using MMD against a domain proxy, evaluated across six domains and multiple base models.

Result: Data-Construction-Skill yields ~20 absolute points improvement over Dolly baseline on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and competes with top agent/DataFlow methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. DAS achieves strongest cross-model correlation in 4/6 domains and r>0.70 in Math, Science, Medical, outperforming existing evaluators.

Conclusion: DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework that treats data construction and data quality evaluation as co-equal targets for progress in LLM-driven data preparation.

Abstract: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

</details>


### [128] [PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20492)
*Rana Muhammad Usman*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LMs fabricate when constrained by required schema fields; a new benchmark (PhantomFill) reveals high coercion of fabrication across models under format pressure, with 2 metrics (Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate); a one-line schema fix reduces it; the problem is pervasive and not solved by scaling alone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how output formats and schema constraints in production-like prompts trigger hallucinations, and to quantify the limits of honesty under format pressure across model sizes and families.

Method: Ask 13 models the same question about the same input, altering only the answer format. Use inputs that cannot be answered truthfully (e.g., a viral post with no visible replies; an untranscribed support ticket). Compare free-text responses to mandated JSON fields or enums. Evaluate explicit guidance (e.g., 'insufficient evidence') and direct instructions (e.g., 'do not infer sentiment'). Analyze across model sizes, including open-weight vs closed-weight families. Develop PhantomFill benchmark with deterministic scoring and report two metrics: Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate. Test a one-line schema fix and report failure modes across fields like required enums and minimum-count arrays.

Result: Fabrication is driven by required fields: 10 of 13 models show 100% coercion in the presence of mandatory fields. In many cases, when sentiment must be provided via schema, models fabricates or quotes data they did not observe. Scale does not solve the issue: small models may refuse, mid-sized models fabricate, larger models again reject; nine open-weight models ignore explicit refusals to infer sentiment. An explicit 'insufficient evidence' option only saves the frontier models, with nine open-weight models failing to respect it. Four of six models override explicit directives not to infer sentiment due to schema pressure. The PhantomFill benchmark provides deterministic scoring and two reportable metrics to reveal these failure modes, and a one-line schema fix reduces the observed fabrication.

Conclusion: Systematic format pressure causes hallucination that persists across model sizes and families. A minimal schema-level fix can mitigate but cannot be trusted to eliminate fabrication. PhantomFill offers a reproducible, metric-driven approach to quantify and diagnose honesty under format constraints and to drive safer schema-aware design in production deployments.

Abstract: Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

</details>


### [129] [The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20512)
*Yufeng Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Orthogonalization (via Newton-Schulz) is the primary driver of Muon's faster grokking; spectral-norm constraints alone do not improve speed and are unstable. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations speeds up convergence but harms stability; five iterations strike a robust balance. Spectral scaling can be dropped without cost. The work emphasizes reporting both first-crossing and sustained grok times under a stability-aware metric and provides reproducible code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle which components of the Muon optimizer (orthogonalized momentum vs spectral-norm constraints) drive faster grokking performance, and to quantify robustness across learning rates and seeds.

Method: Perform multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps; conduct ablation by separating orthogonalization and spectral constraints; mechanistic analysis of spectral-norm behavior; vary Newton-Schulz iteration count (from five to one); evaluate stability across learning rates; assess whether spectral scaling is essential; report both first-crossing and sustained grok times; release full training/analysis code for reproducibility.

Result: Ablation shows orthogonalize-only matches full Muon (speedup stems from orthogonalization); spectral-only comparable to AdamW and unstable. Mechanistic analysis indicates orthogonalized optimizers reach a ~3x lower spectral norm; maintaining controlled embedding movement yields a lower-norm solution rather than simply less movement. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations accelerates threshold attainment but increases fragility, especially at higher learning rates; canonical five iterations are robust across LR. Spectral scaling can be dropped with no measured cost.

Conclusion: Orthogonalization is the dominant mechanism behind Muon's grokking speed; spectral-norm constraints contribute little on their own and may introduce instability. The iteration count for Newton-Schulz trades speed for stability, with five iterations providing a robust default. Stability-aware metrics are essential when evaluating grokking optimizers, and reproducibility is supported by releasing code.

Abstract: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

</details>


### [130] [Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20516)
*Tolgay Atinc Uzun,Radu Timofte,Dmitry Ignatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Denser sampling in closed-loop LLM-guided channel-configuration search improves efficiency and reveals architectural regularities: better frontier performance at lower parameter counts, with non-power-of-two channel widths and structured allocations becoming common.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether the channel-search signal observed in sparse evaluations transfers to a denser sampling regime and uncover additional architectural regularities when more networks are generated and evaluated.

Method: Scale the search to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle, total of 2000 generated candidates across 8 cycles, with 462 CIFAR-100 evaluations after task/metadata filtering. Analyze per-cycle mean accuracy trends, frontier performance, parameter counts, and channel-width patterns (including non-power-of-two widths) to identify regularities.

Result: Per-cycle mean accuracy shows a positive linear trend (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043). Frontier best accuracy rises from 0.3144 to 0.3676. Top-5/Top-10 cycle means also improve. Best model achieves 0.3676 with 11.8M params vs an early high-performer at 0.3144 with 166.5M params. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates. Strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns with moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks.

Conclusion: Scaling the search confirms that the channel-search signal transfers to a denser sampling regime, yielding improved efficiency and revealing architectural regularities (e.g., non-power-of-two widths, structured allocation patterns). These results support further exploration of LLM-guided NAS with denser evaluations to refine design heuristics and potentially reduce parameter counts while maintaining or improving accuracy.

Abstract: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

</details>


### [131] [Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20517)
*Takato Yasuno*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A four-axis multimodal fusion approach (text, keywords, knowledge-graph triples, and images) enables robust retrieval over heterogeneous PDFs, using a coarse-to-fine retriever and triple-filtered indexing to support rapid multi-hop reasoning with strong empirical gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RAG over heterogeneous, multimodal documents is hampered by modality gaps, specialized terminology, and the need to reason across dispersed evidence. The work aims to improve retrieval quality and multi-hop reasoning by integrating multiple evidence axes and structured indexing.

Method: Construct a multimodal index of document blocks (2,403 blocks from 43 disaster PDFs) using dense text embeddings, BM25, image similarity, and knowledge-graph triples. Extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS for fast triple lookup. Use a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-generated captions to support multimodal content. Implement a HippoRAG2-like coarse-to-fine retriever (volume→chapter→block) to prune the search space, and perform Bayesian optimization to learn fusion weights, with triple axis dominating (α_triple=0.44). Evaluate on a 457-pair benchmark, reporting Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. Demonstrate image-to-lesson retrieval via a vision-LMM pipeline.

Result: The system achieves near-perfect retrieval recall on a specialized, multimodal corpus and shows substantial gains in multi-hop reasoning over single-hop baselines. The triple filtration axis dominates fusion weight, indicating the value of structured knowledge graphs in reducing lexical bias and guiding cross-modal evidence aggregation. The coarse-to-fine retrieval significantly narrows the search space, enabling sub-second triple lookup and scalable fusion scoring.

Conclusion: Triple-filtered, multimodal fusion is essential for robust, structured reasoning over noisy PDFs and offers a general framework extendable beyond the disaster domain, including visual inputs via image-to-lesson retrieval.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

</details>


### [132] [Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20519)
*Andrei Cristian Popescu,Haitz Sáez de Ocáriz Borde,Pietro Liò*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adaptive depth in looped Transformers is better understood as a joint trajectory-readout problem, not just gate learning; using fixed-prior depth supervision and simple post-hoc readouts can outperform learned gates, with practical latency gains driven by shorter trajectories.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle the interplay between trajectory formation and exit readout in adaptive-depth looped Transformers, and to diagnose where adaptive compute failures arise (trajectory vs. readout vs. their interaction).

Method: Empirical diagnostic study across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic, binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. Compare (i) fixed-prior depth supervision, (ii) joint gate training, and (iii) post-hoc confidence readouts; analyze gate behavior when fitted on frozen trajectories; report latency and Pareto performance.

Result: Fixed-prior depth supervision yields difficulty-aware trajectories with useful stopping signals; simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or exceed learned linear/MLP gates; fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes failures to trajectory effects from joint training rather than gate expressivity; pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal; measured latency confirms reductions in average exit depth yield practical inference-time savings.

Conclusion: Adaptive depth in looped Transformers should be treated as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, not gate learning alone; this reframing clarifies failure modes and informs design choices beyond optimizing gate expressivity.

Abstract: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints. We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

</details>


### [133] [Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20521)
*Lei Cao,Sihang Feng,Jixin Yan,Tao Sun,Naichen Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a flexible filtering framework that uses pretrained conditional generative models (CVAE) for observation modeling and score-based sampling for online inference, yielding improved accuracy and robustness over baselines on synthetic data and real-world tasks such as manufacturing monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Classical filters (e.g., Kalman) assume linear-Gaussian observation models, which fail for nonlinear, high-dimensional, and heterogeneous sensor data. A flexible, uncertainty-aware observation model is needed to capture complex patterns and provide reliable state estimates.

Method: Replace restrictive observation models with pretrained CVAEs to define a CVAE-induced likelihood. Perform Bayesian prediction-update recursion where the measurement update becomes a posterior sampling problem. Transform the filtering task into a score-based sampling problem and leverage ensemble-based uncertainty quantification.

Result: GBF achieves higher state estimation accuracy and robustness compared with baselines on both synthetic datasets and real-world applications (manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis).

Conclusion: GBF offers a flexible, uncertainty-aware filtering framework that combines generative modeling with Bayesian inference, improving state estimation in nonlinear, high-dimensional settings and demonstrating practical effectiveness in diverse domains.

Abstract: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

</details>


### [134] [Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20522)
*Larry Richards*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A preregistered study tests whether holonomy concentrates on active SAE feature planes in Gemma 2 2B; the prediction is falsified: active planes show less holonomy than controls, with a negative adjusted log contrast; results do not support a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy; area-law findings are limited to a small validation subset and other confounds (transport distortion) are plausible; the cause remains open and several alternative factors are proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically test the semantic-concentration prediction that meaning or semantic engagement concentrates holonomy on active feature planes within a concretely operationalized neural system (Gemma 2 2B) using preregistered measurements and a locality-aware holonomy metric.

Method: Measure holonomy at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by circulating a local frame around small loops with a restricted-Jacobian transport rule and normalizing by enclosed area. Preregistered design and verdict rules. Compare random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes; use area-normalized holonomy as the metric. Post-freeze diagnostics include validation of the area law on a small subset, regression-based controls, and evaluation of transport distortion as a potential confound.

Result: Prediction falsified: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls (adjusted log contrast = -0.29439; 95% CI [-0.43989, -0.14889]). Magnitude-only explanation not supported; common-support failure rendered three-way ordering undefined at matched magnitude. Area law supported in a small validation subset; transport distortion identified as a live mechanism/confound.

Conclusion: The finding is a narrow, auditable operational reversal rather than a causal claim that semantic meaning suppresses holonomy. The underlying cause remains unresolved, with several plausible alternatives (activation-strength geometry, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, transport shear, etc.) to be explored.

Abstract: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

</details>


### [135] [Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20529)
*Jiawei Zheng,Jiazhen Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Uncertainty-aware aggregation for multi-LLMs using Cooke-style log weighting improves robustness in heterogeneous and contaminated expert panels, by calibrating trust based on probabilistic prediction quality rather than assuming equal reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Naive ensemble methods assume equal trust across all models, which is inappropriate for heterogeneous LLMs with varying calibration and reliability, and particularly vulnerable to unreliable/adversarial experts.

Method: Adapt structured expert judgment. Use context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability through Cooke-style log scoring, which penalizes overconfident incorrect predictions and rewards well-calibrated, informative experts. Evaluate on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels.

Result: In homogeneous settings, aggregation performance is similar across methods; in heterogeneous and contaminated settings, Cooke weighting yields superior accuracy-reliability trade-offs and is robust to unreliable experts, outperforming naive aggregation.

Conclusion: Effective multi-LLM aggregation requires calibration of trust under uncertainty. Cooke-style uncertainty weighting provides robustness to model heterogeneity and contamination, enabling more reliable ensemble predictions.

Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

</details>


### [136] [CLOE: Christoffel Loss Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20530)
*Léa Billet,Louise Travé-Massuyès,Elodie Chanthery,Alexandre Gaffet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CLOE combines autoencoder-based dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function detector in latent space, guided by a Christoffel-based loss, with a simple hyperparameter strategy, yielding strong results on high-dimensional anomaly detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Semi-supervised anomaly detection in high-dimensional data is challenging: lightweight Christoffel methods are attractive due to few hyperparameters but struggle with scalability. A scalable, low-tuning approach that preserves simplicity is needed.

Method: Train an autoencoder to reduce dimensionality, apply a Christoffel Function-based detector in the latent space, and introduce a loss term that uses the Christoffel Function to steer the latent representation toward the normal data's support. Provide a principled thresholding procedure and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter.

Result: Experimentation on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks shows CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods while maintaining the lightweight, low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function-based approaches.

Conclusion: CLOE offers a scalable, efficient semi-supervised anomaly detection framework by marrying representation learning with Christoffel Function-based detection, achieving strong performance with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

Abstract: Semi-supervised anomaly detection plays a key role in diverse fields such as process monitoring, healthcare, and finance. However, lightweight methods often struggle with high-dimensional data and typically require careful tuning of multiple hyperparameters. Among existing approaches, Christoffel Function--based methods are attractive due to their simplicity, requiring at most a single hyperparameter. They also benefit from a well-established theoretical foundation that yields several interesting results for data science. However, their main limitation is poor scalability to high-dimensional settings. In this paper, we introduce CLOE, a new method that combines an autoencoder for dimensionality reduction with a Christoffel Function--based detector applied in the latent space. To better align representation learning with anomaly detection, we design a novel loss function that leverages the Christoffel Function to guide the autoencoder toward representations that better capture the support of the normal data distribution. We further propose a principled procedure to set the detection threshold and an efficient strategy to tune the single remaining hyperparameter. Experiments on multiple high-dimensional tabular anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that CLOE achieves superior performance compared to existing methods, while preserving the lightweight and low-tuning advantages of Christoffel Function--based approaches.

</details>


### [137] [Position: Stop Reactively Patching Your Model Every Time and Start Proactive Test-Driven AI Development](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20532)
*Nadine Chang,Maying Shen,Jialiang Wang,Rafid Mahmood,Jose M. Alvarez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proactive, test-driven maintenance flywheel with a test space mapping feedback to objectives, proven to scale longer-term with fewer iterations than a reactive flywheel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reactive maintenance often ignores broader system objectives and underprepares for long-tail edge cases, leading to inefficiency and limited generalization; a proactive, test-driven approach aims to align feedback with task objectives and improve long-term scalability.

Method: Propose a formal framework: construct a test space that maps feedback data to task objectives; develop a mathematical model comparing reactive vs proactive flywheels; prove that the proactive approach achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations; discuss implications for open-world, diverse use-cases.

Result: A mathematical proof is provided showing that a proactive, test-driven flywheel reduces the required iteration count and improves long-term scalability relative to a reactive flywheel.

Conclusion: Adopting a proactive, test-driven maintenance paradigm enhances generalization and efficiency in deployed AI systems; further empirical validation could fortify the theoretical claims.

Abstract: Many modern AI systems are designed to operate under diverse, open-ended, use-cases. To help generalize deployed systems, many deployed-system maintenance pipelines use a reactive AI flywheel that observes emerging feedback from user behavior (errors) and patches the model accordingly. However, when used as the primary maintenance mechanism, these flywheels often ignore the broader context of these errors within the system's objectives, failing to preempt potential future edge cases, which leads to more unnecessary flywheel iterations. Also, it is statistically increasingly difficult to collect remaining errors due to the long-tail nature of open-world use-cases. This position paper argues that a proactive test-driven flywheel is required to address reactive flywheel's limitations and to approach a generalizable system. We advocate for creating a "test space" to technically map feedback data to task objectives, evolving the flywheel from reactive to proactive. We augment our position by mathematically proving a proactive one achieves better long-term scaling with fewer iterations than the reactive flywheel.

</details>


### [138] [Grounding Investor Views: Neural Predicates in the Black-Litterman Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20533)
*Marcos Florencio*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A data-driven Black-Litterman view-generation framework using a hierarchical set of neural predicates to produce P, q, and Omega from structured financial data, enabling interpretable and fully differentiable portfolio construction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the subjectivity and scalability of eliciting views and uncertainties in Black-Litterman by replacing manual inputs with probabilistic, data-driven predicate outputs.

Method: Process structured financial analysis data through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates that output probability distributions over market stances; map these distributions to the Black-Litterman components P, q, and Omega; derive view confidence from predicate outputs; maintain interpretability by tracing back through predicates; ensure end-to-end differentiability for learning.

Result: Proposes a formal framework and data-driven mechanism for generating Black-Litterman views; claims interpretability (traceability) and differentiability; no empirical results reported in the abstract.

Conclusion: Neural predicate-based view generation offers a scalable, interpretable, and differentiable approach to Black-Litterman that automates uncertainty elicitation and links directly to underlying data.

Abstract: Portfolio construction under the Black-Litterman model requires investors to specify views on asset returns alongside explicit uncertainty estimates -- a process that remains largely subjective and difficult to scale. We propose a formal approach in which neural predicates serve as a structured, probabilistic mechanism for view generation. In our formulation, structured financial analysis data is processed through a compositional hierarchy of neural predicates whose outputs -- probability distributions over market stances -- are mapped to the pick matrix $\mathbf{P}$, the view return vector $\mathbf{q}$, and the view uncertainty matrix $\boldsymbolΩ$ of the Black-Litterman model. View confidence is derived from predicate output distributions, providing a data-driven alternative to subjective uncertainty elicitation. The resulting approach is interpretable, in the sense that any portfolio weight can be traced back through the predicate's logical chain to the underlying data, and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end learning.

</details>


### [139] [A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20535)
*Alicia Tierz,Icíar Alfaro,David González,Elías Cueto*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zero-shot digital twins using a thermodynamics-informed GNN with data assimilation enabling real-time, geometry-agnostic simulations for unseen geometries without retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome rigidity and retraining burden of traditional predictive digital twins by enabling real-time, generalizable physics-informed simulation across varying geometries and boundary conditions.

Method: Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (metriplectic thermodynamics) enforcing energy conservation and non-negative entropy locally via graph message passing; auxiliary GNN infers unobserved fields from sparse boundaries; continuous closed-loop data assimilation with deep segmentation and sparse optical flow to correct autoregressive rollout.

Result: Generalization demonstrated across large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and nonlinear sloshing of a viscous fluid on novel unseen geometries without retraining; real-time latency ~25 ms per frame; latent mechanical variables projected via AR.

Conclusion: Unified framework provides physically accurate, geometry-agnostic simulations in zero-shot regimes with real-time performance, indicating broad applicability and potential impact in real-time engineering and AR contexts.

Abstract: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

</details>


### [140] [ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20537)
*Huei-Chung Hu,Hsin-Tai Wu,Koyo Kobayashi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReliableTableQA presents a data-efficient framework to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA outputs, via a ten-category reliability taxonomy and a CFG-generated 50k-label training set; a small schema-stratified SFT (200 examples) yields near-perfect reliability-flagging and parsing, with GRPO providing little benefit when SFT is adequate. The approach reduces UCAR and generalizes across retail domains, highlighting reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In enterprise analytics, syntactically correct queries can produce statistically meaningless results (due to small samples, wide confidence intervals, or confounding). Current systems often respond confidently despite unreliability, leading to UCAR (Unreliable Confidence Answer Rate). A calibrated reliability annotation framework is needed to distinguish meaningful results from spurious ones.

Method: Propose a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) for tabular QA hazards; build a program-first data pipeline generating 50,000 reliability-labeled examples from a CFG over public retail schemas with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; conduct a controlled study comparing supervised SFT and reinforcement GRPO in reliability annotation, including data-efficiency analysis and cross-domain generalization.

Result: Key findings: with only 200 SFT examples, reliability-flag F1 rises from 0.61 to 0.98; parse rate increases from 0.52 to 1.00; UCAR drops to zero; Rel-F1 on held-out H&M reaches 0.997. GRPO provides only marginal gains when SFT is under-trained (+0.06–0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples) and yields no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate; results hold across hard slices, strict exact-match metrics, and out-of-distribution tests.

Conclusion: Reliability annotation is a data-efficient problem: small, schema-stratified SFT suffices for strong generalization and UCAR elimination; reinforcement fine-tuning (GRPO) is beneficial mainly when SFT is under-trained and offers little benefit once SFT is adequate. The work clarifies when GRPO pays off and demonstrates robust cross-domain applicability.

Abstract: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

</details>


### [141] [Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20538)
*Yitao Jiang,Yaoqing Yang,Luyang Zhao,Muhao Chen,Devin Balkcom*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Codec-Gauge is a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing KV-cache compression/quantization backends, concentrating energy in low-frequency layouts to improve fidelity without changing model weights or backends.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context inference with large KV caches faces bandwidth and fidelity bottlenecks. Prior work indicates the channel basis of key/value vectors affects how backends preserve model behavior under compression; a post-training, lightweight transform could improve fidelity without altering weights or coding rules.

Method: Introduce Codec-Gauge: a cache-coordinate layer that applies small orthogonal channel transforms around compression/quantization backends. Optimization uses a frequency-distribution objective: a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss plus a smooth rate proxy to encourage low-frequency energy in codec-facing layouts. Evaluate with measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring across six models at 3/4/6 bits/value, comparing against random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. Also test block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization, plus a 27B model and long-context prompts, with serial storage and timing measurements.

Result: Learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform multiple baselines. They improve quality preservation across block-uniform and KIVI quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context prompts reproduce the trend, and timing measurements validate the compressed-cache paths. Overall, cache-coordinate geometry emerges as a practical post-training variable to boost compression fidelity without changing model weights or backend coding rules.

Conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry provides a practical, weight-free lever to improve KV-cache compression fidelity. Codec-Gauge demonstrates that small, orthogonal, post-training transforms can enhance energy concentration in low-frequency layouts, yielding improved fidelity across diverse backends and quantization schemes while maintaining semantics and coding rules.

Abstract: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

</details>


### [142] [Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20539)
*Kyunghoon Hur,Eunjung Jeon,Hyun Woo Kim,Gyubok Lee,Seongjun Yang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Simulation pre-training on biokinetic ODE curves provides a data-efficient, effective prior for neural networks in bioprocessing, rivaling an architecture-embedded ODE prior; both priors outperform no-prior baselines across diverse datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bioprocess data are costly and scarce; traditional biokinetic ODEs encode domain knowledge, but it is unclear how best to integrate this into neural networks. This study systematically compares data-level priors (simulation pre-training) and architecture-level priors (ODE inside decoder) to learn from limited data.

Method: Compare two priors for neural networks predicting bioprocess trajectories across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species: (1) data-level prior via pre-training a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves; (2) architecture-level prior embedding the ODE inside the decoder. Baselines include models with no prior.

Result: Both priors outperform no-prior baselines. They are substitutable: a generic decoder pre-trained on simulations matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. This suggests simulation pre-training is a simple, data-efficient approach under data scarcity.

Conclusion: Simulation pre-training on simulated biokinetic ODEs provides an effective, data-efficient prior that can rival physics-informed architecture designs, offering a practical path to deploying deep learning in data-scarce bioprocess settings.

Abstract: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

</details>


### [143] [From Atoms to Entropy: Optimal Noise Allocation for Diffusion Training in the Convex Regime](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20540)
*Luca Ambrogioni,Giulio Franzese,Alberto Foresti,Gabriel Raya,Bac Nguyen,Georgios Batzolis,Yuhta Takida,Naoki Murata,Chieh-Hsin Lai,Yuki Mitsufuji*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes a statistical framework for asymptotically optimal diffusion-noise scheduling, showing in fully coupled training the optimizer's schedule is atomic (finite-support) and, in an independent-learner (decoupled) regime, that the sampling density follows a sqrt of the generative entropy rate; validated on Dirac mixtures, manifolds, and MNIST, with larger-scale experiments showing practical gains on discrete domains and competitive performance on continuous images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models hinge on noise schedules that are usually chosen heuristically. The work seeks principled, asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation under two regimes, connecting information-theoretic quantities to practical scheduling and providing empirical validation.

Method: Theoretical analysis under convex/Polyak-Lojasiewicz conditions for a fully coupled regime leading to an atomic minimizer; in a decoupled regime with a feature-noise decoupling condition, use random-matrix analysis to derive a sampling density proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate. Empirical validation in controlled settings (Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, MNIST) and larger-scale experiments comparing sqrt-entropy scheduling to standard EDM-style heuristics.

Result: Optimal schedules in the fully coupled setting are finite-support (atomic). In the decoupled regime, the sampling density aligns with the sqrt of the generative entropy rate. In experiments, entropic scheduling tracks the atomic optimum in neural networks, shows finite-support schedules, and yields substantial efficiency gains on discrete domains while remaining competitive on continuous images. The fully coupled parametric case reveals the theory’s limitations.

Conclusion: The framework provides principled guidance for diffusion-noise scheduling across regimes, with the sqrt-entropy proxy offering a practical scheduling heuristic, particularly effective for discrete domains; broader validation in fully coupled, large-scale settings remains an area for further work.

Abstract: How should a diffusion model decide which noise levels to train on, and how much? Despite the importance of this choice, current noise schedules are based largely on heuristics or empirical tuning. Here, we develop a general statistical framework for studying asymptotically optimal noise-level allocation in diffusion training. Our first main result concerns the fully coupled regime, where information can spread between different time points. Under convexity or Polyak-Lojasiewicz-type assumptions, we show that the optimized training schedule admits an atomic minimizer, concentrated on finitely many noise levels. Our second main result specializes this framework to an idealized independent-learner regime, intended to model temporal specialization in neural networks. Under an additional feature-noise decoupling condition, a random-matrix analysis leads to an information-theoretic proxy: the decoupled sampling density is proportional to the square root of the generative entropy rate, the rate at which conditional entropy grows along the forward process. We test these predictions in controlled settings where the coupled objective can be optimized directly, including Dirac mixtures, low-dimensional manifolds, and MNIST. In these settings, the optimized schedules are consistently finite-support, while the smooth entropic proxy closely tracks the atomic optimum in neural-network models and breaks down mainly in the fully coupled parametric case, as the theory suggests. We then evaluate the entropic schedule in larger-scale experiments, where full schedule optimization is currently intractable. The results indicate that square-root entropy scheduling can substantially improve training efficiency on discrete domains and remains competitive with standard EDM-style heuristics on continuous images.

</details>


### [144] [HypNO: A Graph-Based Neural Operator with Physics-Informed Message Passing for Hyperbolic Conservation Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20541)
*Dimitrije Ždrale,Cassie An Jeng,Katie Wang,Sonia Vanier,Alexandre Bayen,Hossein Nick Zinat Matin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HypNO is a graph-based neural operator that learns scalar hyperbolic conservation laws by operating on a space-time finite-volume graph with physics-informed message passing, achieving accurate, shock-aware predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hyperbolic PDEs with shocks pose challenges for data-driven operators; there is a need to preserve upwinding and entropy to accurately capture discontinuities, with traffic-flow models (LWR and ARZ) as demanding benchmarks.

Method: Construct a space-time graph over finite-volume cells and apply adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing that enforces upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks.

Result: HypNO delivers accurate solution snapshots across varied initial conditions and successfully captures shocks and discontinuities, demonstrating robustness to global transport with shock formation.

Conclusion: Graph-based neural operators with physics-informed messaging can effectively learn hyperbolic conservation laws, showing promise for traffic-flow models and related systems.

Abstract: We introduce HypNO, a graph-based neural operator for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws. HypNO operates directly on a space-time graph of finite-volume cells and uses adjacency-factored, physics-informed message passing to respect upwinding and entropy admissibility near shocks. We benchmark the architecture on the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) and Aw-Rascle-Zhang (ARZ) traffic-flow models, a stress test for operator-learning methods because of their simultaneous global transport and shock formation. HypNO predicts solution snapshots accurately across a range of initial conditions while capturing the shocks and discontinuities of the solution.

</details>


### [145] [Improving Access to Essential Medicines via Decision-Aware Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20542)
*Angel Tsai-Hsuan Chung,Jatu Abdulai,Patrick Bayoh,Lawrence Sandi,Francis Smart,Hamsa Bastani,Osbert Bastani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Decision-aware ML for essential medicines allocation; 19% consumption increase in treated districts; scaled nationwide to 2M beneficiaries; suggests low-cost scalability in LMICs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scarce essential medicines and poor data quality in LMICs hinder efficient, equitable allocation; need data-driven decision support that works with limited data.

Method: Proposes a decision-aware ML framework with multi-task learning to improve sample efficiency and catalytic priors to promote equity; deployed in Sierra Leone as a nationwide decision-support tool; staggered rollout.

Result: Econometric evaluation shows ~19% higher consumption in treated districts; nationwide scaling covering ~2 million women and children under five; claims cost-effective improvement.

Conclusion: Demonstrates potential for ML to improve efficiency and access to essential medicines in resource-constrained settings; scalable, collaborative approach with government.

Abstract: A critical challenge in healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) is the efficient and equitable allocation of scarce resources, particularly essential medicines. This problem is complicated by limited high-quality data, which restricts the applicability of traditional data-driven techniques. We propose a novel decision-aware machine learning framework for essential medicines allocation, which additionally leverages multi-task learning to ensure sample efficiency and catalytic priors to ensure equitable allocation. In collaboration with the Sierra Leone national government, we performed a staggered, nationwide deployment of our system as a decision support tool. Our econometric evaluation finds an estimated 19% increase in consumption of allocated products in treated districts, demonstrating its efficacy at improving access to essential medicines. Our tool was subsequently scaled nationwide, covering an estimated 2 million women and children under five. Our work demonstrates how machine learning methods can improve efficiency at very low cost in resource-constrained global health settings.

</details>


### [146] [When RLVR Shrinks the Reasoning Boundary: Diagnosing Pass@k Inversion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20543)
*Todd Zhou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can improve one-sample accuracy while making a model worse under repeated sampling. We study this pass@k inversion: after training, the policy may solve fewer distinct problems than its base model at large $k$. The failure concentrates on boundary prompts, where the base model contains rare correct trajectories that are recoverable by sampling but too sparse to reliably appear in finite RLVR rollout groups. We argue that a two-mode account explains this as an absence-of-evidence failure: rare correct trajectories may disappear before RLVR samples and reinforces them often enough. The main contribution is this diagnostic and mechanistic framing. Per-Problem Base Anchoring (PBA) is a deliberately simple proof-of-concept: sharpen prompts with sufficient frozen-base correct evidence, and anchor risky prompts to the base distribution. Across three training seeds on Omni-MATH-Test, with MATH500 as a secondary high-coverage validation benchmark, PBA improves both \PassK{1} and high-budget coverage over matched GRPO. A 3000-prompt regime-controlled diagnostic study is consistent across seeds with the expected signature: ordinary GRPO loses base-solvable boundary prompts, while PBA preserves rare verifier-positive trajectories. We use mathematical verifiers as a controlled testbed for verifier-guided optimization; the same pass@k inversion risk applies to ECCV-relevant vision-language agents when repeated visual, spatial, or chart-reasoning attempts are checked by external tools or verifiers. Reasoning post-training should decide not only how strongly to optimize, but which prompts are safe to optimize.

</details>


### [147] [Conflict Resolution under Degraded Surveillance in Air Corridors Using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20547)
*Esrat Farhana Dulia,Syed Arbab Mohd Shihab,Caleb Adams,Ruben Del Rosario*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multi-agent DRL framework using DQN for decentralized conflict resolution between heterogeneous small UAS and eVTOL in a 3D corridor; 14-action policy; evaluated under degraded surveillance; reveals trade-offs between safety and capacity; most conflicts resolved quickly (within ~1 s).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safe Advanced Air Mobility requires reliable conflict-resolution when surveillance is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or unavailable. A decentralized, heterogeneous, reinforcement-learning approach can scale to complex corridors and provide robust performance under degraded sensing.

Method: Deep Q-Network-based multi-agent reinforcement learning with separate policies per aircraft category. Local observations are used with a 14-action space (course maintenance, turns, vertical maneuvering, landing, speed control). Simulation includes aircraft dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delays, information dropout, wind, actuator and model uncertainty. Training evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds.

Result: Loss-of-separation frequency and duration rise with density and separation requirements, but most events resolve within ~1 second. Under safe conditions, agents maintain motion ~79% of the time. Action distribution during conflicts: turning 33%, maintaining 29%, speed control 25%, vertical maneuvers 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations show trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity.

Conclusion: The framework supports simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions, enabling assessment of decentralized, heterogeneous, reinforcement-learning solutions for safe and efficient corridor-based operations.

Abstract: Safe Advanced Air Mobility operations require aircraft to maintain separation when surveillance information is noisy, delayed, incomplete, or temporarily unavailable. This study develops a Deep Q-Network-based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning framework for decentralized conflict resolution among heterogeneous small unmanned aerial vehicles and electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft operating within a structured three-dimensional corridor. Separate policies are trained for the two aircraft categories using local observations and a 14-action space that includes maintaining course, turning, vertical maneuvering, landing, and speed control. The simulation incorporates aircraft-specific dynamics, energy use, corridor constraints, observation noise, communication delay, information dropout, wind disturbance, actuator uncertainty, and model uncertainty. The trained policies are evaluated across 90 combinations of traffic density and minimum separation thresholds. Loss-of-separation frequency and duration generally increase with traffic density and separation requirements, although most events are resolved within 1s. Under safe conditions, agents maintain their motion approximately 79% of the time. During conflicts, turning accounts for 33% of actions, followed by maintaining motion at 29%, speed control at 25%, and vertical maneuvers at 13%. Six Pareto-optimal configurations reveal trade-offs between safety and corridor capacity. The framework supports the simulation-based evaluation of safer AAM conflict-resolution strategies under degraded surveillance conditions.

</details>


### [148] [SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20548)
*Mikail Khona,Aditya Vavre,Boxiang Wang,Deyu Fu,Hao Wu,Mike Chrzanowski,Bryan Catanzaro,Dheevatsa Mudigere,Jeff Pool,Michael Lightstone,Mohammad Shoeybi,Mostofa Patwary,Nima Tajbakhsh,Tijmen Blankevoort*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Adapts and enhances preconditioned gradient methods (SOAP, Muon) for large-scale LLM pretraining to overcome instability and cost, introducing per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning; conducts a unified, fair comparison with AdamW via update-RMS matching; develops a layer-wise distributed optimizer for Megatron-LM; experiments on multi-billion-parameter models show SOAP/Muon outperform AdamW at large batch sizes with maintained stability; releases codebase for emerging optimizers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable faster convergence and practical deployment of higher-order optimizers (SOAP, Muon) at scale, addressing instability and computational overhead that limit adoption in large LLM pretraining.

Method: Identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes; propose per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning; perform unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning-rate transfer; empirically evaluate Muon's orthogonalization quality; develop a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM; implement system-level improvements to accelerate training; release open-source code.

Result: SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at tested scales (multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens); stable training up to batch sizes of 100M tokens for next-token prediction with AdamW degrading; layer-wise optimizer balances memory and communication without compromising optimizer integrity; codebase released for broader research use.

Conclusion: Higher-order optimizers can realize superior convergence at scale when paired with targeted numerical fixes and system-level optimizations; the work provides practical tools and empirical evidence supporting broader adoption of SOAP/Muon in large-scale pretraining.

Abstract: Higher-order optimizers such as Muon and SOAP offer faster convergence than AdamW, but their computational cost and numerical stability challenges have limited adoption at scale. In this work, we adapt and enhance preconditioned gradient methods to overcome the practical challenges of large-scale LLM pretraining. We first identify instabilities in SOAP at large batch sizes and propose algorithmic modifications including per-step QR orthogonalization and improved preconditioning strategies that eliminate loss spikes and enable stable training in these regimes. We then present a unified empirical study of SOAP, Muon, and AdamW using update-RMS matching to ensure fair learning rate transfer across optimizers. As part of this analysis, we empirically evaluate the orthogonalization quality of Muon. Our experiments on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens reveal that SOAP and Muon consistently outperform AdamW at the scales we tested. Notably, at batch sizes of up to 100M tokens for next-token prediction, these optimizers maintain training stability and quality while AdamW degrades. To enable efficient training at large scale, we introduce a layer-wise distributed optimizer compatible with Megatron-LM. Our implementation balances memory and hides communication while avoiding approximations to the optimizer computations, thus retaining their convergence benefits. Additionally, we identify and build specific system-level improvements to further accelerate our layer-wise implementation. To support the research community, we release a codebase that contains emerging algorithms for optimization: https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Emerging-Optimizers

</details>


### [149] [SevDiff: Severity-Conditioned Diffusion for Long-Tail Conflict Trajectory Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20549)
*Eni Solomon Laughter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SevDiff is a severity-conditioned DDPM that generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories conditioned on a target TTC value, achieving high hit-rates for near-term TTC targets on a real expressway dataset and producing physically plausible kinematics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the data imbalance where genuine V2V conflict events are rare in ADAS evaluation datasets, and provide a generator that can enforce a target TTC value to study risk-controlled scenarios.

Method: Severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that takes a scalar target minimum TTC as conditioning input and outputs coordinated vehicle trajectories. Trained on 468 interaction windows from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing). Evaluation uses a hit-rate metric reporting how often realized TTC matches the request. Features include 12 kinematic signals; generated data are checked for physical plausibility (no negative speeds/gaps beyond threshold; out-of-range rates).

Result: Hit-rate of 100% within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets 0.5–1.5 s; 97–99% for 2.0–2.5 s; 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Maximum out-of-range rate 4.7% across 12 features; >96.5% of samples have nonnegative speeds and gaps. Degradation in hit-rate correlates with conditioning strength relative to prior, indicating a precise characterization of the generator’s performance rather than a binary success.

Conclusion: The conditioning signal strength governs generation fidelity, enabling precise, controllable generation of rare-conflict scenarios for ADAS evaluation. SevDiff provides a principled, precision-oriented approach to modeling severity-conditioned interactions, with strong results at near-term TTC targets and physically plausible outputs.

Abstract: Trajectory datasets used in ADAS evaluation are heavily biased toward routine driving; genuine vehicle-to-vehicle conflict events are rare, and the rarer the event, the higher the cost when an ADAS system fails to handle it. Existing generative approaches address this imbalance by conditioning on scene-level properties - spatial goals, agent structure, or natural-language adversarial objectives - but none can accept a target Time-to-Collision (TTC) value as input and be held to producing it within a measurable error. This paper introduces SevDiff, a severity-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that accepts a requested minimum TTC value as a scalar conditioning signal and generates paired vehicle interaction trajectories whose realized conflict severity matches the request, evaluated through a hit-rate metric. Trained on 468 interaction windows extracted from the UTE SQM-W-1 expressway weaving-section dataset (1,041 vehicles, 822,691 observations after smoothing), SevDiff achieves 100% hit-rate within +/-0.5 s for TTC targets of 0.5-1.5 s and 97-99% at 2.0-2.5 s, with graceful degradation to 39% at TTC = 5.0 s. Generated kinematic features are physically plausible, with a maximum out-of-range rate of 4.7% across 12 features and no negative speed or gap values in more than 96.5% of samples. The hit-rate degradation pattern is physically interpretable as the strength of the conditioning signal relative to the training prior, making it a precision characterization of the generator rather than a pass/fail result.

</details>


### [150] [Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20550)
*Tianming Han,Zhijie Pan,Wenchi Ge,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Geometric deep learning enables rational polypharmacology by modeling 3D structures and multiple targets; the review surveys architectures (invariant GNNs, SE(3)-equivariant diffusion), analyzes shared pockets, multi-target bioactivity, and dual-target ligand design, and highlights diffusion-RL conditioning, multimodal omics, and benchmarks as a roadmap for structure-driven therapeutics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional one drug, one target paradigm fails for multifactorial diseases due to compensatory pathways and resistance; geometric constraints across targets hinder ligand design; GDL provides a unifying framework to extract 3D structural interdependencies and integrate multi-omics for polypharmacology.

Method: Systematic survey of GDL architectures and applications: invariant graph neural networks and SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models; evaluation along three dimensions (shared pocket embeddings, heterogeneous graph fusion for multi-target bioactivity, de novo dual-target ligand generation); emphasis on structure-conditioned generative models combining diffusion with reinforcement learning; discussion of omics integration and benchmarking infrastructures.

Result: Synthesizes methodological advances, articulates a paradigm shift from serendipitous to rational polypharmacology; provides a structured guide for navigating multi-target drug design and identifies key challenges and benchmarks.
