Conclusion: Geometric deep learning is a enabling framework for rational design of dual-target ligands; integration with omics and benchmarking will accelerate next-generation structure-driven therapeutics; provides concrete roadmap for researchers.

Abstract: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

</details>


### [151] [SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20551)
*Tianming Han,Li Zhang,Qi Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SenCos-GEM introduces a geometry-enhanced 3D GNN framework that uses physics-guided, law-of-cosines-based constraints and dynamic feature modulation via SE and FiLM for molecular representation learning. It achieves state-of-the-art results on 3D conformation-sensitive tasks (FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, QM9) and demonstrates robust stereoisomer and conformational discrimination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current SSL methods for 3D GNNs often lack explicit physical constraints and are vulnerable to geometric noise from coarse force fields. They also underperform during downstream adaptation due to catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. A need exists for physically grounded representations with dynamic, task-specific feature modulation.

Method: Introduce SenCos-GEM with (i) a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity 3D spatial priors; (ii) lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) adapters in the backbone; (iii) a dual-modulation head that combines FiLM and SENet for dynamic feature recalibration.

Result: Competitive performance across MoleculeNet classification and regression tasks; state-of-the-art on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks (FreeSolv RMSE reduction 12.9%, Lipophilicity RMSE reduction 5.3%, QM9 MAE reduction 8.2%); improved ability to distinguish stereoisomers and conformational perturbations, indicating robust spatial modeling.

Conclusion: SenCos-GEM represents a significant advance in accurate molecular property prediction by integrating physics-informed priors with dynamic adaptation, achieving improved accuracy and robustness on geometry-sensitive tasks.

Abstract: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

</details>


### [152] [Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20552)
*Chitraansh Pandey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A thermodynamics-inspired method (CvAdamW) detects precursors to grokking by tracking attention-variance as a specific heat proxy, then dynamically adjusts weight decay to facilitate generalization within a fixed budget. It identifies and mitigates three failure modes to stabilize learning, demonstrates grokking enablement on a modular-arithmetic task where baselines fail, and reports robust, statistically significant improvements across seeds using a scale-invariant reformulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Grokking (delayed generalization) is inefficient and unpredictable. The authors aim to diagnose precursors to generalization transitions using a physically motivated proxy (Cv) and to intervene online to accelerate or ensure generalization within a fixed compute budget.

Method: Define Cv as variance of attention logits, treat it as a specific heat. Develop CvAdamW a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and scales weight decay to inject 'thermal energy' when a phase transition is detected. Identify and address three failure modes (initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, slingshot blinding) with a memorization gate and an EMA shock absorber. Validate on modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), compare against baseline, and introduce a scale-invariant z-score reformulation evaluated across 10 paired seeds.

Result: Cv peaks before grokking; CvAdamW enables grokking within a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. Cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166; p=0.049, d=0.68). All seeds show Cv peaking before grokking in this task. Paired analysis shows robustness across seeds; code and data are public.

Conclusion: Neural networks may reveal detectable precursors to generalization transitions. A physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget and suggests a pathway to more predictable, tunable learning dynamics.

Abstract: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

</details>


### [153] [Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20555)
*Bryce A. Christopherson,Jack Baretz,Darian Colgrove,Salah Dandan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Double-scoring augments the score-space used by edge-popup to enable fixed-density masks to explore all original subnetworks; this replaces layerwise sparsity search with optimization over larger score tensors to improve strong-ticket extraction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the bottleneck of layerwise sparsity selection in edge-popup when extracting strong lottery tickets, by enabling a richer search over masks and improving robustness to hyperparameters.

Method: Introduce double-scoring: augment the score space and optimize over enlarged score tensors; prove that fixed-density masks in augmented space retain access to all original masks; interpret as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network; perform controlled experiments comparing against fixed-density edge-popup, pruning-at-initialization, rewound sparse-training topologies.

Result: Significant improvement in strong-ticket extraction over baselines; better performance than rewound sparse-training topologies; reduced sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters; ablations show gains arise from augmented score-space competition rather than simply more trainable scores.

Conclusion: Augmented score-space provides a principled mechanism to enable reliable extraction of strong lottery tickets, reframing edge-popup in an augmented network and yielding tangible practical gains in robustness and performance.

Abstract: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

</details>


### [154] [Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20557)
*Hesen Chen,Xinyu Su,Xiaomeng Yang,Yuetan Lin,Zixiong Yang,Junyi An,Fenglei Cao,Yifeng Jiao,Yunqi Zhang,Yuan Cheng,Zhiyu Tan,Hao Li,Libo Wu,Yuan Qi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A unified multimodal model, MKB, learns across six scientific domains using a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum, enabling native outputs and cross-domain understanding generation while preserving base capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Science is increasingly cross-domain; existing systems are domain-specific or rely heavily on text tokenization, limiting cross-domain reasoning and modality-native outputs. There is a need for a shared backbone with modality-tailored components to enable joint understanding and generation across diverse scientific modalities.

Method: Introduce MKB with a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders for six domains (DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, medical images). Train in two stages: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone; Stage 2 integrates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora.

Result: MKB achieves competitive performance on biological/molecular understanding benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs (weather fields, biological strings, segmentation masks), and largely maintains the general capabilities of the Qwen3-VL backbone.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of shared-backbone, modality-tailored multimodal models for cross-domain scientific exploration, providing a foundation for future cross-domain scientific AI with native outputs; code and model are publicly available.

Abstract: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

</details>


### [155] [StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20558)
*Emma Kondrup,Zachary Yang,Anne Imouza,Reihaneh Rabbany*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces StabilityBench, a general benchmark operator that converts single-turn benchmarks into multi-turn interactions with realistic user simulations; reveals instability in LLM performance under context-rich conditions and offers StabilityBench-Mini for cost-effective diversification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world AI assistants exhibit strong context dependence, especially in high-stakes domains. Static, single-turn benchmarks fail to capture multi-turn dynamics, variability, and safeguards required in deployment. A principled, model-agnostic evaluation framework is needed to stress-test stability under realistic user interactions.

Method: StabilityBench is a benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. It augments benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations (demographic proxies, sycophantic baits) while preserving task intent. Applied to four benchmarks across mathematical reasoning, health Q&A, and safety, evaluated on nine large language models. StabilityBench-Mini is proposed as a size-preserving variant that samples across diversification axes to enable realistic evaluation without higher costs.

Result: Model performance is consistently unstable when subjected to the injected multi-turn contexts, with substantial degradation on three of the four benchmarks. This underscores the limitations of static evaluations and motivates more realistic evaluation regimes.

Conclusion: Static benchmarks alone are insufficient to gauge real-world model behavior. StabilityBench provides a principled, general framework for more realistic evaluation; StabilityBench-Mini enables scalable diversification to maintain cost efficiency while enriching evaluation scenarios.

Abstract: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent. We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

</details>


### [156] [Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20559)
*Aditya Dutt,Paul Gader,Aditya Singh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A deep learning framework (JuGAAD) harmonizes census (2001, 2011) with NSSO survey data to produce high-resolution socio-economic indicators via tessellations, autoencoding, and regression, validated against district-level ground truth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address scale mismatch: census data offer wide geographic coverage but coarse, infrequent survey indicators; the goal is fine-grained, up-to-date socioeconomic maps for policy planning.

Method: Three-step pipeline: (1) aggregate census and geospatial data into intermediate village-cluster tessellations to stabilize boundaries; (2) use an autoencoder to compress high-dimensional NSSO data into a low-dimensional latent representation; (3) train a regression model to map upscaled census/geospatial features to the latent NSSO representation and apply it to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against district NSSO indicators.

Result: The approach yields high-fidelity, fine-scale socioeconomic predictions with strong agreement to ground-truth district NSSO indicators, demonstrating effective cross-scale transfer between census and survey data.

Conclusion: JuGAAD provides a scalable framework for producing fine-resolution poverty and food-security indicators from heterogeneous data sources, enabling better-targeted policy analysis where traditional survey data are scarce.

Abstract: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

</details>


### [157] [Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20560)
*Muntaser Syed,Marius Silaghi,Sheikh Abujar,Sharun Akter*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chronofy introduces a three-layer neuro-symbolic Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) to embed temporal validity in RAG, reducing temporal hallucination and enabling principled data re-acquisition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems treat retrieved facts as temporally uniform, causing temporal hallucination when outdated information is used. A temporally aware framework is needed to encode time provenance across representation, retrieval, and reasoning.

Method: Layer 1: a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to structurally separate fact age from representation. Layer 2: learnable exponential decay in graph-based retrieval, with decay coefficients β_j grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3: Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to assess temporal validity of retrieved knowledge and enforce the possibilistic weakest-link principle, tying output confidence to the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain.

Result: Evaluations on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and domain-specific sensitivity analyses show that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

Conclusion: Explicit temporal decay modeling yields more temporally robust RAG systems. The TLDA framework is modular, principled, and generalizable, with practical benefits in domains where timely information is critical and re-acquisition strategies can be invoked.

Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation. Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

</details>


### [158] [CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20561)
*Keumseo Ryum,Joonhyuk Kang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CT-Merging is a LoRA-aware multi-task merging method that derives a common basis from consensus directions across task SVD subspaces and assigns per-task RMS scaling to the final update, improving average accuracy on DC-Merge benchmarks and yielding gains on ViT checkpoints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address mismatch between inherited SVD coefficients and task-induced magnitudes in LoRA merging; reduce reliance on original magnitudes by constructing a shared basis and task-specific RMS scales.

Method: Repeatedly extract task subspace projectors via SVD, build a common basis through consensus directions across tasks, and apply task-level RMS coefficient scaling in the final merged update, reducing sensitivity to rank-wise SVD magnitudes.

Result: CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy on the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark compared with state-of-the-art merging methods, with gains of 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

Conclusion: CT-Merging improves multi-task LoRA merging by aligning directions via a consensus-based shared basis and scaling coefficients with RMS norms, offering better performance and robustness than prior SVD-based merging approaches.

Abstract: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

</details>


### [159] [AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20577)
*Mengda Xing,Jean-Marie Lagniez,Alejandro Franco*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Swin3D Transformer-based surrogate with Gaussian Positional Encoding and Temporal Encoding predicts spatiotemporal lithium‑ion battery discharge from volumetric data, surpassing point-cloud baselines and delivering orders-of-magnitude speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Physics-based electrode-scale simulations of LIB discharge are accurate but computationally prohibitive, hindering high-throughput design and optimization; a fast, accurate surrogate is needed.

Method: Develop a Swin3D Transformer–based surrogate pipeline. Introduce Gaussian Positional Encoding to better encode electrode microstructure geometry and a Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear time evolution; train and validate on the Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset.

Result: The approach achieves higher prediction accuracy than state-of-the-art point-cloud baselines and reduces computational overhead by orders of magnitude, enabling scalable, high-throughput battery design.

Conclusion: The proposed GPE-equipped Swin3D surrogate with temporal encoding offers a scalable and accurate framework for rapid battery discharge simulations, accelerating design and optimization workflows.

Abstract: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

</details>


### [160] [Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21488)
*Gil Lifshits,Igal Bilik,Gilad Katz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MAPS introduces a Master-Agent Proto-plan System for hierarchical MARL in unsignalized intersections; a central Master outputs a compact proto-plan embedding guiding decentralized Worker agents, achieving collision-free navigation with reduced travel time and strong zero-shot generalization to larger agent counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections is hard due to combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, and rigid agent architectures; there is a need for scalable, transferable coordination that decouples strategic planning from execution.

Method: A hierarchical DRL architecture where a centralized Master agent learns a continuous proto-plan embedding representing global coordination; decentralized Worker agents fuse the embedding with local observations to perform vehicle-level control, enabling independent optimization of Master and Workers.

Result: Evaluated on 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv; MAPS achieves collision-free navigation, reduces average travel time, and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines; proto-plans generalize to larger agent counts, achieving 94% success rate in zero-shot transfer from 3-agent training to 5-agent scenarios.

Conclusion: Proto-plan-based hierarchical learning is a promising framework for scalable, transferable multi-vehicle coordination at intersections.

Abstract: Coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections remains a critical challenge for multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) systems, which typically struggle with combinatorial action spaces, reliance on privileged information, or rigid agent designs. We propose Master-Agent Proto-plan System (MAPS), a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architecture in which a centralized Master agent generates a compact, continuous embedding, denoted as proto-plan, that encodes a global coordination strategy. Decentralized Worker agents integrate this embedding with local observations to execute vehicle-specific control, decoupling strategic intent from tactical execution and enabling independent optimization of each module.
  As a proof-of-concept evaluation of this coordination mechanism, we test MAPS across 72 intersection configurations in HighwayEnv. MAPS achieves collision-free navigation while significantly reducing average travel time, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The learned proto-plans further exhibit robust generalization: a system trained with three agents achieves a 94% success rate when deployed zero-shot to five-agent scenarios, confirming that proto-plan-based hierarchical learning provides a promising framework for multi-vehicle coordination.

</details>


### [161] [Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20578)
*Vu Khac Ky*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces primal and inverse Fisher Gaussian-widths to quantify complexity on Fisher-geometry manifolds, linking learning and sparse recovery via two complementary widths and a fundamental product bound.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand statistical complexity on manifolds endowed with the Fisher information metric and its inverse, unifying learning (local fluctuations) and recovery (anisotropic measurements) under a single Gaussian-width framework.

Method: Define w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T) and w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T); derive their properties under Fisher-regular losses, for small Fisher balls, and for anisotropic Gaussian measurements. Obtain two-sided estimates for the statistical dimension, introduce support-sensitive recovery, and prove a multiplicative relation w_G(T) w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2 on common compact T.

Result: Sharp relation w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2; two-sided statistical-dimension bounds; Fisher-ball scalability results; support-sensitive sparse-recovery estimates and curvature-based ordering; demonstrates that Fisher anisotropy redistributes complexity but cannot reduce both widths below Euclidean scale.

Conclusion: Fisher geometry provides complementary and transferable complexity between learning and recovery; the product bound reveals a form of information-geometry uncertainty principle: anisotropy shifts difficulty but cannot beat the Euclidean baseline on both fronts.

Abstract: We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

</details>


### [162] [Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20582)
*Frederik Hauke,Patrick Wienholt,Christiane Kuhl,Dyke Ferber,Jakob Nikolas Kather,Sven Nebelung,Daniel Truhn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Monte Carlo dropout yields epistemic uncertainty in a multi-task chest radiograph classifier, and using this uncertainty as a binary error-risk flag improves decision-support performance by reducing confident misdiagnoses, though raw uncertainty scores are less effective than a flag.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide reliable confidence estimates for medical image classifiers to improve performance on ambiguous or atypical cases and to inform downstream decision-making.

Method: Apply Monte Carlo dropout to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (8 findings; 137,593 training images). Estimate epistemic uncertainty and incorporate it into decision support. Evaluate impact on point predictions (AUROC) and conduct a 2x2 factorial experiment comparing communication modalities (binary flag vs raw scores) for uncertainty in a clinical decision-support agent.

Result: Point-prediction AUROC improved from 0.74 to 0.77 (ΔAUROC 0.023, 95% CI [0.014, 0.033]). In a 2x2 factorial study, the decision-support agent used uncertainty only as a binary error-risk flag, reducing confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%.

Conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty estimation provides decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its practical value depends on how uncertainty is communicated to downstream agents.

Abstract: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions. Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.

</details>


### [163] [Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20586)
*Boldsaikhan Bolorkhuu,Tsogtgerel Gantumur*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper provides an explicit, exact fixed-width ReLU realization for finite affine iterates of vector-valued affine refinement operators, with network depth growing linearly with the iteration count (depth O(n)) for M ≥ 3. It introduces a residual memory-controller to enable backward replay of residuals and Horner-type evaluation of affine forcing, handling arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise-linear forcing terms; a variant for M = 2 addresses seam-separated forcing. It also extends to stage-dependent forcing within a finite-dimensional CPL span and yields linear-depth upgrades for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge vector-valued affine refinement operators with ReLU-based neural realizations, enabling exact, depth-efficient representations of iterative affine systems under piecewise-linear, compactly supported data while controlling forcing dynamics.

Method: Develop a residual memory controller that converts noninvertible residual dynamics into an injective skew-product, allowing exact backward replay required by Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Use offset frames to separate forcing atoms from residual seams, enabling exact recovery via complementary loop readouts. Analyze branch-selection ambiguity and extend the approach for M≥3 to arbitrary CPL forcing; treat M=2 for seam-separated forcing; provide a stage-dependent extension for forcing in a finite-dimensional CPL span and adapt to various recursive constructions.

Result: For M ≥ 3, every finite affine iterate W^n γ has an exact fixed-width ReLU realization with depth O(n). The construction works for arbitrary compactly supported CPL forcing; for M = 2, it applies to seam-separated forcing. A stage-dependent extension yields linear-depth upgrades for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

Conclusion: The work delivers a constructive framework to realize affine refinement operators with ReLU nets of linear depth in iteration count, enabled by a residual memory controller and offset framing. It broadens applicability to general CPL forcing and several recursive schemes, offering practical, depth-efficient realizations.

Abstract: We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

</details>


### [164] [Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20590)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Spectral Drift identifies a frequency-domain instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output, and SDNN uses spectral features across layers to detect failures with a lightweight detector, achieving strong AUROC on CIFAR-10 and outperforming confidence-based baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitations of output-based uncertainty by leveraging internal activations. Internal spectral dynamics may reveal failure signatures that do not manifest in final predictions or confidences.

Method: Define Spectral Drift as the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations. Use multi-scale spectral representations (Short-Time Fourier Transform, Wavelet decomposition) and statistical moments to extract features across network depth. Train a lightweight detector (roughly 5% parameter overhead) via curriculum learning across progressively harder distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.

Result: SDNN achieves 79.0 ± 25.3% AUROC across three seeds on CIFAR-10, outperforming confidence-based baselines (MaxSoftmax 50.5% AUROC, Energy Score 52.9%) by ~25–30 percentage points. Ablations show wavelet and statistical features contribute consistently; STFT impact is unclear. The work demonstrates that spectral analysis of internal activations provides diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

Conclusion: Spectral analysis of internal activations is a promising direction for improving neural-network reliability, enabling failure detection beyond what is possible with output-based metrics.

Abstract: Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

</details>


### [165] [STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20592)
*Jan Linnenbrink,Jakub Nowosad,Marvin Ludwig,Anna Frederike Jablotschkin,Fabian Schumacher,Teja Kattenborn,Hanna Meyer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduce STeMP, a Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol, to standardize reporting of spatio-temporal ML models and guide modelling decisions. Hosted on GitHub with an R-package and web app to fill the protocol, aiming to improve transparency, comparability, and reviewer support; three sections: Overview, Model, Prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current spatio-temporal ML studies suffer from lack of standardized reporting, making it hard to assess model quality, transferability, and applicability; standardized protocols would improve transparency, trust, and comparability.

Method: Propose STeMP protocol organized into Overview, Model, and Prediction sections. Overview captures metadata; Model and Prediction detail predictors, evaluation, software, and workflow. An accompanying R-package and web app help fill the protocol automatically or semi-automatically from modelling objects, with built-in warnings to flag common pitfalls. Protocol hosted on GitHub to invite community contributions.

Result: No empirical results are reported. The paper presents the protocol design and accompanying tooling (R-package and web app) as a framework to standardize reporting and guide modelling practice.

Conclusion: STeMP addresses the lack of standardized SPATIO-TEMPORAL modelling protocols by providing a structured reporting framework and tools, aiming to enhance transparency, comparability, and trust in ML-based environmental maps; community-driven development via GitHub.

Abstract: Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

</details>


### [166] [When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20594)
*Tong Zhang,Junhao Hu,Yun Peng,Tao Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR:  Four findings on weight-tied looped transformers (budget-driven frontier, architecture bias, non-intuitive complexity walls, and transferable mechanisms) with a new convergence-time metric and head-based predictions. 


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Determine when a weight-tied looped transformer actually implements an algorithm on structured problems, and how training budget, depth, and architectural priors shape the learned strategy.

Method: Controlled population experiments on group word problems using a weight-tied looped transformer (block applied T times) across varying budgets, depths, and input schedules; compare with untied variants; introduce convergence-time scaling tau(n,i) and damage-cone validation; test transferability via warm-starting and cross-seed assessments; replicate on an easy-to-hard public benchmark.

Result: (1) Budget law: v ~ n_train/T_train with exponent ~0.98 (R^2 ~0.99); unity when T equals training size; yields halting rule T* ~ ceil(n/v_hat). (2) Architecture prior governs algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans; weight tying switches to serial frontier; untied models at matched depth/params extrapolate poorly and miss A5. (3) Walls not where circuit complexity predicts: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes); group-order costs (S5 operator causes deadlocks); an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatory: warm-starting across budgets transfers the algorithm; imposing seriality via input schedule fails in free training. Convergence-time tau(n,i) introduced; damage cones validate causally; head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate better than tail metrics. Replication on public easy-to-hard benchmark."

Conclusion: The four findings reveal robust, transferable, architecture-dependent algorithms emergent in budgeted, weight-tied looped transformers. They highlight the importance of budget-aware halting, inductive biases from architecture, and training curricula in enabling algorithmic behavior. A new convergence-time metric and head-based predictivity offer practical tools for diagnosing and transferring learned algorithms across seeds and tasks.

Abstract: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

</details>


### [167] [Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20596)
*Seonglae Cho,Zekun Wu,Kleyton Da Costa,Rishi Kalra,Ilham Wicaksono,Adriano Koshiyama*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Cross-family stability of causal effects for single-token sparse-autoencoder features is limited; cross-family differences dominate, implying training methodology shapes interpretability more than activation function or scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether causal effects of SAE-derived features generalize across SAE families in LLMs.

Method: Analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth; evaluate single-token feature localization in decoder space and early layers; quantify ablation effects via logit reductions with BH significance; compare cross-family anchoring and rank recovery; perform controlled activation-function tests.

Result: Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers; 178 of 208 full-layer conditions show BH-significant logit reductions upon ablation; depth modulates cascade vs direct shaping; cross-family causal differences exceed within-family effects; some features remain anchored while others are locally redundant; target token rank recovers to near baseline (96-98%) in 96-98% of cases; activation-function control can reverse sign; training recipe is the residual driver of interpretability.

Conclusion: Interpretability claims across SAE families are sensitive to training methodology; stability of causal roles cannot be assumed across methods; future work should jointly consider training recipes and activation functions when assessing interpretability across SAE families.

Abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

</details>


### [168] [One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20641)
*Afsaneh Mahanipour,Hana Khamfroush*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Analytic federated learning for multi-label classification under task heterogeneity using three closed-form steps, achieving fast convergence (≤2 rounds) and improved accuracy over gradient-based baselines, with reduced communication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In FL, clients annotate only subsets of target disease categories, causing task heterogeneity. Gradient-based FL struggles with slow convergence and systematic false-negative bias due to missing labels.

Method: Three closed-form operations: (1) balanced label projection to neutralize class-imbalance; (2) per-class absolute aggregation to construct independent ridge classifiers from clients' sufficient statistics; (3) optional analytic pseudo-label refinement that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher to non-annotating clients; total communication rounds: at most two.

Result: On ChestXray14 under four missing-class configurations, the method consistently outperforms FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points while reducing communication.

Conclusion: An analytic FL framework effectively handles task heterogeneity in multi-label medical imaging, delivering fast convergence, lower communication, and improved accuracy compared to gradient-based approaches.

Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity. The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients. Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

</details>


### [169] [Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20652)
*Andrew Mack,Kraig Yuheng Tou,Mark Henry,Zhengxun Wu,Lauren Greenspan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ParityTransformer introduces Deep Parity Bottlenecks (DPB) to enable interpretable-by-design sparse representations in a GPT-2-scale model, replacing learned overcomplete bases with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, achieving comparable or better performance on probing tasks and superior interpretability metrics; achieves efficiency via hierarchical sparse MoE and hardware-aware design.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcomplete, post-hoc interpretable bottlenecks (SAEs) are memory- and compute-intensive and don't integrate with forward pass; the phenomenon of superposition implies many features per dimension; there is a need for scalable, interpretable representations built into model architectures.

Method: Replace per-layer learned bottlenecks with DPB: a parameter-free algebraic dictionary; hierarchical sparse bottleneck via multi-level mixture-of-experts; hardware-aware design; ensures sparsity persists through the forward pass; provides a deterministic incoherence guarantee.

Result: ParityTransformers match or exceed post-hoc SAE performance on sparse probing tasks; they outperform on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions.

Conclusion: Interpretable-by-design architectures are feasible at GPT-2 scale; DPB yields native, sparse features aligned with actual computation, addressing the gap between interpretability and performance.

Abstract: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

</details>


### [170] [SalesLoop: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Sales Lead Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20655)
*Chenyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SalesLoop is a reinforcement learning framework for CRM lead ranking that closes the offline-online gap via a performance-aware reward and a discriminative GRPO-based listwise objective; it yields offline metric gains and measurable production lifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline lead-ranking models often perform well offline but underperform in production due to metric misalignment, static baselines, and nonstationary distributions. The paper identifies three gaps: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise–listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift, motivating a closed-loop RL approach.

Method: Introduce a performance-aware reward that weights conversion outcomes by ranking position and conversion velocity; propose Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models; implement a closed feedback loop between predictions and business outcomes; evaluate offline (NDCG@K, P@K) and via a 160-day production A/B test in a real CRM setting.

Result: Offline gains: NDCG@K +7.9%; P@K +15.8% over strongest static baseline. Production A/B: cumulative lift +4.7% (p=0.047) and +8.7% (p=0.002) across 16.5M leads, 280 sales specialists in two markets. Ranking backbone achieves Top-10% recall 44.1% and surfaces high-intent leads with 2.3× the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

Conclusion: SalesLoop demonstrates that an RL-based closed-loop lead ranking can bridge offline-online gaps and deliver meaningful production gains in CRM. The approach is promising for deployment, though considerations such as stability, sample efficiency, and generalization to other settings warrant further work.

Abstract: Lead ranking in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) systems faces a persistent challenge: models achieving high offline accuracy often underperform in production. We identify three fundamental gaps responsible for this disconnect: offline-online metric mismatch, pointwise-listwise objective misalignment, and temporal distribution drift. To address these gaps, we propose SalesLoop, a reinforcement learning framework that establishes a closed feedback loop between model predictions and real-world business outcomes. Our approach introduces (1) a performance-aware reward that encodes conversion outcomes weighted by ranking position and conversion velocity, and (2) Discriminative GRPO, a listwise optimization objective that adapts Group Relative Policy Optimization to discriminative ranking models.
  SalesLoop improves NDCG@K by +7.9\% and P@K by +15.8\% over the strongest static baseline. A 160-day production A/B test at a New Energy Vehicle manufacturer, spanning 16.5M leads and 280 sales specialists across two provincial markets, validates statistically significant cumulative lift of +4.7\% ($p=0.047$) and +8.7\% ($p=0.002$). In production, the ranking backbone achieves Top-10\% recall of 44.1\% and surfaces high-intent leads at $2.3\times$ the conversion rate of specialist baselines.

</details>


### [171] [Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20656)
*Manoosh Samiei,Doina Precup,Paul Masset*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A multi-horizon adaptive discounting method for RL that selects and combines multiple temporal horizons to handle changing rewards and continual task switches, improving adaptability and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed discount factor limits horizon flexibility; biological agents show flexible timescales; need adaptive temporal discounting for robust planning and continual learning.

Method: Introduce a multi-horizon framework that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons (discount factors) to form effective planning horizons; no manual discount tuning; applicable to continual tasks.

Result: Empirical results on MiniGrid show the method identifies effective discount factors across environments, including three-task continual settings; demonstrates improved parameter efficiency and adaptability.

Conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting enhances adaptability and efficiency in RL and aligns with biologically inspired learning; well-suited for continual learning scenarios.

Abstract: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

</details>


### [172] [End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20674)
*Xingjian Li,Kelvin Kan,Deepanshu Verma,Krishna Kumar,Stanley Osher,Samy Wu Fung*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Scalable end-to-end training of high-dimensional systems with hard safety guarantees by integrating a CBF-based safety filter via operator splitting and Jacobian-Free Backpropagation, enabling dimensions up to 1200 state and 400 control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CBF-based safety in end-to-end learning is hampered by computational/differentiation bottlenecks, restricting practice to low-dimensional systems; this work aims to extend safety guarantees to high-dimensional, multi-agent nonlinear control.

Method: Decomposes the QP-based safety filter using operator splitting and differentiates through it with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB), enabling scalable backpropagation while preserving hard safety through the CBF safety filter; provides theoretical justification via nonsmooth analysis.

Result: Demonstrates effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400, maintaining safety guarantees.

Conclusion: The framework enables scalable, safe end-to-end training for high-dimensional control tasks using CBFs, overcoming previous dimensionality and bottleneck limitations.

Abstract: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

</details>


### [173] [Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20675)
*Omran Ayoub,Carlos Natalino,Ali Al Housseini,Felix Foschum,Philipp Morger,Tiziano Leidi,David Hock,Paolo Monti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An explanation-based runtime verification framework checks XAI-derived explanations for each ML decision in optical-network control, ensuring coherence with physics principles before execution; if uncertain, the decision is deferred or rejected. Validated on lightpath QoT classification, intercepting many erroneous decisions while maintaining high automation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ML-driven network control is prone to incorrect decisions that can degrade service and stability; XAI offers insight into predictions, but runtime safety requires that explanations themselves be used to verify decisions before deployment.

Method: Use explanation-based runtime verification that analyzes model explanations (feature importance, interactions) for coherence and physics grounding at runtime; decisions failing these checks are deferred or rejected in the control loop; evaluated on a lightpath QoT classification use case.

Result: The approach intercepts a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving a high automation rate, demonstrating practical benefits for reliability in ML-driven optical network automation.

Conclusion: Explanation-based runtime verification is a promising mechanism to increase the reliability of ML-driven network control by leveraging explanations to gate decisions, potentially reducing service-impacting errors with limited impact on automation.

Abstract: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

</details>


### [174] [Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20694)
*Salavat Ishbulatov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Models drift between planned task budgets and actual actions as a quasi-linear Fisher market, with planned tasks as budget-constrained buyers and performed actions as divisible goods. Uses a fused signal to set valuations; employs seller reserve price and buyer cash option to ensure conservation and hard budgets and to filter junk. Adds a concave completion utility discounting progress; proves existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under a diagonal-dominance condition; validates empirically on random/adversarial instances. Finds sharp zero-entropy equilibria are fragile to affinity noise versus entropy-regularized OT; introduces a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization with a noise-adaptive regularization, facilitating reproducibility and connections to attribution and optimal transport.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the misalignment between planned effort and actual actions in personal and organizational planning systems. Provide a mechanism- and theory-backed bridge that preserves relatedness of plan and execution, avoids false stalls, and offers provable properties and practical robustness.

Method: Formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: buyers = planned tasks with budgets; goods = divisible performed actions; valuations built from fused text/structure/temporal signals. Introduce two market instruments (seller reserve price, buyer cash option) yielding conservation, a hard budget cap, and a junk-filter theorem. Add a concave completion utility that discounts progress as tasks approach their plan. Establish existence via Brouwer fixed-point and local uniqueness under a diagonal-dominance condition. Develop a de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark with affinity-noise corruption to compare equilibrium sharpness against entropy-regularized OT. Propose a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two approaches and a noise-adaptive rule for regularization strength.
