Result: Theoretical results: existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under explicit conditions; algorithm converges in standard market settings but requires new analysis due to progress-discount utility; empirical validation on random and adversarial instances shows a weakness: zero-entropy equilibria are highly sensitive to affinity noise. The entropy-regularized generalization mitigates this, aligning with entropy-regularized OT. Reproducibility parameters are reported; benchmark design isolates affinity effects.

Conclusion: Unifies multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms into a single framework for plan–execution linking. Demonstrates a tunable trade-off between sharp equilibrium and robustness to noise via entropy regularization; highlights limitations (sensitivity to affinity) and offers a noise-adaptive extension. Encourages further exploration of convergence under completion utilities and real-world deployment challenges.

Abstract: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

</details>


### [175] [CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20696)
*Mohammad Fesanghary*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CEDAR is a constraint-based method for discovering lagged causal edges in sparse autoregressive time series, using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation for screening, followed by two targeted CI tests per cross-variable lag, with at most one lag per ordered pair, and stable MCI pruning. Optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for trend-like nonstationarity. It is computationally efficient in sparse settings and edge-level interpretable, best when data are scarce and lag-1 dynamics dominate; less suitable for richer conditioning sets or higher-order/multi-lag effects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Identify lagged causal relationships in sparse autoregressive time series with edge-level interpretability, under limited data, while controlling false positives and accommodating mild nonstationarity.

Method: 1) Screen candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation. 2) Apply two targeted conditional-independence tests for each significant lag candidate. 3) Accept at most one lag per ordered pair. 4) Use a stable MCI pruning step to remove indirect edges. 5) Optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. 6) In sparse regimes, post-screening CI tests scale as O(d^2); preserves edge-level interpretability.

Result: The approach yields a sparse set of lagged edges with a fixed, quadratically scaling CI-test burden after screening, suitable for scarce data with dominant lag-1 self-dynamics; performance diminishes as data grow to reveal higher-order autoregressive effects or require richer conditioning sets.

Conclusion: CEDAR provides an interpretable, computationally efficient framework for lagged edge discovery in sparse time series with lag-1 dynamics and mild nonstationarity, but its effectiveness decreases when higher-order, simultaneous or complex conditioning is needed; it complements more expressive methods that use richer conditioning as data availability and model complexity increase.

Abstract: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

</details>


### [176] [Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20708)
*Hongju Pae*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: In an active inference agent with fast perception (z) and slow global (g) latents, the reward-free regime-switching setting shows Φ_r localizes to g and declines with training; learning effects appear only at the atom level, where decoupling flips Φ_r's sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant, with downward causation driving environmental adjustments. This suggests Φ_r is not a general scalar index of learned integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether the information-theoretic measure Φ_r (Integrated Information Decomposition) indexes learned integration in reward-free predictive agents, and how architectural structure and regime changes influence its distribution and sign.

Method: Analyze an active inference agent with a fast latent z and a slow latent g, where g is prediction-error–driven and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. Use a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol. Compute Φ_r and its atom/compositional contributions, examine how learning and decoupling affect sign and regime dependence, and identify the locus of Φ_r-relevant temporal organization.

Result: Φ_r concentrates in the slow latent g in the reward-free regime-switching setting; its aggregate magnitude is largely determined by architecture and decreases with training. The learning effect becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips Φ_r's sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These findings identify g as the architectural locus of Φ_r-relevant temporal organization in the active inference agent, arguing against reading the scalar Φ_r as a direct index of learned integration.

Conclusion: In this active inference context, Φ_r reflects architectural organization and its atomistic decomposition, not a simple scalar measure of cumulative learned integration; interpretation of Φ_r must consider latent decomposition and regime structure.

Abstract: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

</details>


### [177] [LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20734)
*Jihoon Tack,Philippe Laban,Jennifer Neville*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Static single-turn benchmarks fail to predict LLM performance when user intent evolves over a multi-turn dialogue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether LLMs can track and act on user intent as it changes during an interaction, a capability essential for effective collaborative agents.

Method: Transform static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations where user intent is incrementally revealed, revised, and redirected, while preserving original evaluation protocols to reuse existing benchmarks.

Result: Across multiple tasks, strong performance in static settings collapses in the evolving-intent setting; substantial performance drops observed across model families.

Conclusion: Current LLMs do not reliably track or act on evolving user intent in conversation, revealing a gap hidden by static evaluations and signaling a need to develop dynamic intent-tracking capabilities for future agents.

Abstract: As LLMs become more capable, they are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, taking on user-delegated tasks through iterative interaction. Yet genuine interaction is inherently dynamic: users rarely specify their intent upfront, instead disclosing, revising, and reshaping it as the conversation unfolds. Despite this, LLMs are still predominantly evaluated or trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings, leaving open a fundamental question: how well do LLMs track and act on user intent as it evolves over the course of a conversation? To study this, we introduce a framework that transforms static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations in which the user's intent evolves across turns--incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation--while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol, enabling existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without new annotation. Across multiple tasks, we surface a consistent phenomenon: strong static-setting performance does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial drops across model families. Our findings point to a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on the user's evolving intent, a capability invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

</details>


### [178] [Cardinality-Decomposed Loss: Matching Training Objectives to Relation Structure in Heterogeneous Recommendation Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20737)
*Parul Maheshwari,Amulya Paruchuri,Yiqing Zou,Alireza Sahami Shirazi,Farhad Farahani,Prakhar Mehrotra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) is proposed for heterogeneous bipartite graphs to jointly optimize for one-to-one and one-to-many relations by combining Cross-Entropy (CE) and BPR, preventing attribute embedding collapse and improving discriminability and downstream tasks; the lambda parameter trades off CE and BPR, with dataset behavior governed by semantic alignment and topology leakage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BPR, while effective for ranking, causes attribute embeddings to collapse in heterogenous graphs with mixed relation cardinalities, contaminating user/item embeddings and harming downstream tasks. A single loss is insufficient to capture multi-cardinality relations; a cardinality-aware loss is needed.

Method: Introduce CDL that couples CE (for one-to-one relations) and BPR (for one-to-many relations) within a shared encoder, and analyze the CE-BPR conflict in the encoder parameter space. Evaluate on five datasets with two structural configurations (1-1 attributes on user nodes: MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing; and on item nodes: Yelp) to assess attribute embedding discriminability. Use a lambda to balance CE and BPR; perform a lambda sweep to reveal behavior, guided by semantic alignment (attribute-to-preferences predictiveness) and topology leakage (graph connectivity encodes preferences).

Result: CDL consistently improves discriminability of attribute embeddings across datasets. Ranking performance (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal, but can degrade or conflict if the correlation is weak. The lambda sweep indicates the dataset behavior is governed by two graph properties: semantic alignment and topology leakage; a higher emphasis on CE benefits cases with low alignment, while BPR benefits high-alignment scenarios.

Conclusion: Incorporating cardinality-aware losses yields more faithful attribute representations and can improve ranking when signals are strong, with the lambda parameter enabling adaptation to data properties. Graph structure properties—semantic alignment and topology leakage—explain when ranking signals help or hurt and guide hyperparameter tuning.

Abstract: Graph Neural Networks trained on heterogenous bipartite graphs form a common basis in recommendation systems. These graphs often express relations that vary in cardinality, for example, user-item preferences are one-to-many and user-attribute features are one-to-one. Traditionally, a unique loss function is applied for all of the network components which is often Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR). While BPR works well for the recommendation task, we find that it causes attribute embeddings to collapse to near-random geometry -- a silent failure that leaves standard ranking metrics largely unaffected and therefore invisible to conventional evaluation. This in turn pollutes user node embeddings, which are shaped by both edge types simultaneously, hurting downstream tasks like personalization, segmentation, etc. Here we propose a Cardinality-Decomposed Loss (CDL) that combines both Cross Entropy (CE) and BPR to enable the model to collectively optimize for relations across cardinalities. We confirm this CE-BPR conflict by showing the two losses compete in the shared encoder's parameter space. We evaluate CDL on five datasets spanning two structural configurations -- one-to-one attributes on user nodes (MovieLens-1M, Last.fm-360K, PayPal Audience Factory, BookCrossing) and on item nodes (Yelp) -- and find that CDL consistently improves discriminability in attribute embeddings. We also show that ranking (NDCG) improves when attributes carry meaningful preference signal, but conflicts with it when the correlation is weak. We use a lambda parameter to navigate this trade-off, and a lambda-sweep reveals that dataset behavior is governed by two graph properties -- semantic alignment and topology leakage. Semantic alignment measures whether the attribute predicts preferences, while topology leakage measures whether the graph's connectivity already encodes it.

</details>


### [179] [Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion for Trustworthy Multi-Omics Multimodal Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20742)
*Mohammad Raahemi,Ali Sekhavati,Alireza Maleki,Hamid Nasiri*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ACE introduces a Confidence-weighted expansion for multimodal fusion with intra-modality generated modalities and a dual confidence mechanism, achieving better accuracy and calibration on four multi-omics datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address robustness and trustworthiness of multimodal fusion in noisy or uninformative data streams and provide a trustworthy global confidence score for final predictions in safety-critical settings.

Method: Generate new modalities by exploiting intra-modality correlations to enrich the multimodal space; apply a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweights all modalities by reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused decision.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, ROSMAP) in both classification performance and confidence calibration.

Conclusion: ACE yields more stable and robust multimodal fusion with improved predictive performance and calibrated confidence, facilitating deployment in high-stakes applications.

Abstract: Multimodal learning is a robust approach to improve predictive performance in applications such as medical prognosis. However, the clinical applicability of models that use multimodal learning is hampered by their poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams. Present fusion approaches often lack robust mechanisms for the dynamic assessment of data quality and for the provision of a trustable confidence score on the final prediction. This dissuades their deployment in safety-critical settings. To address these limitations, we introduce Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE), a novel framework to enhance the trustworthiness of multimodal fusion models. ACE first enhances the multimodal space by generating new, complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweighs all modalities by their reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused, final decision. To evaluate ACE, we used four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, and ROSMAP). ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration. Our framework provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates the use of multimodal learning in addressing high-stakes problems.

</details>


### [180] [GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20757)
*Miguel P. Bento,João Seabra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GaugeQuant uses a LogSumExp loss to break transformer symmetry, selecting a rotation-based basis to minimize activation outliers, enabling in-training quantization improvements with minimal overhead.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Transformers exhibit continuous internal symmetries that preserve outputs but hinder quantization; breaking these symmetries in training can reduce activation outliers and improve quantized model perplexity without calibration data.

Method: Add LogSumExp term to loss to break symmetry; use stop-gradient so only rotation matrices are updated; no calibration data or quantization simulation; training objective unchanged otherwise; tested on LLaMA-2 7B under W4A4 and W4A16.

Result: Perplexity improvements: W4A4 8.22 -> 6.73; W4A16 11.16 -> 5.45; competitive with post-training methods requiring frozen models and calibration data; code available.

Conclusion: In-training, data-free quantization with negligible overhead can yield substantial gains by selecting a symmetry-breaking basis, making quantized transformers more accurate with minimal disruption to the language modeling objective.

Abstract: Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

</details>


### [181] [Memory-Computation Tradeoffs in Semi Amortized Parametric Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20769)
*Shijie Pan,Agustin Castellano,Zeyu Shen,Enrique Mallada*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This work studies amortized optimization: offline memory of solved instances is used to warm-start online K-step projected gradient descent, and it derives bounds on the offline memory needed to achieve a target accuracy under a fixed online budget. It handles μ-strongly convex and β-growth objectives, reveals a phase transition in K where extra memory stops helping, provides a general framework for memory-acceleration cost, and validates findings on parameterized ridge regression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify the offline data (memory) requirements needed to achieve a specified accuracy when online computation is constrained, thereby clarifying the memory–computation–accuracy tradeoffs in learning-enabled decision systems.

Method: The offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances; the online phase retrieves a warm start via a nonparametric predictor constructed from offline solutions and performs K steps of projected gradient descent on smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain. The study provides matching upper/lower bounds for μ-strongly convex objectives and near-matching bounds for β-growth convex objectives, along with a general proof framework that isolates the memory cost of acceleration and the roles of convergence rate and Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map. Experiments employ parameterized ridge regression to validate the theory.

Result: For μ-strongly convex objectives, matching upper and lower bounds on memory ensure ε-accuracy under fixed K. For convex objectives with β-growth (β>2), near-matching bounds are obtained and a phase transition in K is identified beyond which additional memory yields no gain. A general framework quantifies memory cost and highlights two driving quantities: online convergence rate and Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the predicted tradeoffs.

Conclusion: The study characterizes the memory cost of acceleration as a function of the online convergence properties and the sensitivity of the solution map, showing substantial offline memory can reduce online iterations up to a limit. The results offer principled guidance for designing amortized optimization systems and delineate when accumulating more offline memory ceases to help.

Abstract: Learning-enabled decision systems often use offline data or computation to reduce online compute cost. Despite the empirical success of such approaches, there is limited general understanding of how much offline information is needed to achieve a desired accuracy under a fixed online computation budget. We study this question through the lens of amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances, and an online phase produces a solution to a new instance by retrieving a warm start and applying $K$ steps of projected gradient descent. We analyze this setup for smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain, using a nonparametric predictor built from the stored offline solutions. For $μ$-strongly convex objectives, we establish matching upper and lower bounds on the memory required to guarantee $\varepsilon$-accuracy under a fixed online iteration budget $K$. For convex objectives satisfying a $β$-growth condition ($β>2$), we obtain near-matching bounds and identify a phase transition in $K$ beyond which additional memory provides no benefit. We further provide a general proof framework that (i) explicitly quantifies the memory cost of acceleration---how much offline memory is required to achieve a prescribed speedup over the unaided online optimizer---and (ii) identifies two key quantities driving this cost: the convergence rate of the online optimizer and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map to the problem parameter. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the predicted memory--computation--accuracy tradeoffs.

</details>


### [182] [Toward Mechanistic Interpretability of an AI Foundation Model Fine-Tuned for Atmospheric Chemistry](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20778)
*Jason Y. Hu,Ivan Higuera-Mendieta,Patrick Obin Sturm,Makoto M. Kelp*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FM for atmospheric chemistry shows a limited alignment with true chemistry: first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen is captured, but chemical constraints are not enforced; internal representations are meteorology-centric; sparse autoencoders reveal causally relevant components that do not map cleanly to processes; framework needed to test mechanistic learning for policy relevance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether weather forecasting foundation models fine-tuned for atmospheric chemistry learn real physical/chemical mechanisms or merely statistical regularities from reanalysis data; establish a framework for mechanistic interpretability with implications for policy.

Method: Impose controlled chemical perturbations on Aurora forecasts and test against known photochemical relationships; analyze internal representations of forecasts; use sparse autoencoders to identify internal components and their causal influence on chemical predictions; examine ozone response to reactive nitrogen and the treatment of emissions features like wildfires; compare learned constraints to process-based chemical knowledge.

Result: Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce chemical constraints; generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and relaxes localized emission features toward background; internal representations remain largely organized around pretraining meteorology with limited chemistry-specific structure; sparse autoencoders reveal internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes.

Conclusion: Forecasts should be evaluated by their internal mechanisms, not solely by skill; provides a framework to test whether AI atmospheric chemistry forecasting models learn true chemical processes, with important policy implications for using such models in decision-making.

Abstract: Weather forecasting foundation models (FMs) are increasingly fine-tuned to predict air quality, offering fast global pollution forecasts at lower computational cost than conventional chemical transport models. These FMs are typically trained on reanalysis data and generate forecasts through autoregressive rollout. They do not explicitly represent governing physical or chemical processes. Therefore, high forecast skill does not reveal whether a model has learned physical mechanisms or exploits statistical regularities in its training data. Here, we present the first study of what a FM fine-tuned for atmospheric chemistry has learned by examining Microsoft's Aurora model. We impose controlled chemical perturbations on its forecasts and test them against known photochemical relationships. We then examine the internal representations that generate these forecasts. We find that Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce the chemical constraints that a process-based model encodes. It generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and relaxes localized emission features such as wildfire plumes toward background. Internally, its representations remain largely organized around the meteorology inherited during pretraining, with little structure specific to chemistry. Using sparse autoencoders, we identify internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes. This work provides a framework for testing whether AI forecasting systems learn atmospheric chemistry from reanalysis data. As these models are increasingly positioned to inform environmental policy decisions, we argue that composition forecasts should also be judged by their internal mechanisms rather than by benchmark skill alone.

</details>


### [183] [Synthetic minority data is redundant or invalid: a data-dependent validity theory and a de-biased test](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20787)
*Ahmad B. Hassanat,Ahmad S. Tarawneh,Ghada A. Altarawneh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Debiased validity of synthetic minority oversampling reveals that classical checks are systematically biased. A population-level validity metric, estimated with held-out real data, shows most synthetic data fail to be valid or informative. Across 91 methods, 3 classifiers, and diverse datasets, no approach clears both validity and information gain; an open-source pip-installable audit is released to shift the burden of proof to synthetic minority data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The conventional validation of synthetic oversampling relies on a generator-scored check that is biased toward the generating data. The study proposes a debiased, population-level validity measure to assess whether synthetic minority points truly belong to the minority class, using withheld ground truth.

Method: Define a debiased estimator for validity as P(synthetic point is minority) evaluated against withheld real data. Compare this to the classical check, which uses the generator’s own data. Conduct a large-scale audit (91 methods, 3 classifiers, datasets including medicine and finance) and include a generator designed to pass the classical check. Release an installable audit tool to assess both validity and information gain.

Result: The classical check underestimates true invalidity in 96–99% of method–imbalance-ratio cells; the debiased estimator tracks invalidity more accurately. Across the broad evaluation, gains over a trivial baseline are noise-thin (median F1 gain < 0.01) and calibration is often degraded. No method clears both validity and information gain. The authors provide a pip-installable audit to flip the burden of proof onto synthetic minority data.

Conclusion: Validity is a data property governed by class overlap: when classes are well separated, oversampling adds no value and is often harmful; when they overlap, synthetic data remain invalid. Synthetic minority data should demonstrate both validity and information gain on the data at hand, or be avoided.

Abstract: For two decades, the standard remedy for class-imbalanced learning has been to fabricate synthetic minority examples, and the standard evidence of their validity has been a check that cannot fail: synthetic points are scored against the very data that generated them. We de-bias the check. Validity becomes a population quantity -- the probability that a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class -- with a consistent estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data. Where held-out ground truth is available, the classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96-99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells, while the de-biased estimator tracks it closely. We prove validity is a property of the data, not the method: class overlap sets an invalidity floor no faithful generator escapes, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap. Across 91 methods, three classifiers, and datasets spanning medicine and finance -- including a generator engineered to pass the classical check -- none clears both bars: gains over the best trivial baseline are noise-thin (median below 0.01 F1, a decision threshold's reach), and most damage calibration. We release the audit as a pip-installable test and flip the burden of proof: synthetic minority data must now demonstrate, on the data at hand, both validity and information gain.

</details>


### [184] [Memoir: Should a Model Write to Its Memory While It Thinks?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20792)
*Jaber Jaber,Osama Jaber*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Coupled fast-memory rewrites during pondering slow early learning under fixed budget; read-only pondering outperforms on short runs; by 960 steps both arms converge to perfect recall; energy signaling robust; kernel optimization yields speedups; code provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate the impact of allowing memory rewriting within pondering iterations (coupled arm) versus a read-only pondering baseline on procedural associative recall with key interference.

Method: Two arms (81,738 parameters; 76,362 trainable) matched for compute, data, optimizer, schedule, seeds. 240 steps across 12 seeds; 960 steps across 8 seeds. Paired design per seed. Measures recall accuracy with 95% CIs. Statistical comparison via paired t-tests on seed-differences. Tracks energy margin and delta-rule forward time; reports code at GitHub.

Result: At 240 steps: coupled recall 0.5203 [0.4522,0.5883] vs read-only 0.6557 [0.5953,0.7160]. Paired difference 0.1354 [0.0431,0.2277], t(11)=3.23, p in 95% [0.0431,0.2277], read-only favored in 10/12 seeds. After 960 steps, both reach 1.0000, indicating a learning-speed penalty under fixed budget rather than a capability penalty. No observed energy-signal failure; energy margin persisted. Kernel restructuring reduced forward delta-rule time from 0.907 ms to 0.351 ms on the device.

Conclusion: Coupled memory rewriting imposes a learning-speed penalty under fixed budget; not a demonstrated capability penalty. Ceiling effects limit conclusions about non-saturating tasks. Energy signaling remains robust to rewriting. Implementations yield speedups in forward computation; code available for replication.

Abstract: Memoir combines per-sample fast memory, shared slow parameters, variable-depth latent recurrence, and a future-latent energy objective. We test its riskiest coupling: each pondering iteration may rewrite the fast tier that the same iteration reads. On procedural associative recall with key interference, we compare a coupled arm against an otherwise identical read-only pondering arm. Both arms contain 81,738 parameters, including 76,362 trainable parameters, and use matched declared forward multiply-accumulate counts, data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. After 240 training steps across 12 seeds, coupled recall is 0.5203 with a 95 percent interval of [0.4522, 0.5883], while read-only recall is 0.6557 with [0.5953, 0.7160]. The arms are paired per seed, and the read-only lead of 0.1354 gives a paired t of 3.23 on 11 degrees of freedom with a 95 percent interval of [0.0431, 0.2277] on the difference, winning on 10 of 12 seeds. After 960 steps across 8 seeds, both arms reach 1.0000, so the measured effect is a learning-speed penalty at a fixed budget, not a demonstrated capability penalty. That longer control is ceiling limited, leaving convergence on a non-saturating task unmeasured. A predicted failure in which memory rewriting corrupts the energy signal did not occur: the energy margin grew and held. Kernel restructuring also reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907 ms to 0.351 ms on the stated device. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/RightNow-AI/Memoir

</details>


### [185] [External Clustering Validation by the Homogeneity-Parsimony Trade-off](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20799)
*Andreas Tiffeau-Mayer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores for clustering, built on a refined information bottleneck, with set-matching and pair-based extensions and ROC-level interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scalar clustering metrics often obscure the trade-off between preserving class-relevant information and avoiding unnecessary fragmentation; a normalized, principled score system is needed that does not reward lossy compression.

Method: Define normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores within a modified information bottleneck framework that does not reward lossy compression; establish monotonicity under cluster refinement; derive set-matching and pair-based variants; show that the pair-based trade-off recovers ROC; apply framework to feature selection and algorithm comparison.

Result: Theoretical properties proven: scores vary monotonically with refinement; unified evaluation criteria across formulations; set-matching and pair-based scores derived; in the pair-based setting, homogeneity–parsimony trade-off mirrors ROC curves; demonstrated utility for feature selection, algorithm comparison, and Pareto-optimal clustering solutions.

Conclusion: Jointly considering these scores clarifies clustering operating points, identifies Pareto-optimal solutions, and extends evaluation beyond entropy-based measures into set-matching and pair-based contexts.

Abstract: Scalar metrics are often used to evaluate clusterings against known classes, but they can obscure a fundamental trade-off: clusterings should be informative about class labels while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation. Here we describe normalized scores of cluster homogeneity and parsimony that quantify this trade-off. These scores build on the information bottleneck principle, modified to not reward lossy compression. We show by example and mathematical proof that our definitions of these scores have the intuitive property of varying monotonically under cluster refinement in contrast to related proposals. Extending the information-theoretic framework beyond Shannon entropies, we furthermore derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts of the homogeneity and parsimony scores. These unify commonly used evaluation criteria and show that, in the pair-based setting, the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the receiver operating characteristic of binary classifiers. We demonstrate the framework's utility for feature selection and algorithm comparison, illustrating how considering scores jointly can clarify clustering operating points and identify Pareto-optimal solutions.

</details>


### [186] [New Complexity-Theoretic Frontiers of Tractability for Neural Network Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20811)
*Cornelius Brand,Robert Ganian,Mathis Rocton*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper presents new polynomial-time training algorithms for specific neural network architectures with linear or ReLU activations, notably ReLU nets with hidden out-degree of 1 and linear nets under a data-throughput condition, advancing tractability beyond prior work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the computational complexity of optimally training neural networks and push the boundary of tractable architectures beyond the currently known results for linear and ReLU activations.

Method: For ReLU networks, develop a polynomial-time training algorithm for architectures where hidden neurons have out-degree 1. For linear activations, derive a polynomial-time algorithm under a novel data-throughput condition, enabling optimal training.

Result: Establishes polynomial-time tractability for ReLU networks with out-degree-1 hidden nodes and identifies the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class of linear-activation networks under the throughput condition.

Conclusion: Demonstrates that certain architectural constraints yield tractable optimal training, expanding the frontier of tractable neural-network training; invites further work to generalize these conditions and understand the limits of tractability.

Abstract: In spite of the fundamental role of neural networks in contemporary machine learning research, our understanding of the computational complexity of optimally training neural networks remains incomplete even when dealing with the simplest kinds of activation functions. Indeed, while there has been a number of very recent results that establish ever-tighter lower bounds for the problem under linear and ReLU activation functions, less progress has been made towards the identification of novel polynomial-time tractable network architectures. In this article we obtain novel algorithmic upper bounds for training linear- and ReLU-activated neural networks to optimality which push the boundaries of tractability for these problems beyond the previous state of the art. In particular, for ReLU networks we establish the polynomial-time tractability of all architectures where hidden neurons have an out-degree of $1$, improving upon the previous algorithm of Arora, Basu, Mianjy and Mukherjee. On the other hand, for networks with linear activation functions we identify the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class of networks by obtaining an algorithm that can optimally train network architectures satisfying a novel data throughput condition.

</details>


### [187] [Robust Asynchronous Q-Learning under Reward and State Corruption via Batching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20822)
*Sreejeet Maity,Aritra Mitra*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BR-Async-Q is an epoch-based robust Q-learning algorithm that batched online data to defend against adversarially corrupted feedback (both rewards and states) under the Huber contamination model. It provides a high-probability l_infty error bound that matches vanilla Q-learning up to a small additive term dependent on the corruption fraction, and offers the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under joint reward and state corruption; with corruption limited to rewards, the bound's dependence on corruption is minimax optimal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robust reinforcement learning in harsh environments where an adversary can contaminate observations and rewards. The goal is to learn an near-optimal policy despite data corruptions, with theoretical guarantees against Huber-type contamination.

Method: An epoch-based, batched (batch-wise) robust Q-learning algorithm named BR-Async-Q. It partitions the data stream into batches to reduce variance and constructs robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using batched data. The algorithm combines asynchronous Q-learning with robust statistical estimation to mitigate the effect of corrupted samples.

Result: The authors prove a high-probability l_infty error bound for BR-Async-Q that matches vanilla Q-learning up to an additive term that scales with the corruption fraction. This constitutes the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under joint reward and state corruption. When only rewards are corrupted, the bound’s dependence on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal.

Conclusion: This work advances robust RL by providing formal guarantees for asynchronous Q-learning under both reward and state data corruption. It highlights batching as a viable strategy to reduce variance in robust updates and establishes optimal rates in the reward-only corruption regime. Potential future directions include empirical validation, extending to function approximation, and exploring different corruption/adversarial models.

Abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning in harsh environments, we consider the problem of learning an optimal policy subject to adversarially corrupted feedback. Specifically, at each time-step, an adversary can perturb both the reward and state observations of the learner following the Huber contamination model. To defend against such data corruption, we propose {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}}: a novel, epoch-based, robust \(Q\)-learning algorithm built upon two key ideas: (i) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using such batched data. We prove a high-probability $\ell_\infty$ error bound for {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}} that matches that for vanilla \(Q\)-learning, up to a small additive term that scales with the fraction of corrupted samples. To our knowledge, this provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous \(Q\)-learning subject to both reward and state corruption. Furthermore, when only rewards are corrupted, the dependence of our algorithm's bound on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal.

</details>


### [188] [Beyond Heavy Log Curation: Perplexity-Based APT Detection via Unsupervised, Context-Augmented Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20832)
*Shoya Otsu,Kei Suzuki,Toshiaki Koike-Akino,Jing Liu,Ye Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A perplexity-based detector CAPTAIN uses pre-trained language models with minimal preprocessing to detect APT-related activity in long logs by encoding recent history via an encoder and a Q-Former-style bridge, injecting compact context into the decoder input, and applying smoothing to perplexity; it achieves competitive performance on APT benchmarks with reduced data-preprocessing effort.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce analyst workload and engineering cost by leveraging general pre-trained LMs with domain-agnostic preprocessing, addressing the scalability challenge of detecting sparse attack signals in large-scale logs.

Method: Encode recent history with an encoder; use a Q-Former-style bridge to create compact context tokens; inject these tokens into the decoder input so perplexity reflects temporal context; compute perplexity as the detection score; apply smoothing filters to the perplexity time series for stability.

Result: CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines on APT-oriented benchmarks and remains robust when inputs are substantially less curated, reducing development and operational cost of advanced log preprocessing.

Conclusion: A scalable, low-preprocessing perplexity-based detection approach that leverages general LMs to robustly detect APT activity, offering reduced engineering effort while maintaining competitive performance.

Abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) remain difficult to detect because only a small fraction of events in large-scale logs are attack-related, and investigation is expensive and hard to scale. Prior machine-learning approaches can reduce analyst workload, but they often rely on heavily curated training data and sophisticated preprocessing pipelines. Building and maintaining such pipelines require substantial domain expertise and engineering cost. Motivated by insights from a study of a strong APT detection baseline, we propose CAPTAIN (Context-Augmented Perplexity-based Threat Activity log detectIoN), a perplexity-based detector that leverages general, pre-trained language models with minimal, domain-agnostic preprocessing, enabling robust scoring of long, minimally processed log entries. CAPTAIN encodes recent history with an encoder model and a Q-Former-style bridge, then injects the compact context tokens into the decoder input so that perplexity reflects temporal context. To improve stability, CAPTAIN additionally applies smoothing filters to the perplexity time series. Across APT-oriented benchmarks, CAPTAIN competes with strong existing baselines and remains robust under substantially less curated inputs, that reduces the development and operational cost of advanced log preprocessing.

</details>


### [189] [Offline RL with Hierarchical Action Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20834)
*Ahad Jawaid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HiQC combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking to enable unbiased k-step backups in offline goal-conditioned RL, improving long-horizon tasks on OGBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon value estimation in offline RL suffers from compounding errors; hierarchical methods reduce horizon but often rely on myopic, biased low-level controllers and still struggle with long chains.

Method: Introduce Offline HiQC: condition the low-level critic on temporally extended action sequences (action chunks) and perform high-level latent planning. This dual horizon compression yields unbiased k-step value backups. The approach includes theoretical analysis showing a tighter error bound under a bounded per-backup error model, and empirical evaluation on the OGBench suite against baselines.

Result: HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance among the compared methods on OGBench, with the most pronounced gains on long-horizon navigation tasks (e.g., humanoid-giant).

Conclusion: Dual decomposition—latent high-level planning plus low-level action chunking—tightens value error bounds and effectively scales offline goal-conditioned RL to long horizons, outperforming standard hierarchical or flat-chunk baselines.

Abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning general-purpose policies from static datasets. However, scaling these methods to long-horizon tasks remains a challenge due to the curse of horizon, where value estimation errors can compound through long chains of bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical approaches mitigate this by decomposing tasks into subgoals, yet they often rely on low-level controllers that suffer from myopic execution and biased value estimates. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Implicit Q-Chunking (HiQC), an offline goal-conditioned RL algorithm that combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking. By conditioning the low-level critic on temporally extended action sequences, HiQC enables unbiased k-step value backups, compressing the horizon at both the planning and execution levels. We theoretically demonstrate that this dual decomposition results in a tighter bound on value error under a bounded per-backup error model compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking alone. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance among the compared methods on the OGBench suite, with its largest gains on long-horizon navigation tasks such as humanoid-giant.

</details>


### [190] [Multilevel Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing with Scale-Aware Neural Recovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20857)
*Amirhossein Nouranizadeh,Sarang Rajendra Patil,Alan John Varghese,Varsha Narayanan,Amit Chakraborty,Mengjia Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GWCS compresses graph signals via spectral graph wavelets with a multilevel importance sampler and scale-aware GNN, achieving high fidelity and compression on synthetic and PDE datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate data requirements and data-preparation costs in scientific ML (neural operators, PINNs) by efficient offline compression of graph signals while preserving essential information.

Method: Represent signals with the spectral graph wavelet transform; use a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler to retain high-energy coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio; reconstruct signals from sparse coefficients using a scale-aware graph neural network.

Result: On synthetic approximately band-limited graphs and PDE mesh datasets (Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, Dynamic Stall), GWCS achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantially better data compression than graph sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines.

Conclusion: GWCS provides an effective, interpretable compressed representation for graph signals, reducing data requirements for training physics-informed ML models and neural operators, with potential applicability to a broad class of graph-based scientific data.

Abstract: Scientific machine learning methods such as neural operators and physics-informed neural networks have advanced engineering applications and inverse problems, but their training typically requires large volumes of simulated data. This makes data preparation and model training expensive. We propose Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing (GWCS), a learning-based framework for offline compression of graph signals by representing them as sparse, interpretable wavelet-domain representations using the spectral graph wavelet transform. The framework combines a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler, which retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio, with a scale-aware graph neural network that reconstructs the signal from the sparse coefficients. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic approximately band-limited graph signals over random graphs and four PDE simulation datasets over meshes, which include Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, and Dynamic Stall. We compare against graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to existing benchmarks.

</details>


### [191] [Position Bias is Hidden Behind Ceiling Effects: A Permutation Diagnostic for LLM Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20864)
*Hiroki Tamba*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exhaustive answer-order permutation reveals position bias in LLM MC evaluations within a Goldilocks zone; introduces inspect_permute; finds two bias mechanisms; bounds detectable region; open-source under MIT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Position bias confounds capability comparisons; single-shuffle measurements mix bias with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity; exhaustive permutation aims to isolate the bias signal.

Method: Run exhaustive answer-order permutations per question; compute chi-squared / Cramer’s V; bootstrap confidence intervals; apply to four vendors across five MMLU subjects; 24k API calls at temperature 0; preregistered predictions via SHA-256 hash; data split with half observed.

Result: Detectable position bias only within roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone; below that, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above that, ceiling effects compress variance; two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity in a narrow capability band); frontier-tier models lie above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased.

Conclusion: Brackets the detectable region for position-bias measurement; makes the central question verifiable in a rigorous form; open-source package, data, and preregistration under MIT; complements prior ceiling-effect work (arXiv:2606.26185).

Abstract: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is widely cited as a confound in capability comparisons, but published measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles whose results confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. I introduce inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports the chi-squared / Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. I apply the tool across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, with falsifier predictions pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed. Position bias turns out to be statistically detectable only within a roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress the variance below the chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells separate into two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. Together with the ceiling-effect characterisation in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and makes the field central question askable in a verifiable form. Package, data, preregistration under MIT.

</details>


### [192] [TwistedMerge: Certified Higher-Order Diagnostics and Abstention for Model Merging](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20887)
*Ting Gong,Shitan Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TwistedMerge reframes model merging as a finite descent problem with local checkpoints and transitions, delivering a conservative, abstention-based certification pipeline. It shows that cycle residuals are not reliably predictive of merge degradation and establishes a falsifiable framework for safe merging through inverse-consistency, centrality, and closure tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global consistency in merging multiple independently trained or fine-tuned models cannot be guaranteed by pairwise alignability alone. A formal, certifiable framework is needed to identify true obstructions and to abstain when merging would be unsafe.

Method: Formulates merging as a descent with checkpoint-local objects, transitions as alignment maps, and cycle products as residuals. TwistedMerge splits into fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a chosen comparison complex, and analysis of nonabelian holonomy. A residual becomes a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains or returns a fallback (ordinary or synchronized). The paper proves a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity, plus experiments including planted defects, central systems, noisy estimates, and an audit of low-rank adapters; finally, tests on natural checkpoint collections.

Result: The policy yields abstention rather than unsafe merges in many cases; cycle residuals do not reliably predict degradation, and no natural central or period-index class is certified. Naive factor averaging is shown to depend on the GLr representative, while global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD demonstrate stability. The framework provides a falsifiable certification/abstention approach for model merging, and descent theory is positioned as a practical, test-driven tool for safe composition of models.

Conclusion: TwistedMerge demonstrates a principled, conservative approach to model merging with explicit tests that promote abstention in uncertain cases. It positions descent theory as a falsifiable framework for certification and highlights the limits of cycle-based diagnostics, while offering robust alternatives (global synchronization, dense-delta SVD) when conditions permit.

Abstract: Model merging combines independently trained or fine-tuned models, but pairwise alignability does not imply globally consistent alignment. We formulate merging as a finite descent problem in which checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge is a conservative certification pipeline that separates fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a specified comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains and returns an ordinary or synchronized fallback. We prove a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, showing that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover the predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior, while noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on the tested controls. A trained low-rank-adapter audit shows that naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoint collections, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified. The results position descent theory as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework.

</details>


### [193] [Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20890)
*Hyeong-Gun Joo,Songnam Hong,Dong-Joon Shin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an information-theoretically secure, single-round aggregation framework for sign-based federated learning, using MV polynomial, inverse-form exponent reduction, and secure multiplication to minimize communication/latency while ensuring robustness via MDS-based decoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address privacy risks of exposing gradient signs in sign-based FL and the inefficiency of existing secure aggregation schemes, enabling low-overhead, end-to-end security for on-device learning.

Method: Compute the majority-vote (MV) polynomial through a single-round secure multiplication with linear offline complexity; apply inverse-form exponent reduction to halve MV polynomial degree; use MDS-code-based decoding to tolerate dropouts and adversaries, ensuring information-theoretic security under honest-majority; reveal only the final aggregated sign to the server.

Result: Online communication reduced up to 99.5% and latency up to 85.7% versus conventional approaches; robustness against dropouts and adversarial behavior yields accuracy gains up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively; end-to-end security with only the aggregated sign exposed.

Conclusion: A practical foundation for scalable, low-latency, information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL, combining efficient secure multiplication, degree reduction, and MDS-based robustness.

Abstract: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

</details>


### [194] [HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20896)
*Kritanu Chattopadhyay,Soumya Chatterjee,Ondrej Krejcar,Debotosh Bhattacharjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A dual-graph hierarchical model that predicts spatial gene expression from H&E with domain-aware edge typing and PPI-informed gene graphs; yields better correlation and calibrated uncertainty across tissue types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome cost/complexity of spatial transcriptomics and lack of tissue-structure-aware predictions; provide uncertainty estimates for clinical deployment.

Method: Two graphs: spot graph with Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolution, edges typed as inter-domain, intra-domain, boundary via Leiden clustering; gene-level graph fusing STRING-DB protein–protein interactions with tissue-specific co-expression via learned attention gating; evidential uncertainty estimation for calibrated confidence intervals.

Result: Outperforms 13 baselines across six Visium sections from breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissues; gains robust under multi-seed reproducibility and negative controls; ablations show domain-aware edges and hierarchical depth are necessary; calibrated uncertainty identifies low-confidence predictions for pathologist review.

Conclusion: HierarchicalDAEW delivers accurate, interpretable spatial gene-expression predictions with calibrated uncertainty, leveraging tissue architecture and prior biology; promising for clinical use with built-in reliability checks.

Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

</details>


### [195] [Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20908)
*Quazi Ishtiaque Mahmud,Nesreen K. Ahmed,Ali Jannesari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CudaPerf: a reflective RL framework for GPU code generation that combines verifiable execution rewards with structural code-aware rewards. It uses a two-stage training pipeline (offline pairwise ranking via contrastive learning, then online RL with a unified reward for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency) and iterative refinement. Evaluated on C->CUDA and PyTorch->CUDA tasks, it surpasses strong baselines with up to 5x speedups and up to 17% correctness gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing RL-based rewards predominantly rely on outcome signals (e.g., correctness, speed). For GPU code, structural properties (memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, synchronization patterns) critically influence performance but are underutilized in RL signals. Incorporating such signals can guide generation toward optimized CUDA implementations.

Method: Two-stage approach: (1) offline pairwise ranking using contrastive comparisons to distinguish strong vs weak candidates; (2) online RL training jointly optimizing for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency via a unified reward. Iterative refinement uses execution feedback to progressively improve candidates. Dataset with 2.9k C→CUDA and 1k PyTorch→CUDA programs, each with diverse inputs and multiple CUDA implementations. Evaluation on benchmarks for both translation directions.

Result: CudaPerf outperforms strong baselines (Qwen-3-32B for C→CUDA; CUDA Agent for PyTorch→CUDA) with up to 5× speedup and 3.32× speedup, and gains of 17% (C→CUDA) and 7% (PyTorch→CUDA) in correctness.

Conclusion: Integrating verifiable execution rewards with structural, code-aware rewards yields substantial gains in GPU-targeted code generation. The two-stage learning and iterative refinement framework effectively leverages execution feedback and structural signals, suggesting broader applicability to optimizing compilers and other performance-critical code generation tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capacity of LLMs for optimized code generation. However, existing RLVR approaches primarily rely on outcome-based signals such as correctness and speedup, overlooking performance-critical structural properties of programs that are essential for generating optimized code. In this work, we propose CudaPerf, a reflective RL framework that incorporates both verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards derived from parallelization features (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy, Arithmatic Intensity, and synchronization patterns). CudaPerf operates in two stages: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong and weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through a unified reward signal. To further enhance learning, CudaPerf utilizes iterative refinement using execution feedback enabling progressive improvement of generated candidates. We also introduce a dataset comprising 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs, each paired with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations encompassing diverse optimization strategies. CudaPerf is evaluated across multiple benchmarks comprising both C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations. Empirical findings suggest that CudaPerf significantly outperforms strong baselines, including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA) by achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively.

</details>


### [196] [Three-Pronged Spectral Control for Federated Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20914)
*Shiva Raj Pokhrel,Dipsan Bhattarai,Anwar Walid*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRISHUL is a spectral-control framework for robust federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) that mitigates non-IID client heterogeneity in LoRA-like setups. It uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to enable exact aggregation, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers via a concave water-filling budget rule. It incurs negligible extra computation/communication and improves convergence, stability, and final performance across vision and language benchmarks, especially under strong heterogeneity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Federated PEFT with LoRA achieves communication efficiency but suffers from fragility under non-IID client data due to spectrally misaligned local update subspaces, leading to high-variance aggregation and poor transfer globally.

Method: (TRISHUL) Shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases enable algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates. Before upload, apply nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components. Adaptation heads are allocated non-uniformly across layers using a concave water-filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Shrinkage is applied only to small core matrices to keep computation and communication overhead minimal, and no additional per-round communication is introduced beyond the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. The approach adheres to the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting, without formal privacy guarantees.

Result: Empirical evaluation across CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B shows that TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with larger gains as data heterogeneity increases.

Conclusion: TRISHUL provides a robust spectral-control mechanism for federated PEFT that addresses spectral misalignment in non-IID federated learning with negligible overhead. It enhances convergence and final accuracy across modalities, though it lacks formal privacy guarantees and relies on shared bases and shrinkage choices that may influence certain subtleties of the learned representations.

Abstract: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables communication-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models on decentralized edge data, but it remains fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity. In low-rank adaptation (LoRA), different clients may learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, causing high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. We propose TRISHUL, a spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT. TRISHUL follows the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting but does not itself provide formal privacy guarantees. TRISHUL uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to obtain algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Because shrinkage is performed only on small core matrices, TRISHUL adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication over the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. Across vision and language benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.

</details>


### [197] [Best-of-Evidence: Best-of-N Selection under Partial Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20950)
*Cenwei Zhang,Teng Fang,Yuxia Wang,Derek Li,Bryan Dai,Lei You*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BoE extends Best-of-N by operating on a fixed pool and using a signed candidate-factor graph to manage partial, verifiable evidence under a limited budget, improving decision quality when evidence is reliable and decoupled from full-response verification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: BoN assumes fully verifiable complete candidates, but many vision-language tasks offer only partial verifications (e.g., findings, spans, regions) and allow conflicting claims across candidates. A framework is needed to allocate limited evidence to influence selection under partial verification.

Method: Introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE) with a fixed candidate pool, a signed candidate–factor graph to encode reusable claims, and a score-based controller that allocates a budget to evidence actions. Zero budget reduces BoE to standard BoN; theoretical results characterize evidence capacity and query efficiency; experiments in medical VQA assess performance.

Result: Theoretically, residual evidence capacity bounds improvement and shared factor queries can achieve O(log K) vs Θ(K) query complexity in a factor-code model. Empirically, BoE improves fixed-pool selection and rescues some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant across four medical VQA settings; it also reveals limits set by channel quality and candidate generation.

Conclusion: BoE formalizes selection under partial verification, delivering a practical controller and exposing the conditions under which evidence-driven gains are achievable; gains are not universal and depend on evidence quality and how well claims are represented and shared across candidates.

Abstract: BoN improves model outputs by sampling several candidates and selecting one with a proxy score, but it assumes that complete candidates can be evaluated reliably. Many vision-language tasks instead provide only partial verification: a finding, span, value, region, or relation may be checkable even when no dependable whole-response verifier exists. Moreover, the same claim may recur across candidates with opposing stances, allowing one observation to support part of the pool and contradict another. We introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE), an inference-time selection framework that keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims with a signed candidate--factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can change the final choice. BoE formalizes selection under partial verification and provides a practical score-based controller, with the zero-budget case recovering the underlying BoN decision. Theoretically, we show that residual evidence capacity limits any evidence-driven improvement and that shared factor queries can achieve an O(log K) versus Θ(K) query separation in a factor-code model. Common-ledger experiments on four medical VQA settings show that BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant, while also revealing the channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that prevent universal gains.

</details>


### [198] [The Weight of Silence: A Causal Case for Weights Over the Scratchpad in Latent Chess Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20952)
*Ishan S. Kshirsagar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Reinforcement learning with a staged latent-reasoning curriculum improves chess performance and steals robustness, not reliance on internal thoughts as an inference-time scratchpad.


<details>
