More broadly, the results support a growing body of evidence indicating that effective representation-level unlearning requires objectives that act directly on latent representations rather than on increasingly sophisticated weight-selection strategies.

</details>


### [223] [Emergent Misalignment Recruits a Pre-existing Persona Subspace](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21356)
*Mohammed Suhail B Nadaf*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Emergent misalignment arises from a reusable low-rank persona subspace; projecting it out during fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To explain why narrowly targeted misalignment generalizes to unrelated questions and whether a latent persona structure governs this generalization.

Method: From a frozen instruction-tuned model, extract per-domain persona subspaces via contrastive teacher forcing; identify a shared low-rank core across four domains; test effects of the first optimizer step, subspace projection in the residual stream, projection in the weight gradient, and post-hoc edits; compare with injecting the subspace into a never-fine-tuned model; evaluate on a 14B model; examine data distribution effects across four domains.

Result: Found a common low-rank core spanning domains; the core has most of its mass outside a separate style core; projecting the subspace from the residual stream during fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (reducing judged generations from 27.7% to 0%), while a matched-rank random subspace does nothing. Injecting the subspace into a never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose (up to ~45%). Projections on the weight gradient are inert, and post-hoc edits do not remove the structure; the misalignment trace re-forms under edits. Spreading bad data across domains yields more broad misalignment than either weight superposition or diversity alone. The results come from a single 14B model; provenance and remediation details remain open, though the preventive subspace intervention also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.

Conclusion: Broad misalignment appears to arise from a transferable, latent subspace (a persona-like structure) present before fine-tuning; targeted intervention on this subspace can prevent misalignment and also erases the narrow behavior, highlighting a potential mechanism behind emergent misalignment.

Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow stream of bad advice can make it broadly misaligned on questions unrelated to the training data, a phenomenon called emergent misalignment. We ask why the narrow lesson generalizes at all, and we find that narrow fine-tuning recruits a persona structure that is present in the model before the fine-tune exists. From a frozen instruction-tuned model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct) we extract per-domain persona subspaces by contrastive teacher forcing and find that 4 unrelated domains share one low-rank core at 657x a random-subspace null, with 82% of that core lying outside a style core built at matched diversity. The literal first optimizer step of fine-tuning on insecure code climbs a broad-misalignment margin harder than the same code framed as educational, and forecasts realized margin movement out to 375 steps. Projecting the subspace out of the residual stream throughout fine-tuning prevents broad misalignment (27.7% to 0.0% of judged generations) while a matched-rank random subspace changes nothing; injecting it into the never-fine-tuned model induces misalignment that grows with dose to 45.4%, past the fine-tuned model it is measured against. The same projection applied to the weight gradient is inert, and three post-hoc weight edits leave the disposition in place: the sharpest edit suppresses the behavior rather than removing it, and the ablated structure re-forms inside the subspace the edit cleared. Spreading a fixed budget of bad data across 4 domains produces more broad misalignment than mechanical weight superposition and matched diversity jointly account for. All measurements come from one model at 14B; the extraction is from an aligned instruction-tuned checkpoint, which leaves the structure's provenance open; and the intervention that prevents misalignment also abolishes the narrow trained behavior.

</details>


### [224] [Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21366)
*Hossein Mobahi,Peter L. Bartlett*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HOPE proposes a Hilbert-space progressive encoding framework for neural network compression, modeling neurons as rank-1 Hilbert–Schmidt operators to unify pruning, neuron merging, and macro-block eviction via low-rank subspace projections; data-free and hyperparameter-free, with proof-of-concept demonstrations in compression and fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand and decompose learned representations in deep networks by tying learning to compression, addressing scale-symmetry and architectural biases in standard compression heuristics, and enabling a unified, architecture-agnostic analysis across layers.

Method: Represent neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators in a Hilbert space; use low-rank subspace projections to realize pruning and neuron merging; extend the framework to macro blocks to cover multi-layer constructs like residual connections; operate in a data-free and hyperparameter-free manner, providing a unified metric for decisions across diverse architectures.

Result: Conceptual framework with proof-of-concept experiments demonstrating potential for model compression and fine-tuning, illustrating the viability of a continuous, operator-based approach to representation deconstruction.

Conclusion: HOPE provides a unified, data-free, hyperparameter-free scheme for progressive encoding in neural networks, enabling unbiased architectural decisions across heterogeneous layers and pointing to a promising direction for representation analysis and compression research.

Abstract: Deep neural networks encode complex representations, but deconstructing this internal knowledge remains a challenge. Given the link between learning and compression, network compression offers a promising lens to analyze this knowledge. However, standard compression heuristics often suffer from scale symmetries and architectural biases. To resolve these, we introduce Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE), a mathematical framework to gradually deconstruct the representations in trained network weights.
  HOPE shifts network compression from the discrete domain into a Hilbert space of continuous functions. By modeling individual neurons as rank-1 Hilbert-Schmidt operators, HOPE unifies pruning and neuron merging as low-rank subspace projection. Extending this formulation, HOPE introduces macro block eviction to encompass multi-layer structures like entire residual pathways under the same unified metric. This unified approach enables unbiased architectural decisions across layers with different types and sizes. HOPE is a data-free and hyperparameter-free framework. We present proof-of-concept experiments in model compression and fine-tuning to highlight the practical potential of our theory.

</details>


### [225] [Mean-to-Score Discrete Diffusion: Posterior-Mean Denoisers for Score Entropy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21372)
*Jingyuan Li,Xiaoyi Jiang,Yixuan Jiang,Wei Liu,Yi Zhu,Zuoqiang Shi,Pipi Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SEDD can violate Bayes realizability; projecting scores onto the bridge polytope fixes negative weights and improves generative performance. The proposed mean-to-score (M2S) maps clean-token posterior means to exact scores, improving CTMC-based diffusion across budgets, with strong CIFAR-10 and OpenWebText results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure that discrete diffusion score vectors are jointly realizable as posteriors under the forward kernel, addressing violations from positivity alone and reducing invalid sampling weights.

Method: 1) Project raw scores onto the bridge polytope to enforce Bayes realizability. 2) Introduce mean-to-score (M2S): map a clean-token posterior mean to a score via a kernel-dependent linear transformation, applicable to coordinate-wise CTMC with mild support conditions. 3) Analyze uniform corruption (maps simplex to bridge polytope) and absorbing-mask corruption (recovers MD4). 4) Empirically compare on CIFAR-10 and OpenWebText-scale models, across sampling budgets.

Result: Projection onto the bridge polytope eliminates negative pre-normalization weights and improves external generative PPL from 203.6 to 175.1 without changing the sampler. M2S achieves CIFAR-10 test BPD 3.129 (down from 3.173) and improved FID-50k (specific numbers not stated). A 170M-parameter M2S trained on ~262B tokens yields PPL 143.3 at 128 steps vs 183.6 for the strongest pure-uniform baseline, outperforming SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints at all tested budgets.

Conclusion: M2S provides a general, exact mapping from posterior means to scores for CTMC-based discrete diffusion, enforcing Bayes realizability, removing negative weights, and delivering consistent gains across datasets and model scales.

Abstract: Score Entropy Discrete Diffusion (SEDD) parameterizes discrete reverse processes with unconstrained positive score ratios. While positivity guarantees nonnegative reverse jump rates, it does not ensure Bayes realizability: ratios at a noisy state need not be jointly induced by any clean-token posterior under the forward kernel. The score-entropy loss has the correct population optimum but does not enforce this constraint away from it. In a trained pure-uniform SEDD checkpoint, roughly one quarter of complete score vectors violate the coordinate box, while more than half lie inside it yet remain materially incompatible with any valid posterior. Such violations can produce negative pre-normalization weights in finite-step sampling. Projecting raw scores onto the bridge polytope removes all observed negative weights and improves external generative PPL from $203.6$ to $175.1$ without changing the sampler. We introduce \emph{mean-to-score} (M2S), which predicts a clean-token posterior mean and converts it to the score through an exact kernel-dependent linear map. The construction applies to any known coordinate-wise continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) satisfying a mild support condition. For uniform corruption, it maps the probability simplex onto the bridge polytope; for absorbing-mask corruption, the resulting objective recovers MD4 exactly. In a controlled 28.4M-parameter CIFAR-10 comparison, M2S lowers test BPD from $3.173$ to $3.129$ and FID-50k from $\CifarSEDDFID$ to $\CifarMtwoSFID$. A 170M-parameter M2S model trained on about 262B OpenWebText token slots outperforms the evaluated pure-uniform SEDD, GIDD, and Neural CTMC checkpoints at every tested sampling budget, reaching generative PPL $143.3$ at 128 steps versus $183.6$ for the strongest pure-uniform baseline.

</details>


### [226] [A Diffusion-Model Subpopulation Digital Twin for Mobile Health Deployment: A Case Study on the HeartSteps Intervention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21403)
*Ziping Xu,Yuyi Chang,Chenshun Ni,Nithin Sugavanam,Asim H. Gazi,Pedja Klasnja,Emre Ertin,Susan A. Murphy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A conditional diffusion-based digital twin (JITAI-Twin) for simulating target populations to vet JITAI algorithms before deployment; validated on HeartSteps data, outperforming simpler simulators, enabling pre-deployment testing of online algorithms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prevent burden and disengagement from poorly designed algorithms by vetting online algorithms in realistic simulated users before real-life deployment; require temporally consistent, adaptable digital twins that can be updated with multiple data sources.

Method: Develop JITAI-Twins using a temporally consistent conditional time-series diffusion model. Three-phase updating: (1) pre-train on a large observational dataset, (2) fine-tune on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, (3) inference-time calibration to the next target population from domain-scientist expertise. Validate by treating successive HeartSteps deployments (v2–v4) as upcoming studies to assess the twin's fidelity in reproducing temporal and between-participant structure versus simpler simulators.

Result: The JITAI-Twin reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators, suggesting it can be used to simulate a target deployment before it runs and inform online algorithm design decisions.

Conclusion: JITAI-Twins offer a practical, validated workflow to pre-simulate target deployments for JITAI design, supporting safer and more effective online decision-making before real-world rollout.

Abstract: Mobile-health interventions increasingly use online learning and decision making algorithms to personalize when to nudge users toward healthier behavior, but a poorly designed algorithm can burden and disengage participants. New algorithm design decisions should therefore be vetted against realistic simulated users before each real-life deployment. We propose a method to develop ``JITAI-Twins'': digital twins of a target subpopulation for comparing candidate online algorithms before a just-in-time adaptive intervention (JITAI) deployment. The method builds on a conditional time-series diffusion model that is temporally consistent (future actions do not affect the generated past), and it supports repeated updating from three sources of information, in three steps: pre-training on a large observational dataset, fine-tuning on small prior intervention deployments in related populations, and inference-time calibration to the next target population from domain-scientist expertise. We validate the twin at each pre-deployment stage of the long-running HeartSteps series (v2 through v4) of physical-activity suggestion intervention deployments, treating each successive deployment as an upcoming study. The proposed method reproduces the target subpopulation's temporal and between-participant structure better than simpler simulators. These results suggest that our twin can be used to simulate a target deployment before it runs, the prerequisite for testing and informing online algorithm design decisions.

</details>


### [227] [Semantic-Aware Task Clustering for Constructive and Cooperative Multi-Tasking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21426)
*Ahmad Halimi Razlighi,Maximilian H. V. Tillmann,Edgar Beck,Bho Matthiesen,Armin Dekorsy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CMT-SemCom benefits from semantic-aware clustering of tasks into semantically aligned groups, followed by intra-cluster end-to-end training; this reduces negative transfer and improves accuracy versus unclustered or single-task baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In cooperative multi-task semantic communication, task interactions can be constructive or destructive depending on semantic relationships. There is a need to identify and exploit positive task correlations while avoiding detrimental interference to improve performance and efficiency.

Method: A two-stage optimization: (i) semantic clustering using hierarchical density-based spatial clustering to group semantically aligned tasks after a short initial training phase; (ii) intra-cluster end-to-end CMT-SemCom learning conducted only within discovered groups, enforcing within-cluster cooperation and isolating clusters.

Result: Simulation results indicate effective mitigation of destructive cooperation and negative transfer, with accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual (single-task) training baselines.

Conclusion: Semantic-aware task clustering enables constructive cooperation in CMT-SemCom by partitioning tasks into coherent groups for intra-cluster E2E learning. While effective in the reported simulations, performance may depend on clustering quality and stability; opportunities exist for dynamic clustering, robustness analysis, and evaluation of computational overhead.

Abstract: Cooperative multi-task semantic communication (CMT-SemCom) improves task execution performance by leveraging shared representations. However, as we demonstrated in [1], cooperative multi-tasking can be either constructive or destructive, depending on the semantic relationships among tasks. To ensure constructive cooperation, we propose a semantic-aware task clustering method for CMT-SemCom. We have formulated a sequential multi-stage optimization problem in which semantically aligned tasks are clustered once after a short initial training phase, and then end-to-end (E2E) joint training is conducted exclusively within the discovered groups. Specifically, the problem decomposes into two stages: (i) a semantic clustering problem leveraging hierarchical density-based spatial clustering, and (ii) an intra-cluster E2E CMT-SemCom learning problem. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively mitigates destructive cooperation and negative transfer, yielding accuracy gains compared to unclustered multi-tasking and individual training baselines.

</details>


### [228] [Context-weighted Discrete Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21427)
*Daniil Cherniavskii,Daniel Severo,Karen Ullrich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Context-aware CTMC modifications for discrete flow matching; a context-weighted sampler and scaled cross-entropy loss reduce perplexity and improve sampling, while matching semi-autoregressive baselines and enabling order-agnostic generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evidence that token uncertainty correlates with local context density; standard factorized objectives mix tokens of different difficulty, hindering training and sampling.

Method: Modify CTMC with local-context information: introduce a context-weighted sampler and a scaled cross-entropy loss that reweights token-specific training signals according to neighborhood context.

Result: Generation quality improves with negligible overhead; up to 63% perplexity reduction on OpenWebText; performance comparable to semi-autoregressive block diffusion baselines; retains arbitrary-order generation.

Conclusion: Local context is a key factor in discrete generative modeling; simple, context-aware modifications can yield substantial gains in both sampling efficiency and training efficiency.

Abstract: Discrete flow matching provides a flexible framework for generative modeling on discrete structures. However, the standard factorized training objective exposes the model to targets of varying difficulty, mixing well-conditioned, predictable tokens with ambiguous, high-entropy ones. We empirically demonstrate that the uncertainty over the value of each token is closely related to the density of available context in its neighborhood. Motivated by this observation, we propose a simple modification to the underlying continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) that incorporates local context information. Our context-weighted sampler improves generation quality with negligible computational overhead, while our scaled cross-entropy loss function reweights the training signal from different tokens and reduces generative perplexity by up to 63% on OpenWebText. Moreover, our approach matches a strong semi-autoregressive block diffusion baseline in quality while retaining the ability to perform generation in any order. These results highlight the role of local context as an important factor in discrete generative modeling and show that simple context-aware modifications can significantly improve both sampling and training efficiency.

</details>


### [229] [KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21446)
*Yann Bouquet,Alireza Khodamoradi,Kristof Denolf,Mathieu Salzmann*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KroQuant introduces a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform for post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers, enabling block-wise activation quantization with reduced parameter count and lower online cost, achieving higher fidelity at W4A4 than competing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PTQ of diffusion transformers at very low precision (W4A4) suffers from activation outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. Existing fixes trade accuracy for inference cost: per-channel scaling is cheap but harms channel magnitudes; Hadamard transforms improve accuracy but require large blocks; full dense invertible transforms yield high online cost. A compact, hardware-friendly transform is needed to maintain quality without skyrocketing latency.

Method: Apply a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of activations. This block-local structure enables small tensor-core GEMMs and stores less than half the parameters compared to per-channel scaling. Offline LoRaQ calibrates the residual per-weight quantization error. The approach emphasizes a balance between quantization quality and inference cost, with a focus on efficient hardware execution on GPUs such as MI350.

Result: On MI350 GPUs, KroQuant’s quantizer kernel is up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant. Evaluated on PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant yields outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

Conclusion: KroQuant offers a parameter-efficient, hardware-friendly PTQ solution for diffusion transformers that improves accuracy at low precision with favorable runtime characteristics, outperforming key baselines in both quantization fidelity and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

</details>


### [230] [Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21453)
*Rajiv Shailesh Chitale,Rahul Madhavan,Taneesh Gupta,Deepanway Ghosal,Aravindan Raghuveer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TTEL introduces Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization, an inference-time method that localizes the first erroneous step in a reasoning trajectory using feedback, enabling truncation and branching to reuse valid prefixes while reducing tokens generated; it achieves superior efficiency and performance across sequential reasoning benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard approaches to scaling inference-time computation (e.g., independent sampling, sequential refinements) lack token-level credit assignment, causing valid prefixes to be discarded and inefficient use of compute. TTEL targets token-level error attribution at test time to improve efficiency and performance.

Method: TTEL uses fixed or environment feedback to compare conditional probabilities under an informed feedback context against a null-context baseline. It localizes the error step in the chain of thought, truncates the trajectory at that point, and branches a new generation from the identified prefix, maximizing reuse of the valid prefix.

Result: TTEL achieves strictly dominating Pareto frontiers in sequential reasoning tasks, optimizing pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. On Qwen3-8B with LiveCodeBench, TTEL reaches pass@64 of 71.0% while generating ~360k tokens vs 735k with independent sampling. Generalizes to AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, outperforming competing test-time baselines on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

Conclusion: TTEL provides an effective inference-time scaling mechanism with token-level credit assignment, delivering significant efficiency gains and competitive or superior accuracy across multiple reasoning benchmarks.

Abstract: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

</details>


### [231] [Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21475)
*Peng Xie*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Deterministic KV-cache eviction loses identifiability: evicted values can be altered so that the observed outputs stay the same while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, making a serving-time estimator of that error inconsistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, a single logit offset implements the Hájek correction inside softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set yields a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads, seven claims were pre-registered and three were lost: question-aware eviction at 25–50% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73–0.75 vs 0.47–0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To assess the reliability and interpretability of KV-cache eviction in serving transformer models. Deterministic eviction lacks identifiability of the actual error introduced by eviction, hindering trustworthy error estimation and repair. The work seeks to restore identifiability and provide an actionable error certificate for per-step decisions.

Method: Prove impossibility result for deterministic eviction failing to bound or identify the true error. Propose randomized eviction with a Poisson-sampled tail and known inclusion probabilities. Apply a single logit offset to perform the Hájek correction inside softmax. Use a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set to construct a per-step error certificate. Empirically evaluate on real workloads; pre-register seven claims and report which hold.

Result: Deterministic eviction cannot bound or identify the true error; randomized eviction yields identifiability. The Hájek-corrected softmax with Poisson tail achieves an error certificate with 0.97 coverage and no loss in accuracy. On real workloads, seven claims were preregistered and three were not supported. The certificate enables attribution, achieving AUC 0.73–0.75 (vs 0.47–0.54 for output confidence) and better recomputation scheduling than random or confidence gating; randomization improves attribution but not predictive accuracy.

Conclusion: Randomization provides attribution through a usable error certificate, enabling separation of cache-induced versus inherent failures and more efficient recomputation scheduling. However, some claimed benefits (e.g., claim about budget savings at certain budgets) may not hold; output log-probability is not as effective as the certificate for identifying failures. Overall, randomized eviction with a certificate is a robust approach for reliable and interpretable serving.

Abstract: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the Hájek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

</details>


### [232] [Finite-Sample Coverage Audits for High-Recall Candidate Generation: Certification and Learning-Theoretic Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21480)
*Martin Anthony,Kaveh Salehzadeh Nobari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper studies how many audit labels are needed to certify that the mass of missed relevant items in an initial high-recall stage is small, providing finite-sample guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To quantify audit label requirements for certifying missed mass in a high-recall pipeline, ensuring that unrecovered relevant items are bounded with finite-sample validity.

Method: The authors prove a lower bound showing that only sampling from the excluded pool yields any non-trivial certificates; they derive a matching finite-corpus lower bound on the required label effort. They develop an exact finite-sample toolkit using binomial and hypergeometric inversion, construct a two-pool design to convert missed mass to recall, and provide certificates for nested candidate generators and perturbation mechanisms.

Result: Any valid audit that guarantees fewer than m missed relevant items with high probability in the zero-miss regime must inspect roughly N0/m labels from the excluded pool; excluded-pool auditing is minimax rate-optimal. The toolkit yields certificates that hold under fixed candidate generator family and audit rule, enabling stress-testing and selection of low-burden generators meeting missed-mass targets.

Conclusion: The work establishes minimax-optimal audit strategies for missed-mass certification in zero-miss scenarios, provides exact finite-sample certificates, and offers a practical framework for choosing candidate generators under a desired missed-mass target with observable review burden.

Abstract: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

</details>


### [233] [Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21535)
*Alagappan Valliappan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Windowed-MTP: a training-free, drop-in method that uses a sliding attention window to limit the speculative draft head's KV cache reads, preserving verification accuracy while reducing per-step and end-to-end latency for long contexts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speculative decoding relies on a cheap draft head (MTP/NEXTN) but with million-token contexts the draft head's full-attention KV reads become prohibitive, undermining speedups. A fresher approach is needed to bound draft cost without sacrificing correctness.

Method: Introduce StreamingLLM-style sliding window with an attention sink to the draft's attention (Windowed-MTP). The draft's KV working set is bounded to a constant; unread draft KV entries are reclaimed with a compact ring buffer. The full-attention target still decides accepted tokens, so windowing changes only proposed tokens. Evaluations across Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang.

Result: Per-decode-step draft cost reduced by 28%-44% with windowing; end-to-end latency improved by the same margin at matched acceptance. The approach is input-invariant and scales with context; ~7.7-11% of KV remains unread and is reclaimed without affecting acceptance or quality.

Conclusion: Windowed-MTP provides a training-free, drop-in, lossless method to curb draft KV reads, enabling speculative decoding to remain beneficial at ultra-long contexts and across diverse architectures.

Abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

</details>


### [234] [Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21542)
*Yakun Wang,Leyang Wang,Song Liu,Taiji Suzuki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Zero-Flow Discrepancy (ZFD) and Zero-Flow Two-Sample Test (ZF2ST) for two-sample testing using learnable witnesses with valid calibration; separates witness learning from hypothesis evaluation; provides regression-based and power-maximized witness learning; demonstrates strong power on structured distributional changes with calibrated Type-I error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of existing two-sample tests in capturing local, structured misalignments between samples. Leverage a zero-flow criterion to quantify discrepancy and enable flexible neural witnesses while maintaining statistical validity.

Method: Define a zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD) based on the zero-flow criterion. Learn a witness function that captures local misalignment between the two distributions; implement two learning strategies—regression-based and power-maximized. Use the learned witness within a hypothesis-testing framework that separates witness learning from hypothesis evaluation to ensure calibrated p-values.

Result: Proves the validity of ZFD. Proposes the practical ZF2ST framework. Empirical results on synthetic and image datasets show strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated Type-I error.

Conclusion: ZF2ST offers a flexible, calibration-preserving two-sample testing approach based on zero-flow discrepancy. It effectively detects structured distributional differences using neural witnesses and can be extended with additional witness-learning schemes or datasets.

Abstract: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

</details>


### [235] [X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21550)
*Dongjie Fu,Di Cao,Xize Cheng,Zihan Zhang,Wenxu Jia,Yifu Chen,Shengpeng Ji,Yu Zhang,Tao Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A cross-modal on-policy distillation method (X^3-OPD) transfers textual reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student, using a three-tier corpus and on-policy trajectories to improve audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought while preserving domain-shift robustness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data compared to text; bridging the gap between audio-language models and text-based LLMs in deep reasoning; enabling reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and dialogue.

Method: X^3-OPD trains the student to generate reasoning trajectories conditioned on acoustic perception; the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers; constructs a three-tier symmetric corpus: textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning with paralinguistic cues; extends cross-modal distillation to non-linguistic content.

Result: Empirical evaluation on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR shows substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning quality and chain-of-thought, with the model's capabilities kept robust under domain shift.

Conclusion: Demonstrates viability of cross-modal distillation for audio reasoning, broadens reasoning grounding to prosody and dialogue, and contributes a scalable dataset framework; future work could address remaining gaps and broader generalization.

Abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

</details>


### [236] [Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21561)
*Aaron Feller,Kris Deibler,Maxim Secor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EnsembleEGNN shows ensemble-aware molecular property prediction by per-conformer EGNN encoding and set-attention pooling; pretrained on CREMP improves cyclic-peptide property prediction over sequence-only baselines; end-to-end hybrid with BERT yields best accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Molecular property prediction often relies on a single conformation, ignoring conformational ensembles; need thermodynamically informed representations to capture ensemble effects.

Method: Encode each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network layers; pool using Set Attention Block to form ensemble representation; pretrain on CREMP with multi-task self-supervised objectives: masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction; evaluate on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB; compare scratch vs pretrained; also train a hybrid end-to-end with BERT sequence encoder.

Result: From scratch on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB, R^2≈0.005. Pretrained EnsembleEGNN achieves R^2=0.477, Pearson r=0.699, outperforming BERT baseline (R^2=0.439, r=0.667). End-to-end hybrid with BERT yields R^2=0.538, r=0.737.

Conclusion: Ensemble-aware embedding of conformational ensembles substantially improves cyclic-peptide property prediction; pretraining on ensemble data is crucial; combining ensemble embedding with sequence information yields further gains.

Abstract: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

</details>


### [237] [Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21573)
*Hongnan Ma,Yiwei Shi,Mengyue Yang,Weiru Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TimePNS presents a necessity-aware time-series explanation framework that uses counterfactual interventions to identify subsequences that are not only sufficient but necessary for a model's prediction, via a two-stage process combining causal generative modeling and a necessity-refining gate; experiments show improved sufficiency-necessity trade-offs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current explanations emphasize sufficiency but may highlight spurious subsequences; there is a need to identify necessary subsequences to ensure explanations reflect true decision-critical factors.

Method: Two-stage design: Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process and a sufficiency mask; Stage II intervenes counterfactually on temporal factors to derive necessity signals and trains a gate that suppresses non-essential components and emphasizes counterfactually necessary ones.

Result: Empirical results on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show TimePNS better identifies decision-critical subsequences and improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

Conclusion: TimePNS provides a principled framework for necessity-aware explanations in time-series, combining causal discovery with counterfactual intervention to refine sufficiency-based explanations.

Abstract: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

</details>


### [238] [Expanding Flow Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21585)
*Sophia Tang,Pranam Chatterjee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows) and Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs) that enable flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality via an expanding interpolant; decomposes the map into an expand operator and a transport map; recovers fixed-canvas flows as a special case; extends to the discrete simplex for variable-size graphs and sequences; frames output size as a learnable degree of freedom in continuous and discrete modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the rigidity of traditional flow models that operate at fixed dimensionality or fixed sequence length, by enabling generative models where the output size (dimensionality/sequence length) is itself a controllable, learnable quantity.

Method: Define flows between distributions of growing dimensionality using an expanding interpolant that augments the state with conditional noise. Introduce Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs) that factor the timestep map into an expand operator (adds coordinates/tokens conditioned on the current state) and a transport map (pushes the expanded state along the interpolant). Compose these operators to obtain a single map that expands and denoises the state. Show that fixed-canvas flows arise when the expand operator is the identity. Extend the framework to the discrete simplex to support variable-size graphs and variable-length sequences.

Result: Proposes a unified, principled framework (EFlows and EFMs) for settings where output size is a learnable degree of freedom, applicable across continuous and discrete domains; provides a construction that subsumes existing fixed-dimensional flow models as special cases and enables variable-size generation.

Conclusion: EFlows and EFMs offer a general paradigm for controllable generation with learnable output size, unifying continuous and discrete modalities and enabling tasks such as variable-size graph and sequence generation.

Abstract: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [239] [AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20452)
*Vinil Pasupuleti,Shyalendar Reddy Allala,Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu,Shrey Tyagi,Srinivasateja Songa*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes AINTMA, a six-agent, cloud-native QA architecture that autonomously manages testing using RL prioritization, generative quality narratives, and secure multi-agent communication; evaluated on 12 projects with strong gains and ROI, scalable yet reliant on historical data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the need for autonomous, intelligent quality assurance in distributed cloud environments to improve test effectiveness, efficiency, and security beyond traditional test management.

Method: Six specialized agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated via secure multi-agent messaging over a cloud-native microservices stack. RL Prioritization models test selection as an MDP with 47 features over a rolling 36-month window. Generative module uses LLMs to produce plain-language narratives and recommendations. Zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT for secure communications and multi-tenant isolation.

Result: Empirical evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months showing 88.4% APFD prioritization accuracy (vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% reduction in test cycle time; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback; supports 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response; Generative module rated 4.3/5 by developers.

Conclusion: Agentic AI with autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence, and secure connectivity can substantially advance software quality management in cloud-scale environments.

Abstract: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

</details>


### [240] [Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20462)
*Melanie Rieff,Robin Staab,Thibaud Gloaguen,Stefan Hegselmann,Martin Vechev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Domain-specific evaluation reveals that watermarking LLMs harms medical reasoning and terminology, with standard benchmarks masking clinically meaningful degradations; domain-aware testing is essential for safe medical deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To ensure traceability of model outputs in medicine without compromising clinical quality, and to assess whether watermarking introduces clinically consequential errors that domain-agnostic benchmarks miss.

Method: Benchmark five watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on unimodal and multimodal clinical tasks; implement a human-expert-validated pipeline to audit medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and hallucinations; analyze error modes such as lexical corruption and image-findings misattribution/omission.

Result: Watermarking induces substantial degradation across several failure modes (lexical errors, terminology hallucinations, misattribution/omission of image findings); domain-agnostic metrics fail to reveal these issues, highlighting the need for domain-specific analyses.

Conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a prerequisite for safely deploying watermarked models in medicine; current benchmarks can obscure clinically consequential degradations.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

</details>


### [241] [ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20463)
*Wojciech Michaluk,Tymoteusz Urban,Mateusz Kubita,Soveatin Kuntur,Anna Wróblewska*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Hybrid ML-based clickbait detector as a browser extension using transformer embeddings + linguistics features + baitness score; XGBoost achieves F1 0.91; provides pre/post warnings, score, explanations, and spoiler; includes demo video.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mitigate misinformation/attention-grabbing content by enabling proactive, interpretable detection of clickbait in real-time; address limitations of single-technique detectors.

Method: Hybrid feature engineering: transformer embeddings, linguistically motivated features, custom baitness score; evaluate various NLP techniques from classic vectorizers to LLM embeddings; final XGBoost classifier; post-hoc explanations; spoiler generation; browser extension integration; evaluation on open combined dataset; includes user-facing warnings before and after article access.

Result: F1-score of 0.91 on the open combined dataset; real-time warnings; post-read score; explanation using analyzed metrics; spoiler summary; demonstration video.

Conclusion: Demonstrates effective, user-centric detection with interpretable outputs; promising for deployment; suggests further work on generalization, privacy, and user experience.

Abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

</details>


### [242] [Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20464)
*Izhar Ali*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Self-consistency yields per-question uncertainty; but cross-question structure requires diverse ensembles; a homogeneous single-model variation reveals little cross-question structure, whereas a 24-model ensemble reveals multiple correlated factors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether variation from sampling (self-consistency) exposes cross-question structure and to compare it with cross-question structure revealed by a diverse ensemble, using random-matrix theory on multiple benchmarks.

Method: Compare two regimes on same questions: 100 runs of a single model at τ=1 vs ensemble of 24 LLMs at τ=0. Apply Marchenko–Pastur random-matrix test to separate signal from noise. Evaluate eigenvalues across MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K.

Result: Within a single model, at most one eigenvalue rises above the noise across five families and three benchmarks. Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues exceed the noise edge; a Bernoulli null yields at most 1 in 500 Monte Carlo draws.

Conclusion: Self-consistency provides accurate per-question uncertainty but does not reveal cross-question structure; diverse ensembles are needed to surface what a model does not know.

Abstract: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

</details>


### [243] [JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20466)
*Arya Tschand,Charles Hong,Julian Walker,Nina Cai,Shangkun Wang,Suvinay Subramanian,Sundar Dev,Vijay Janapa Reddi,Amir Yazdanbakhsh,Sethu Sankaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A TPU-native benchmark suite (JAXBench) for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs, showing context-aware optimization improves correctness and speedups; provides datasets, baselines, and evaluation harness to advance open-source TPU kernel work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: No standardized TPU kernel-optimization benchmark exists analogous to rigorous GPU benchmarks; need a shared target to drive progress and fair evaluation of optimization methods on TPUs.

Method: Assembles 50 JAX workloads, extracting 17 production ML operators from MaxText architectures and translating 33 operators from KernelBench, with new problem sizes to maximize TPU MXU utilization. Eight production operators ship hand-optimized Pallas kernels from Tokamax tuned for upper-bound baselines. Evaluates four feedback-driven methods for generating Pallas kernels on JAXBench using Gemini 3 Flash; compares against XLA; analyzes effect of conditioning on curated TPU documentation and search structures (Autocomp beam search).

Result: Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48/50 benchmarks with 1.28x geomean speedup. Autocomp beam-search achieves 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA; on 8 hand-tuned kernels it reaches 1.60x over XLA, nearly matching Tokamax’s 2.08x upper bound but underperforms on specialized paged/ragged attention. Overall, high-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging, and the authors release JAXBench and evaluation harness for open-source contributions.

Conclusion: TPU kernel optimization remains difficult but tractable with context-aware guidance; JAXBench provides a standardized benchmark, datasets, and baselines to spur research and reproducibility in TPU kernel optimization.

Abstract: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

</details>


### [244] [DC-Leap: Training-Free Acceleration of dLLMs via Draft-Guided Contiguous Leaping Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20467)
*Yanhua Jiao,Tianyi Wu,Xiaoxi Sun,Yulin Li,HuiLing Zhen,Libo Qin,Baotian Hu,Zhuotao Tian,Min Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DC-Leap is a training-free framework that accelerates diffusion LLMs during parallel decoding by addressing JPDE through dynamic contiguous verification and draft-guided look-ahead decoding, achieving substantial speedups with comparable quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome overly conservative confidence thresholds driven by Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE) that impede parallel decoding efficiency in diffusion LLMs, without requiring additional training.

Method: Introduce Dynamic Contiguous Verification (DCV) to enforce strictly-ordered causal constraints during parallel decoding and progressively verify token dependencies, neutralizing JPDE. Incorporate a draft-guided decoding mechanism that uses drafts to leap forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context while preserving bidirectional attention at inference.

Result: Empirical results show substantial speedups (up to 53.19x on MBPP for long sequences; up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache) with generation quality comparable to baselines.

Conclusion: DC-Leap offers a training-free path to reliable acceleration of dLLMs in moderate-confidence regimes by combining DCV and draft-guided decoding, effectively mitigating JPDE while preserving output quality.

Abstract: While parallel decoding is central to the efficiency of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs), current strategies are often hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds. These thresholds, necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), result in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. To overcome this, we propose DC-Leap, a training-free framework that enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in the moderate-confidence regime. DC-Leap introduces a Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process. By progressively validating token dependencies, this mechanism effectively neutralizes the JPDE, enabling reliable acceleration with comparable performance. Furthermore, DC-Leap incorporates the draft-guided decoding mechanism, where the draft helps extend the context by leaping forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context and retaining the structural benefits of bidirectional attention during inference. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DC-Leap achieves substantial speedups, up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache with comparable generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/ffh-wyls/DC-Leap .

</details>


### [245] [InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20468)
*Jehyeok Yeon,Ben Rank,Maksym Andriushchenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InferenceBench benchmarks optimizing LLM inference speed on a single OpenAI-compatible server with a two-hour budget, revealing limits of memorized solutions and the need for diverse exploration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether AI agents can perform real optimization in open-ended engineering tasks beyond recalling known recipes.

Method: Four scenarios targeting prefill latency, decode latency, concurrent throughput, and all three; 15 agent configurations; compare to PyTorch baseline and vLLM; two-hour budget; qualitative trajectory analysis.

Result: Agents improve up to 8.08x vs baseline, approach or beat vLLM default settings (4.05x); but a simple hyperparameter search yields up to 11.53x improvement, indicating that exploration matters; agents tend to converge on a single framework and re-measure rather than exploring diverse configurations.

Conclusion: The bottleneck lies in proposing diverse configurations and systematic evaluation rather than domain knowledge; true open-ended AI engineering requires better search strategies and experimentation discipline to surpass memorized solutions.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

</details>


### [246] [DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20469)
*Zishan Shao,Lixun Zhang,Kangning Cui,Yixiao Wang,Ting Jiang,Hancheng Ye,Qinsi Wang,Zhixu Du,Yuzhe Fu,Fan Yang,Danyang Zhuo,Yiran Chen,Hai Helen Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Identify a small, decode-time, task-general subspace shared across tasks; removing it during decoding causally harms performance and clarifies decode-time vs prefill roles; steering signals align with decode-time subspace; code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand whether a task-general structure exists specifically in decode-time hidden states under KV-cached inference and quantify its causal role.

Method: Discover a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states (DecodeShare). intervene by projecting out/removing that subspace only during decoding; compare with prefill-derived and random subspaces under a fixed intervention budget; evaluate impact on task performance; analyze steering directions and practical deployment implications; provide code.

Result: Disturbing the decode-time shared subspace degrades decision performance more than disturbing prefill-derived or random subspaces; the decode-shared subspace overlaps common steering directions; projecting it out separates decode-time vs prefill functional roles; decode-time evaluations yield more reliable downstream signals; the subspace is compact yet high-leverage as a causal channel.

Conclusion: DecodeShare reveals a compact, causal decode-time subspace that governs cross-task dynamics and informs activation steering and deployment; these insights refine understanding of decode-time structure and offer practical techniques for robust decoding.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

</details>


### [247] [PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20470)
*Jiacheng Wang,Weiyan Zhang,Guangya Yu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PlanE proposes a plan-based framework to tailor LLMs for tasks via data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference, plus a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner to select the best base LLM and DTI configurations for a given dataset. It is validated across datasets and base LLMs, and shows generalizability under different objectives; code is released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the high annotation cost of large instruction-tuning data and the lack of optimization methods for task-specific LLM adaptation, by introducing a planning-based approach to efficiently construct attractive LLMs.

Method: Introduce PlanE framework comprising data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference; develop a DTI planner to select the optimal base LLM and DTI combinations for specific datasets; evaluate across multiple datasets and base LLMs; test generalization of the DTI planner under various objectives; provide open-source code.

Result: PlanE is reported to be effective across different datasets with the same base LLM and across the same dataset with different base LLMs; the DTI planner shows generalizability under different optimization objectives.
