Conclusion: PlanE offers an efficient, flexible framework for task-specific LLM enhancement, enabling efficient data-driven planning to select suitable base LLMs and tuning strategies; results support cross-dataset and cross-LLM robustness, with publicly available code.

Abstract: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

</details>


### [248] [Benchmarking the Personalization Capabilities of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20471)
*Ashutosh Srivastava,Siddharth Yedlapati,Vinay Aggarwal,Yaman Kumar Singla,Shashwat Dixit,Jitendra Ajmera,Balaji Krishnamurthy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs show a personalization plateau in two-party persuasion; a large, public, reproducible benchmark (SDR-Bench) and a real-world field test find no model clearly outperforms baseline in inducing action, though some content is rated useful; resources released for reproducible study.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether generative agents can achieve classical customization in persuasion, where sender and receiver have potentially divergent objectives, by adapting Bayesian Persuasion to LLM-powered outreach and evaluating on real-world outcomes.

Method: Adapt Bayesian Persuasion (Kamenica & Gentzkow, 2011) to generative agents. Build SDR-Bench: 6,279 customer success stories across 22 industries ~200 enterprises, with temporally constrained simulation to avoid future-data leakage. Evaluate frontier LLMs and research agents on their ability to tailor outreach to inferred receiver states. Conduct a field deployment with 12 professional sales reps. Measure effectiveness via action outcomes, immediate usefulness ratings (human evaluators), and expert agreement (Pearson correlations). Release SDR-Arena/SDR-Bench for reproducible study.

Result: Across frontier models and agents, a consistent personalization plateau observed; in a Fortune 100 tech cohort, no model statistically distinguishes successful from unsuccessful outreach. Field deployment: 48% of model-generated content rated immediately useful; senior-expert agreement with model judgments: Pearson r = 0.82.

Conclusion: Public datasets (SDR-Arena/SDR-Bench) enable reproducible study of large-scale generative personalization. Current generative personalization exhibits limited two-party persuasion capabilities; significant gaps remain between predicted usefulness and actual action, underscoring the need for improved evaluation frameworks and possibly new modeling approaches.

Abstract: Personalization, the act of varying a message to induce action from a specific receiver while keeping sender, channel, and time fixed, has a long tradition in psychology and marketing as a two-party problem in which sender and receiver have independent objectives. Large language models remove the bounded-inventory constraint of classical retrieval-and-ranking approaches by generating a continuum of message variants conditioned on inferred receiver state, raising the question of how well current models perform personalization in the classical sense. Existing LLM personalization benchmarks measure sender-side adaptation, in which the receiver is the same user the model is serving. The two-party question, whether a generated message induces its intended action in a third party, has been investigated only through A/B tests and small-scale human studies that cannot be re-run against a new model on demand. We adapt the Bayesian Persuasion framework of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) to generative agents and instantiate the formulation in sales, where receiver actions are routinely logged against the outreach that induced them. We release SDR-Bench, a public corpus of 6,279 customer success stories spanning 22 industries and approximately 200 enterprises, served through a temporally constrained simulation that prevents future-data leakage. Across frontier LLMs and deep-research agents, we observe a consistent personalization plateau and on a Fortune 100 tech cohort no model statistically separates successful from unsuccessful outreach. A field deployment with 12 professional sales representatives validates the framework, with 48 percent of model-generated content rated immediately useful and senior-expert agreement at Pearson 0.82. We release SDR-Arena and SDR-Bench publicly to support reproducible study of generative personalization at scale.

</details>


### [249] [Robust Critics: Defending LLMs Against Multi-Turn Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20472)
*Roman Belaire,Arunesh Sinha,Pradeep Varakantham*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DCGS reframes adversarial dialogue as an MDP and uses per-turn intent inference with token- and utterance-level critics to reweight candidate responses, improving safety in multi-turn chats and transferring robustness to frontier models without fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ambiguity in user intent in multi-turn dialogue makes safety decisions hard: worst-case interpretation hurts legitimate users, best-case exploitation is easy. Also, dialogue context trajectory is ignored by many safety frameworks.

Method: Model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value- and regret-based critics at token and utterance levels. Use an action-value critic to score candidate responses. Infer user intent at each turn from full history and apply inference-time reweighting that approximates exponential tilting of the base policy. Evaluate on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, Harmbench; demonstrate transfer to frontier models without additional fine-tuning.

Result: DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks across several benchmarks. It also improves robustness when transferred to frontier models without fine-tuning.

Conclusion: Inference-time intent-aware reweighting can safely and effectively modulate model responses in multi-turn adversarial dialogue, offering better safety without sacrificing performance and enabling transfer to other models.

Abstract: When a user asks a language model something harmful, is it a genuine attack or a misunderstood but well-meaning question? This ambiguity is one of the central challenges of LLM safety. A model that assumes the worst harms legitimate users; one that assumes the best is easily exploited. The problem is compounded in multi-turn dialogue, where an attacker's true intent may only reveal itself gradually across many exchanges, yet existing safety frameworks apply a contextual bandit treatment, ignoring the trajectory of the conversation.
  To that end, we propose Dialogue Critic Guided Sampling (DCGS), a framework that addresses this by inferring user intent at every turn of dialogue. Instead of applying a fixed rule about what is or is not safe, DCGS learns what the user's intent is likely to be based on the full conversational history and generates responses accordingly. Formally, we model adversarial dialogue as a Markov Decision Process and learn value and regret-based critics at both the individual token and utterance (full response) levels, scoring candidate responses via an action-value critic. We prove that this inference-time reweighting approximates exponential tilting of the base policy, guaranteeing improvement in expected return for any finite candidate pool, a property that group-relative objectives do not exhibit. Evaluated on CARES-18k, WildJailbreak, Redbench, and Harmbench, DCGS outperforms strong robust baselines and frontier models on adversarial dialogue tasks. DCGS also transfers to frontier models, improving their robustness without fine-tuning.

</details>


### [250] [Incomplete Prompt Jailbreaks in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20473)
*Yeonjea Kim,Bumjin Park,Jaesik Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Formalizes incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) in LLMs, characterizes when incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations, shows refusal delay, simple parameter tuning fails to generalize, and identifies termination/continuation neurons as potential intervention points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the susceptibility of open-weight LLMs with safeguards to incomplete harmful prompts and improve robustness against IPJ through mechanistic insights.

Method: Empirical analysis of incomplete sentence continuations across diverse attractor types; evaluation of refusal behavior and generalization across content domains; finetuning experiments; neuron-level analysis to identify termination and continuation neurons.

Result: IPJ is a systematic vulnerability where models delay refusals until sentence end; finetuning alone does not generalize across domains/attractor types; two functional neurons (termination and continuation) govern sentence completion.

Conclusion: Neuron-level interventions targeting termination and continuation neurons may enable more precise and robust IPJ defenses, highlighting a promising avenue for strengthening LLM robustness against incomplete prompts.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly released as open-weight models with safeguards against harmful requests. Nevertheless, sentence completion remains vulnerable to incomplete harmful prompts. In this work, we formalize this phenomenon as incomplete prompt jailbreaks (IPJ) and provide a systematic empirical characterization of when and how incomplete prompts elicit harmful continuations. We analyze diverse attractor types associated with incomplete sentence continuation and show that LLMs systematically delay refusal until sentence termination. We further demonstrate that training models to refuse incomplete harmful prompts via parameter tuning is insufficient, failing to generalize across both content domains and attractor types. To enable fine-grained control, we identify two functional neurons: termination and continuation neurons. By clarifying their roles in sentence completion, we highlight the potential of neuron-level interventions for more precise and robust IPJ defenses.

</details>


### [251] [VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20474)
*Sumaya Abdul Rahman,Seckhen Ariel Andrade Cuellar,Ghani Raissov,Mohammad Raza*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR:  VeriSimpl introduces a simplification-based verification framework that uses solver-generated diagnostic queries to enable LLMs to robustly translate natural language problem descriptions into optimization formulations, achieving higher accuracy and offering a high-precision self-verification signal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation:  Existing NL-to-optimization systems can produce formulations that execute but do not faithfully implement the intended task. There is a need for tractable, internal verification to ensure formulations match the task description.

Method:  VeriSimpl leverages the optimization solver to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation. It introduces simplification strategies across problem constraints and decision variables, enabling the LLM to reason locally under fixed global context and perform robustness checks.

Result:  Evaluations on optimization benchmarks show consistently improved accuracy over existing methods and reveal a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

Conclusion:  The framework demonstrates that simplification-based verification can enhance the reliability of NL-to-optimization formalization and provide a useful self-check mechanism, with implications for more trustworthy NL-driven optimization pipelines.

Abstract: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

</details>


### [252] [SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20475)
*Pragaash Ponnusamy,Shivam Sahni,Jue Wang,Tri Dao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SonicSampler unifies and accelerates the full LLM sampling pipeline inside a single, tile-aware Triton kernel suite, enabling dynamic per-request behaviors and CUDA Graph compatibility, with hierarchical two-stage top-k that yields major speedups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing implementations accelerate only parts of the sampling pipeline, use multiple kernel launches, or assume uniform sampling across a batch, hindering dynamic, workload-aware serving and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution.

Method: A suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse the entire sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware, batched kernel. Supports dynamic per-request features (grammar constraints, repetition, penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-k/p/min-p filtering, speculative verification) and CUDA Graph compatibility. Introduces a hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm to efficiently select tokens by exploiting low-entropy output distributions.

Result: Demonstrates up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines for the top-k component and up to 16x speedup across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, while maintaining flexible batched execution and CUDA Graph compatibility.

Conclusion: SonicSampler provides a unified, efficient, and dynamic sampling solution for LLM inference that maximizes hardware efficiency and serving flexibility by fusing the entire pipeline and leveraging a novel top-k approach.

Abstract: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

</details>


### [253] [Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20476)
*Faizan Iqbal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Empirical benchmark of five LLMs on multisensor hazard data; multi-sensor cases yielded no precautionary warnings below individual limits, while single-sensor thresholds were detected reliably; prose prompts slightly outperform structured tables for ChatGPT-4o; implications for safety-monitoring deployments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate reliability and failure modes of large language models in multi-sensor physical hazard assessment to inform safe deployment in safety-critical systems.

Method: Tested five LLMs (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) across 60 scenarios in three categories (multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, pattern disambiguation) using 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0; compared performance on multi-sensor (Category A) versus single-sensor (Category B) scenarios; also contrasted structured tabular prompts with plain prose.

Result: All models scored near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) and near-perfect on single-sensor thresholds (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). ChatGPT-4o's performance improved under prose prompts relative to tabular prompts (p = 0.001).

Conclusion: Multi-sensor data fusion presents a significant risk of missed precautionary warnings in current LLMs; caution is warranted when deploying LLMs for physical safety monitoring. Further work should address multi-sensor fusion capabilities, standardized evaluation metrics, broader model coverage, and defensive system-level safeguards.

Abstract: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

</details>


### [254] [Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20477)
*Yurui Lai,Samir Moustafa,Renchi Yang,Tsz Nam Chan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes roma core method named \algo{} for semi-supervised learning on Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) using a dual-pathway encoder, Wasserstein-distance-based graph sketching, and an LLM-synthesis module to generate readable summaries for condensed nodes, achieving strong performance with compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: TAGs fuse graph topology with textual semantics but existing methods face scalability bottlenecks, label scarcity in semi-supervised settings, and lack human-readable textual attributes for downstream LLM tasks. A unified, scalable framework is needed to capture cross-modal interactions and enable efficient LLM integration.

Method: A graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) operating inside a collaborative self-training loop to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. A theoretically grounded Wasserstein Distance (WSD) based graph sketching algorithm. A cost-effective LLM text synthesis module that uses cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes.

Result: Empirical evaluation on benchmark TAGs shows state-of-the-art performance and compression: strong results for both GNN-based and LLM-based downstream tasks, demonstrating effective TAG learning under resource constraints.

Conclusion: The framework delivers a unified semi-supervised approach that scales TAG learning, provides interpretable textual summaries for condensed nodes, and enables effective integration with LLMs through WSD-guided sketching and collaborative pseudo-labeling.

Abstract: {\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

</details>


### [255] [Beyond Liars' Bench: The Impact of Lie Typology, Depth, and Sparsity on Deception Detection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20479)
*Amr Moustafa,Max Feser,Florian Mai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Deception-detection probes are highly dependent on dataset and lie type; diversity in deception data and representation choices shape detectability, with depth and sparsity playing varying roles and gains limited for expressive probes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate why deception-detection probes fail to generalize across lie types and assess how representation depth, probe expressivity, sparsity, and training data typology influence detectability; address out-of-domain transfer by augmenting data with diverse deception types.

Method: Systematic experimental study across seven probe types; vary representation depth, probe expressivity, use sparse representations (feature representations and sparse autoencoders); augment benchmark data with a supplementary dataset including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration; evaluate detection performance across conditions and lie typologies.

Result: Key findings: optimal representation depth depends on dataset; more expressive probes provide limited gains beyond linear baselines; sparse autoencoder features do not outperform dense hidden states; training data composition and lie typology substantially change detectability.

Conclusion: Deception detection is highly dependent on representation and data; transferability across lie types is challenging; to build robust detectors, diversify lie typologies in training data and tailor representation choices to dataset characteristics.

Abstract: Training probes to detect deceptive outputs from large language models is still an open problem. Recent work has demonstrated that detection probes fail especially in out-of-domain scenarios -- training on one type of lie does not transfer well to deception scenarios involving other types of lies. In this work, we conduct a systematic study on how various factors impact detection performance: representation depth, probe expressivity, sparse feature representations, and the lie typology of the training data. To this end, we augment standard benchmark training data with a supplementary dataset containing diverse types of deception, including fabrication, omission, and exaggeration examples. Analyzing these factors across seven probe types, our experimental results show that the optimal representation depth is highly dataset-dependent, more expressive probes provide only selective gains over linear baselines, and sparse autoencoder features perform similarly to dense hidden states. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the choice of training data and lie typology substantially changes detectability, highlighting that deception detection is a highly representation-dependent problem.

</details>


### [256] [Enabling Scalable Topology Inference in Distribution Systems via Constrained Multi-Source Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20480)
*Haoran Li,Lihao Mai,Muhao Guo,Jiaqi Wu,Yang Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Constrained-inference framework refines a base distribution topology using heterogeneous evidence, achieving high accuracy with localized reconnections and a falsification-driven reliability metric.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Accurate distribution topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and grid operation, but reliable connectivity records are hard due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing methods relying on electrical similarity or spatial records falter in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata; scalable, data-fusion approaches are needed.

Method: Instead of building topology from scratch, the framework refines a provided base topology by detecting inconsistencies, performing localized reconnections within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforcing physical feasibility. It uses a falsification-driven reliability metric to quantify support for each inferred connection relative to alternatives, guiding verification priorities.

Result: Validated on three feeders with over 8,000 AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Achieves >95% topology reconstruction accuracy and substantially reduces computational effort vs. global inference. Demonstrates that correlation-based methods alone yield ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, while combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust, scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

Conclusion: The approach yields scalable, reliable topology identification with a verifiability metric, improving observability and operation of distribution grids, particularly in dense or data-incomplete deployments.

Abstract: Accurate distribution system topology is essential for outage localization, voltage analytics, and operation of distribution grids, yet maintaining reliable connectivity records remains challenging in practice due to heterogeneous and imperfect utility data. Existing topology identification methods often rely primarily on electrical similarity or spatial records alone, which become unreliable in dense feeders and under inconsistent metadata conditions. This paper formulates distribution topology identification as a constrained inference problem that refines a utility-provided base topology using heterogeneous evidence while enforcing spatial feasibility and physical operational constraints. Instead of reconstructing connectivity from scratch, the proposed framework detects inconsistent assignments, performs localized reconnection within constrained neighborhoods to ensure scalability, and iteratively enforces physical feasibility to produce operationally consistent topology estimates. In addition, a falsification-driven reliability metric evaluates how strongly each inferred connection is supported relative to alternative feasible assignments, enabling utilities to prioritize verification efforts while preserving system-wide observability. The framework is validated using operational data from three feeders comprising more than $8{,}000$ AMI meters in collaboration with a large U.S. utility. Results demonstrate over $95\%$ topology reconstruction accuracy while significantly reducing computational effort compared with global inference approaches. The study further shows that correlation-based methods alone produce ambiguous assignments in dense urban feeders, whereas combining electrical measurements with spatial and operational constraints enables robust and scalable topology recovery under realistic deployment conditions.

</details>


### [257] [Routing Without Training: Controllable-Ratio LLM Offloading via Reliability Gating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20481)
*Evan Chen,Shiqiang Wang,Kevin S Chan,Su Wang,Christopher Brinton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A training-free routing method that uses prompt-varied sampling and Bayesian early stopping to decide between local or cloud execution, enabling strong local–cloud collaboration without trained routers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the reliance on trained routers or collaboration-specific finetuning in local-cloud LLM setups by leveraging the local model's own response agreement as a trust signal.

Method: Estimate agreement by sampling responses under prompt variations; apply Bayesian early stopping for efficient uncertainty control; calibrate at deployment time to achieve any target collaboration ratio; compatible with diverse LLM families, scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models.

Result: CARGO consistently outperforms training-free baselines and, in several settings, surpasses supervised learned routers across a range of reasoning and QA tasks.

Conclusion: Effective local–cloud collaboration can emerge from the local model’s intrinsic response behavior without the need for an additional trained router.”

Abstract: Local-cloud collaboration is a practical way to deploy large language models under resource constraints, but existing methods often rely on trained routers or collaboration-aware finetuning that tie routing behavior to a particular operating regime. In this work, we show that such training may be unnecessary: the local model's own inference-time agreement across sampled responses already provides a strong signal for deciding when to trust local execution and when to offload to a stronger cloud model. We propose CARGO, a training-free routing framework that estimates this agreement through prompt-varied sampling, applies Bayesian early stopping for sample-efficient uncertainty control, and supports arbitrary target collaboration ratios through lightweight deployment-time calibration. Across diverse reasoning and question-answering tasks, multiple local LLM families and scales, and both pretrained and finetuned local models, CARGO consistently outperforms other training-free baselines and in several settings surpasses supervised learned routers. These results suggest that effective and adaptable local-cloud collaboration can emerge directly from the local model's intrinsic response behavior, without requiring an additional trained router.

</details>


### [258] [PersonaTrail: Benchmarking Personalized Web Agents through Browsing Trails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20482)
*Seungbin Yang,Chaewoon Ki,Dohyun Lee,Jaegul Choo,ChaeHun Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduce PersonaTrail and PACMem for personalized web agents: a benchmark using realistic browsing trajectories and a memory framework that separates factual and preference memories, achieving superior results to baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks do not capture personalization from underspecified prompts and history, hindering evaluation of agents that must infer user preferences from browsing history in a managed open web environment.

Method: Create PersonaTrail with realistic browsing trajectories as user history; develop PACMem that splits raw histories into factual memories (session summaries) and preference memories (recurring patterns); retrieve relevant memories to guide personalized navigation.

Result: PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on tasks related to personalized web navigation within PersonaTrail.

Conclusion: Structured memory of factual and preference information enables more effective personalized navigation; PersonaTrail provides a realistic benchmark for evaluating web agents under underspecified prompts.

Abstract: Recent advances in large language models have enabled web agents to autonomously execute complex tasks. In practice, users frequently provide underspecified instructions, requiring agents to infer the missing context from their raw browsing histories. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this form of personalization, as they either restrict tasks to fully explicit prompts or abstract web interaction history into simplified forms. To bridge this gap, we introduce PersonaTrail, a benchmark for personalized web agents operating in a managed open web environment. By leveraging realistic browsing trajectories as user history, PersonaTrail evaluates an agent's ability to infer user preferences and recall information from past browsing sessions. We further propose Preference-Aware Contextual Memory (PACMem), a framework that decomposes raw browsing histories into two types of structured memory: factual memories that summarize individual sessions and preference memories that distill recurring behavioral patterns. At inference time, the agent retrieves the most relevant entries from these memories to guide personalized navigation. Extensive experiments show that PACMem consistently outperforms existing memory-based baselines on both tasks.

</details>


### [259] [Tractable Hierarchical Control of Autoregressive Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20483)
*Max Scribner,Antonio Vergari,Vaishak Belle*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Polynomial-time satisfaction of LR(k) grammars for steering autoregressive LLMs toward syntactically valid output, enabling efficient constraint enforcement during code/data generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure syntactic validity of LLM-generated outputs (SQL/JSON) to integrate with formal systems; prior methods were exponential.

Method: Distill LLM into a tractable probabilistic model and compute the probability of outputs satisfying an LR(k) grammar of finite duration, then use this to steer/mask generation.

Result: Showed that satisfaction can be computed in polynomial time for any LR(k) grammar of finite duration, improving over previous exponential-time approaches.

Conclusion: Enables efficient constraint-based steering of LLM generation to satisfy formal syntactic constraints, improving output validity for program synthesis and data generation.

Abstract: Constraining the generation of autoregressive large language models (LLMs) is an important component of integrating language models into formal systems. In the generation of code and data for tasks like program synthesis, ensuring that language models produce syntactically valid output is a prerequisite for processing such output. These languages (such as SQL or JSON) are often designed as $LR(k)$ context-free grammars. By distilling the LLM to a tractable probabilistic model, its autoregressive generation can be steered and masked to incorporate the probability of satisfying logical constraints, ensuring high quality output that is guaranteed to be valid. This paper demonstrates that the satisfaction of any $LR(k)$ grammar of finite duration can be calculated in polynomial time, an improvement over the exponential time of applying previous methods to such grammars. This result enables efficient constraint and steering of LLM generation towards output that better satisfies formal syntactic constraints.

</details>


### [260] [The Devil is in the Spectrum: Mitigating Representation Collapse in LLMs via Topologically Regularized Side-Path](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20484)
*Yiheng Tao,Kaiwen Cheng,Yao Lu,Chang Liu,Jie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: TRSP provides topological regularization to balance spectral mixing efficiency and information capacity in LLM attention, mitigating homogenization and isolation collapses; achieves strong long-context performance via a parameter-free Triangular Box with a length-aware gate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs suffer representation collapse that degrades long-context performance. Two pathological extremes—homogenization collapse (attention sinks, rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (local attention, context disconnection)—limit effectiveness. A balance between mixing (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) is needed.

Method: Spectral analysis of attention dynamics; introduce Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP) with a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight length-aware gate. Regularizes token interaction topology via proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation for robust mixing, without altering core attention.

Result: TRSP yields significant improvements on general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Specifically, on NoLiMa with 8× the training length, TRSP retains 83% accuracy and outperforms Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by ~30 and ~50 percentage points, respectively. Code is available at the provided URL.

Conclusion: TRSP achieves spectral balance and a healthier transition operator while remaining non-invasive to core attention. It improves long-context performance without structural changes to the attention mechanism, demonstrating practical advantages and replicability.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally limited by representation collapse, a bottleneck that severely degrades long-context performance. We identify that existing approaches risk drifting into one of two pathological extremes: homogenization collapse (e.g., attention sinks causing rank deficiency) and isolation collapse (e.g., local attention causing context disconnection). Through spectral analysis of attention dynamics, we derive an intrinsic trade-off between mixing efficiency (spectral gap) and information capacity (effective rank) that standard mechanisms struggle to balance. To resolve this dilemma, we propose the Topologically Regularized Side-Path (TRSP), a non-invasive architectural intervention that achieves spectral balance. TRSP employs a parameter-free Triangular Box mechanism, scaled by a lightweight, length-aware gate, to regularize the token interaction topology. By integrating proximal coupling to preserve effective rank and distal propagation to support non-degenerate mixing, TRSP promotes a geometrically healthier transition operator without altering core attention. Experiments show significant improvements across general capabilities and long-context benchmarks. Notably, on NoLiMa at $8\times$ the training length, TRSP retains $83\%$ accuracy and surpasses the Differential Transformer and Gated Attention by approximately 30 and 50 percentage points, respectively. Code available at: https://github.com/Eziotao-tyd/TRSP.

</details>


### [261] [Expectation Alignment of Language Models for Real-World User Expectations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20485)
*Miaomiao Li,Yang Wang,Bin Liang,Shudong Liu,Zhiwei Zhang,Kam-Fai Wong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes ExpectBench benchmark and LENS framework to study and improve alignment with real user expectations in LLM interactions; evidence of misalignment in current models; approach to extract semantic expectations and latent expectation-aware generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation methods miss diverse, subtle user expectations; misalignment persists between what users want and model outputs; need principled extraction and modeling of expectations.

Method: 1) principled procedure to extract semantic user expectations from real interactions; 2) ExpectBench benchmark grounded in real user expectations; 3) LENS framework to integrate latent expectations into response generation.

Result: Analyses show models struggle to satisfy and anticipate user expectations; LENS improves expectation satisfaction; results suggest explicit expectation modeling yields better alignment.

Conclusion: Modeling and benchmarking user expectations is crucial for realistic human-AI alignment; ExpectBench and LENS provide a path forward and show potential gains.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance on standard benchmarks, yet it remains largely unexplored whether they truly meet user expectations. Existing evaluation approaches, relying on model heuristics, expert rubrics, or user simulation, fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, causing models to appear competent while misaligning with what users actually seek. We present the first systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, proposing a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and introducing ExpectBench, a benchmark grounded in real user expectations. Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

</details>


### [262] [OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20486)
*Zhongzheng Li,Tiancan Feng,Wenhao Li,Qingsong Ran,Shikun Feng,Xiaoyuan Zhang,Yue Wang,Xiaoguang Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPTScientist is a theory-guided, multi-agent framework that discovers optimizers in a typed DSL, combining evolutionary search with DSL extensions to overcome representational bottlenecks, yielding RS-MR that improves transformer pretraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning is hard due to optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and generalization. Existing automated methods either search unconstrained code spaces (flexible but often invalid) or stay within narrow families (stable but limited in novelty). A middle ground using theory-guided, typed DSLs promises more reliable yet expressive optimizer discovery.

Method: OPTScientist deploys four agents—Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer—within a single orchestration loop. Candidate updates are composed from modules for direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping in a typed DSL. The search combines evolutionary optimization over programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small extensions to the DSL when repeated failures signal representational bottlenecks. The framework compiles and evaluates discovered optimizers under a native evaluation protocol and validates them with theory-guided constraints.

Result: The framework discovers RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer, which improves transformer pretraining performance versus strong baselines under the native evaluation protocol.

Conclusion: This work demonstrates a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programming, compiler-validated DAGs/DSLs, and closed-loop experimentation, enabling systematic discovery of novel, reliable optimizers.

Abstract: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

</details>


### [263] [Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20487)
*Chendi Wang,Liam Cunningham,Tom Yishay,Jieying Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A reproducible framework measures LLM hallucinations as signals of ideological drift in political QA; using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles, it finds model differences in hallucination rates and a robust leftward drift in hallucinated content, with uncertainty correlating to drift in some models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess how LLMs propagate ideological distortions in election-adjacent political information and provide auditable safeguards.

Method: (i) create article-specific questions, (ii) obtain document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference comparison, (iv) classify ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, (v) analyze logits to relate token uncertainty to hallucination and drift.

Result: Hallucination rates vary by model and topic; source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest, but hallucination content shows strong leftward drift, including from right-leaning sources. Higher entropy generation contexts increase hallucinations; uncertainty sometimes predicts leftward drift, supporting an “uncertainty to guessing” mechanism.

Conclusion: Auditing AI-mediated political information and designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments require attention to model-specific hallucination behavior and observed leftward ideological drift, with logit-level insights informing uncertainty-aware safeguards.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

</details>


### [264] [Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20488)
*Bronislav Sidik,Chaya Levi,Nizzan Kimhi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ATM enables dynamic runtime topology mutation in multi-agent LLM frameworks to alleviate overload, using telemetry-driven detection and safety invariants; yields large gains in task success and privacy safety with minimal latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fixed topologies in multi-agent LLM systems constrain scalability and reliability; runtime overload (e.g., many action categories, tool errors, or queuing) necessitates dynamic restructuring to maintain performance and safety.

Method: Telemetry-driven Bottleneck Index (six signals: queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, cross-agent wait) triggers when thresholds breach for consecutive ticks. The overloaded agent is factorised into specialized sub-agents; the parent is hot-swapped into a coordinator while preserving its identity. State transfer uses privacy-level-aware routing; memory atoms routed only to permitted child sets or dropped with logged reasons. No topology accepts live traffic until shadow validation. Safety invariants include capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.

Result: Across 720 DeepSeek-V3 task runs and four ablation conditions with three workloads, the ATM factoriser boosts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. Privacy exposure events drop from 2.0 to 0.0 per task. Overflow-related latency adds <500 microseconds p99 on the hot path. An external live-tool probe supports validity. The framework, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

Conclusion: ATM demonstrates safe, scalable runtime topology mutation for multi-agent LLM frameworks. Dynamic specialization via controlled mutation yields substantial task-success gains and privacy improvements with minimal latency, and is viable for practical deployment.

Abstract: Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality. The runtime rails carrying ATM's invariants add less than 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution is included as an external-validity check. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

</details>


### [265] [EvoSQL: Memory-Augmented Critic-Generator Co-Evolution for Text-to-SQL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20489)
*Jiawei Zhou,Jianwei Wang,Chenyu Zhou,Chaojian Shi,Ming Dong,Kai Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EvoSQL is a memory-grounded co-evolution framework for Text-to-SQL that couples a generator and a critic with iterative memory, execution-based verification, and a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization stage to inject execution-aware supervision; it yields consistent gains on Spider and BIRD datasets, especially BIRD-Dev, with code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address beyond-one-shot reasoning in Text-to-SQL by enabling multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction, via a memory-informed generator-critic loop and supervision to backbones.

Method: Iterative generator-critic interaction with a contextualized candidate memory; verification using execution signals and LLM-based critique; memory updated through utility-guided aggregation; SDPO fine-tuning to inject execution-aware supervision into coding LLM backbones.

Result: EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines on Spider and BIRD. Large gains on BIRD-Dev (e.g., +1.37% to +9.19% across models like Qwen3-4B and Qwen2.5-Coder-3B). SDPO initialization also boosts performance on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev.

Conclusion: Memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems; the authors provide code for replication.

Abstract: Text-to-SQL has advanced rapidly with large language models, but complex database queries still require reasoning beyond one-shot generation, including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. We present EvoSQL, a co-evolution framework that formulates SQL synthesis as an iterative interaction between a generator and a critic. EvoSQL maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates with both execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates its memory through utility-guided aggregation. To strengthen the underlying generator-critic pair, we further introduce a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones. Experiments on Spider and BIRD show that EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with particularly large gains on BIRD-Dev, ranging from +1.37% for Qwen3-4B to +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev. These results suggest that memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/EvoSQL.

</details>


### [266] [CRAWO: Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20490)
*Eugênio Santos,Daniel Maia,Stefano Loss,José Manoel Silva,Aluizio Rocha Neto,Thais Batista,Everton Cavalcante,Nélio Cacho,Eduardo Nogueira,Daniel Araújo,Frederico Lopes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CRAWO provides a hardware-aware, controller-loop framework for adaptive, edge-wide AI pipeline orchestration using CRDs and microservices on lightweight Kubernetes, reducing cloud dependency in latency-sensitive scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address heterogeneity and dynamic resource constraints in edge AI deployments; existing platforms lack adaptive scheduling and efficient resource allocation across diverse edge devices.

Method: Control-loop orchestration that decouples allocation from execution; hardware-aware allocator with pluggable MD layer using real-time metrics; domain modeling via CRDs; operator reconciles state; microservices on K3s; inter-stage data flows.

Result: Demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced cloud reliance in latency-sensitive vehicle surveillance with license plate recognition.

Conclusion: CRAWO advances edge AI deployment by enabling adaptive, hardware-aware workload placement across distributed edge infrastructures via a practical CRD-based architecture and reference implementation.

Abstract: Edge Intelligence has emerged as a key paradigm for enabling real-time applications in smart cities by shifting computation from centralized cloud data centers to the network edge, thereby reducing latency and bandwidth consumption. However, deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures remains challenging due to the wide range of device capabilities, from low-power microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems. Existing edge orchestration platforms primarily focus on deployment automation and infrastructure management, but these approaches are often inefficient and limit the ability to adaptively allocate resources under dynamic conditions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces CRAWO (Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration), an architectural framework for coordinating AI pipelines across distributed edge environments. CRAWO follows a control-loop-based model that separates allocation intelligence from execution by managing placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows while instantiating services on edge nodes. The framework incorporates a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that leverages real-time infrastructure metrics to enable adaptive workload placement. The reference implementation adopts a microservices architecture deployed on a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation. Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.

</details>


### [267] [DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20491)
*Raffi Khatchadourian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DFAH-Bench: a replay benchmark for measuring observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across tool-use trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration; reveals that outcome agreement is insufficient to gauge stability; identifies three behavioral profiles; provides dataset and code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard benchmarks evaluate decisions, not the stability of the reasoning/process; need to detect divergent tool paths and evidence usage that lead to the same decision; to improve reliability and interpretability in real-world tool-using agents.

Method: Replay-based benchmark analyzing 8,127 episodes across 10 models and 3 financial tasks; measures three channels (tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, decision concentration) without requiring hidden reasoning text; compute agreement vs path divergence; cluster models into pattern matchers, stable executors, trajectory divergers; release resources.

Result: Found high outcome agreement (95%) but only 77% tool-path agreement, an 18-point gap; many high-agreement cases still show trajectory divergence (>55%); three behavioral profiles emerge; provides empirical evidence that outcome-only metrics miss instability.

Conclusion: Outcome-centric benchmarks miss critical instability; DFAH-Bench offers a multi-channel approach to assess behavioral stability in financial agents; supports more robust evaluation and interpretability; accompanying repository released.

Abstract: Standard evaluation benchmarks measure what a tool-using agent decides, not whether it arrives at that decision through the same process each time. We introduce DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark that measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across three channels -- tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration -- none of which require access to hidden reasoning text. Across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks, we find that outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal: frontier models can agree on decisions 95% of the time while following the same tool path only 77% of the time -- an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) that outcome-only evaluation misses entirely. Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. We identify three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers that achieve near-perfect agreement by collapsing to a single output regardless of input, stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and trajectory divergers that reach the same conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts. The benchmark code, metric scripts, replay logs, benchmark card, dataset README, and release manifest are released in the accompanying repository.

</details>


### [268] [Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20493)
*Quentin Besnard,Nicolas Ragot*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A continual time-series forecasting framework that uses an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention to adapt to changing data distributions while mitigating forgetting, achieving stable or improved performance with reduced retraining on benchmarks and a piezometric dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-stationary, dynamic environments cause distribution shifts in time-series data; static forecasting models struggle to adapt. There is a need for continual learning methods that preserve prior knowledge (stability) while integrating new information (plasticity) under computational constraints.

Method: Extends static forecasting models by incorporating an Experience Replay memory guided by Attention mechanisms to select informative past samples for rehearsal, enabling online adaptation to new contexts while preserving previously learned knowledge.

Result: Empirical results show maintained or improved predictive accuracy over time and reduced retraining data requirements and costs on standard benchmarks and a diverse piezometric time-series dataset.

Conclusion: The Attention-guided replay framework offers a practical path to deploy adaptive forecasting in dynamic settings, mitigating catastrophic forgetting and reducing data/computation needs; further work should explore replay strategies and attention architectures.

Abstract: Deep learning has led to remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, particularly in robotics, imaging and sound processing. However, a major limitation of neural networks remains their strong dependence on large and stationary datasets. In many real-world applications, these conditions are rarely met due to evolving and dynamic environments where data distributions change over time. Continual learning aims to address this challenge by developing models capable of adapting incrementally while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under computational constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for continual time series forecasting, designed to extend existing static forecasting models commonly used in the literature by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This approach allows the model to adapt dynamically to new contexts while preserving prior knowledge, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks as well as on a piezometric dataset exhibiting diverse temporal behaviors. Results show that our approach effectively increases or maintains predictive performance over time while reducing retraining costs and data requirements, thus facilitating the deployment of forecasting models in dynamic and real-world settings.

</details>


### [269] [Isolating LLM Alignment from Regex: Zero Coverage and Metric-Dependent Divergence Under Adversarial Mutation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20494)
*Alexandre Cristovão Maiorano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Disabling the nine-pattern regex in L5-no-regex does not improve coverage over a substring filter; alignment’s impact is metric-dependent, offering detectable refusals for adversarial probes via an LLM judge but no improvement for natural-language harmful probes under substring matching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Test whether a corpus designed to bypass the regex reveals alignment gains when a live Gemini backend is used with a regex filter, challenging the previously observed ceiling.

Method: Introduce L5-no-regex (identical to L4-real but with the regex disabled) and evaluate against N=45 adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified via Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ~1,555 probe-run pairs over N=5 replications. Use a primary substring classifier and a secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants to measure block rates across five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories; assess differential predictions across sub-corpora and report statistical significance.

Result: Primary substring classifier: L5 block rate = 0% across all five OWASP categories; Wilson upper bound <5%; p=1.00 vs L0. LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants shows 56–100% block rates (p<0.01), indicating alignment responds to adversarial framing, but refusals are too nuanced for substring matching. Sub-corpus differential prediction not supported (p=1.00). Alignment’s contribution is metric-dependent: zero added coverage for natural-language probes beyond regex; some added refusals for adversarially framed probes detected by an LLM judge.

Conclusion: Alignment’s impact depends on the evaluation metric: no additional coverage for natural-language harms beyond the regex filter; detectable refusals for adversarially framed probes emerge under LLM-judge metrics, suggesting nuanced alignment behavior. The authors provide the locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts for replication.

Abstract: Production LLM applications commonly stack a regex filter in front of model-side alignment; prior work found no measurable coverage gain from adding a live Gemini backend behind an active regex filter. We ask whether that ceiling holds when the corpus is \emph{designed to bypass the regex}. We introduce $L_5$-no-regex -- identical to $L_4$-real (Gemini-2.5-flash, token-budget cap, rate limit, output scrub) but with the nine-pattern filter disabled -- and evaluate it against $N{=}45$ adversarial probes across three sub-corpora (carry-forward, regex-bypass, alignment-isolate), amplified by Gemini paraphrase and PAIR to ${\sim}1{,}555$ probe-run pairs over $N{=}5$ replications. Under the primary substring classifier, H1 is refuted: $L_5$ block rate is $0,%$ across all five OWASP LLM Top-10 categories ($Δ\text{pp}{=}0$ vs.\ $L_0$, $p{=}1.00$; Wilson upper bound ${<}5,%$). A secondary LLM-judge metric on PAIR variants shows $56$--$100,%$ block rates ($p{<}0.01$), revealing alignment does respond to adversarially-framed probes -- but produces refusals too nuanced for substring matching. The sub-corpus differential prediction is not supported ($p{=}1.00$). Alignment's contribution is \emph{metric-dependent}: on natural-language harmful-request probes, it adds zero observed coverage beyond the regex; on adversarially-framed variants, an LLM judge detects refusals the substring classifier misses. The locked corpus, mutation artifacts, and export scripts are released for replication.

</details>


### [270] [Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20495)
*Anas Mohamed,Kaizan Haque,Azal Ahmad Khan,Chetan Sharma,Shuwen Ge,Ali Anwar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Workload-aware cache eviction for multi-agent DAG execution; a scoring-based policy combining recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency to retain high-value cache entries under memory limits; demonstrates substantial latency reductions and near-unbounded-cache performance, and is complementary to other optimizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Uniform eviction policies ignore structural/workload cues inherent to agent-based workflows; leveraging DAG structure and reuse signals can maximize cache effectiveness under memory constraints.

Method: Introduce a unified scoring function that blends three signals: recomputation cost (cost to recompute an entry), DAG dependency count (how many downstream tasks depend on the cached item), and agent invocation frequency (how often the cached result is requested). Evaluate across three multi-agent benchmarks with varying reuse patterns; compare against uncached, finite-capacity baselines, and unbounded cache; assess latency and accuracy; analyze compatibility with plan-level caching and parallel execution.

Result: Latency reduced up to 64.7% vs uncached baseline; average 31.1% latency reduction over the next-best finite-capacity baseline; performance approaches unbounded cache while maintaining accuracy on par with or better than competing finite-capacity methods.

Conclusion: Workload-aware caching effectively improves throughput in multi-agent pipelines and is complementary to other optimization techniques; the approach targets distinct bottlenecks and can be integrated with plan-level caching and parallelism to maximize efficiency.

Abstract: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

</details>


### [271] [From Errors to Rules: Iterative Prompt Optimization for Text Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20497)
*Yueying Cui,Renhao Xue,Yi Zhang,Mukul Prasad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ERGO is an error-driven prompt optimization method for text classification that complements demonstration-based ICL and exploration-based search by focusing on error patterns to derive decision rules; it excels on boundary-learnable tasks and offers interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To empirically map strengths and limitations of major prompt optimization paradigms for text classification and to offer a unified framework that guides practitioners in selecting the most appropriate paradigm based on task characteristics.

Method: Performed a comprehensive empirical study across diverse benchmarks (2–150 classes) comparing demonstration selection, exploration-based search, and error-driven diagnosis. Introduced ERGO, which iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses errors, and uses a diagnose–prescribe–rewrite feedback loop to generate targeted decision rules. Evaluated on boundary-learnable tasks (e.g., TREC, CLINC150).

Result: ERGO achieves the best accuracy on boundary-learnable tasks (TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%), converges in 3–5 iterations, and yields interpretable decision rules. It does not achieve the highest overall average, but is complementary: ICL excels on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration on many-class intents, and ERGO on boundaries learnable from error patterns.

Conclusion: Task structure dictates the most effective prompt optimization paradigm. The proposed complementarity framework helps practitioners select methods based on task characteristics and provides a practical path to leverage the strengths of multiple paradigms.

Abstract: Prompt optimization for text classification spans diverse approaches, from demonstration selection to exploration-based search to error-driven diagnosis, each with known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (2 to 150 classes) comparing these paradigms through both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces, revealing that each paradigm excels on structurally different task types and that no single method dominates. Guided by these insights, we propose Error-Guided Optimization (ERGO), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules through a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop. ERGO achieves the best accuracy on tasks where errors concentrate in specific confused label pairs (which we term boundary-learnable tasks): TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%, converges in 3-5 iterations, and produces interpretable decision rules. While ERGO does not achieve the highest overall average, it fills a complementary role: demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent, and ERGO wins where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns. We provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical guidance for practitioners.

</details>


### [272] [AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20498)
*Fanjin Zhang,Zhengyang Wang,Ruixuan Huang,Kefan Zhang,Amy Xin,Yuanchun Wang,Shu Zhao,Evgeny Kharlamov,Jie Tang,Juanzi Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A real-world benchmark (AISE-Bench) for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs, with 1,133 QA pairs, full API execution traces, and ground-truth references. Evaluates 14 methods; strongest model shows only moderate performance, highlighting challenges in API planning/execution and grounded, traceable reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill gaps in existing tool-using benchmarks that rely on synthetic templates or narrow tasks by addressing realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, parameterization, grounding with references, and comprehensive process-and-outcome evaluation.

Method: Cre ated AISE-Bench with 1,133 QA pairs, annotated full API execution trajectories, validated API parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. Implemented a customized annotator workflow enabling planning, execution, and revision of complex API workflows. Defined a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, grounding accuracy, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Evaluated 14 methods (including PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro).

Result: AISE-Bench provides a challenging new testbed; strongest model achieves only moderate performance, particularly in API planning/execution; offers datasets and code for replication and further research.

Conclusion: AISE-Bench enables quantitative evaluation of stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning in multi-step API-using LLM agents and is poised to drive improvements in real-world information-seeking tasks over academic knowledge graphs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with tools are emerging as autonomous agents capable of using Web engine, APIs, and code to solve complex, long-horizon tasks. Current tool-using benchmarks for information seeking on academic graphs rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow tasks such as paper-centric tasks, leaving key challenges underexplored - realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling for APIs, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive evaluation of both the process and the outcome. We introduce AISE-Bench, a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs. AISE-Bench release contains 1,133 QA pairs, including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. To support high-quality annotation, we design a customized agent workflow to enable annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows efficiently. We develop a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Among the 14 evaluated methods, even the strongest model (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution.
