AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving the stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents. Our code and data are available at https://aise-bench.github.io/.

</details>


### [273] [ExecuGraph: A Multi-Agent, Execution-Grounded Framework for Reliable Backend Code Synthesis with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20499)
*Sai Deekshith Lekkala,Jothi Prabha Appadurai,Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu,Manpreet Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Multi-agent ExecuGraph framework improves backend code synthesis with execution-based validation, using six agents and a bounded retry budget; configurability enables ablations and controlled measurement of each lever's contribution; gains are modest on internal-30 but notable cross-model, especially with stronger base models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-pass LLM code generation is prone to incorrect or unreliable output. Execution-based validation and modular multi-agent decomposition can improve correctness, reliability, and allow precise measurement of each component's marginal contribution.

Method: Six agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, Explainer) coordinate via a typed directed workflow on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer. A subprocess sandbox with wall-clock timeout guards evaluations. Evaluations are performed on internal-30 (n=30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, comparing ExecuGraph against a one-shot baseline and an execution-retry baseline (Reflexion-style ablation). Extensive ablations include per-agent effects, retry-budget sweeps, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit.

Result: On internal-30, differences among configurations are statistically indistinguishable. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 percentage points. Cross-model gains are larger: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, accuracy goes from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump, supporting a scaling hypothesis where multi-agent decomposition becomes more valuable with stronger base models.

Conclusion: The work's main contribution is methodological: a configurable, single codebase that unifies one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablations to quantify each lever's marginal contribution. It presents per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit, highlighting that multi-agent decomposition yields measurable gains, especially with higher-capability models.

Abstract: Large Language Models generate plausible backend code, but a single-pass paradigm provides no guarantee of correctness or runtime reliability. We present ExecuGraph, a multi-agent framework that places execution-based validation at the center of backend code synthesis. Six specialized agents (Planner, Code Generator, Logical Reviewer, Evaluator, Optimizer, and Explainer) are coordinated by a typed directed workflow with a bounded retry budget, implemented on LangGraph with locally hosted models (Ollama) and an optional retrieval layer for algorithmic technique recall. A subprocess-isolated sandbox with a wall-clock timeout guards every evaluation. We evaluate on a curated 30-problem DSA suite (internal-30), HumanEval (n=64), and an APPS-introductory subset, contrasting ExecuGraph against a single-agent one-shot baseline and a single-agent execution-retry baseline (a Reflexion-style ablation that isolates the contribution of multi-agent decomposition). On internal-30, the three conditions are statistically indistinguishable (n=30; paired Wilcoxon p=0.59 MF vs. SO, p=0.08 SR vs. SO); 95% bootstrap confidence intervals on all pairwise mean differences include zero. On HumanEval, multi-full edges ahead by +3.1 pp. The strongest signal is cross-model: with DeepSeekCoder V2 Lite, graph-category accuracy improves from 57.5% (oneshot) to 80.0% (multi-full), a +22.5 pp jump that supports a scaling hypothesis: the value of multi-agent decomposition grows with base-model capability. The framework's primary contribution is methodological: a single codebase that collapses by configuration into one-shot, execution-retry, and per-agent ablation conditions, enabling controlled measurement of each lever's marginal contribution. A per-agent ablation, retry-budget sweep, error-class taxonomy, and test-source audit are reported.

</details>


### [274] [FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20500)
*Sizhe Tang,Guangyu Jiang,Yu Li,Rongqian Chen,Ioannis G. Kevrekidis,Tian Lan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FlowEdit introduces a branch-aware, information-theoretic framework to regulate internal reasoning in LLMs for ill-posed open-world problems, enabling generation of diverse, valid alternative responses. It demonstrates strong empirical gains in accuracy and informativeness, with observable entropy dynamics in token streams.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ill-posed real-world tasks feature inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or incompatible requirements that defy a single correct answer. Conventional next-token prediction in LLMs struggles to surface hidden conflicts or sustain multiple hypotheses; a mechanism is needed to maintain, compare, and output competing reasoning branches in one pass.

Method: FlowEdit applies two dual information-theoretic objectives on internal reasoning representations: (1) maximize information flow from each selected hypothesis to its branch outcome, and (2) minimize overlap/conditional dependence across sibling branches. This is realized via tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, yielding a branch-aware reasoning process that produces a full set of alternative responses corresponding to valid hypotheses.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, with exact-set-match accuracy up by 68% and overall response informativeness up by 24%. The token stream exhibits redistributed next-token entropy concentrated within branches, peaking at flow boundaries, and scaling with the number of required flows.

Conclusion: FlowEdit offers a principled approach to ill-posed reasoning by enforcing multiple competing hypotheses and delivering diverse, informative responses. It provides a theoretical and empirical framework for information-flow regulation in LLMs, though questions remain about measurement of internal flows, generalization across tasks/models, and computational overhead.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

</details>


### [275] [MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20501)
*Jason Yoo,Rajarshi Saha,Shaowei Zhu,Tao Yu,Wei Tang,Youngsuk Park*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular co-evolution framework for kernel generation (MKEvolve) that jointly evolves PyTorch module decompositions and LLM-generated subkernels, yielding configurable, interpretable kernels with better correctness and speed and lower token usage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Kernel development for hardware accelerators remains a bottleneck despite advances in LLM-based code generation. A modular, interpretable, and adaptable approach is needed to ensure correctness and performance across model architectures while reducing dependence on end-to-end synthesis.

Method: Iteratively co-evolve a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule. Across iterations, split/fuse the decomposition, while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The final kernels are compositions of independently verified subkernels, enabling swappability, traceability of errors/speedups to specific subkernels, and easy adaptation to related architectures.

Result: Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, covering multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve achieves higher correctness and speedups than end-to-end direct synthesis baselines and reduces LLM token usage by up to 35%.

Conclusion: MKEvolve provides a configurable, interpretable, and adaptable pathway to scalable kernel generation for ML workloads, with demonstrated gains in correctness and performance and reduced dependency on large-scale token usage.

Abstract: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

</details>


### [276] [Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20502)
*Jan Speller,Malte Luttermann,Marcel Gehrke,Tanya Braun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Laplace-based extension scheme to lift two probabilistic graphical models with non-identical variable sets to a common measurable space, preserving semantics while enabling distributional comparisons.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable principled, quantitative comparison of probabilistic graphical models defined on different variable sets by placing them on a shared measurable space.

Method: Extend unmatched components using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions so that joint distributions are equal up to multiplicative constants and coincide under projection; prove invariance of the joint under projection; provide deterministic algorithms to compute minimal structural extension to the smallest common space and to a common graphical structure; analyze structural and measure-theoretic properties.

Result: Induced joint distribution is invariant under projection; extension yields minimally extended factor graphs on the smallest common space and on a common structure; enables well-defined distributional discrepancy measures and informs comparison methodologies.

Conclusion: The proposed extension framework preserves probabilistic semantics, supports principled comparison across non-identical variable spaces, and offers a deterministic method for constructing a shared representation with useful measure-theoretic properties and criteria for evaluation.

Abstract: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

</details>


### [277] [LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20503)
*Lazar Milikic,Simon Guilloud,Khanh Nguyen,Viktor Kuncak*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LeanFlow enables translating mathematical papers into Lean projects with efficient runtimes and token usage; Kimi2.6 completes within 2000 calls, GPT5.5 achieves full document-level completion with low token cost, and benchmarks show strong formalization performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, and efficiency in document-to-project formalization and to identify configurations that yield reliable, scalable leanification.

Method: Perform two case studies on previously unformalized papers in number theory and measure theory, conducting ablations across model, proof-workflow, and toolset using Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; report task outcomes, API calls, input/output tokens.

Result: With Kimi2.6, full document-level workflows complete within a 2000-call budget; no-queue variants reach the budget limit. With GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the workflow shows the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost across sources. LeanFlow attains 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in GPT5.5 runs.

Conclusion: Configuring runtime mechanisms (model choices, workflows, and toolsets) materially impacts completion, auditability, and efficiency in document-to-formalization; LeanFlow demonstrates robust effectiveness across diverse papers and benchmark suites, suggesting practical guidelines for scaling AI-assisted formal verification workflows.

Abstract: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

</details>


### [278] [Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20506)
*Houda Khrouf,Pedro Fillastre,Sebastiao Correia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperGraphRAG extends GraphRAG with hypergraphs for richer semantics, addressing extraction and retrieval bottlenecks via self-consistency prompting and Personalized PageRank.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Graph-based RAG struggles with representing n-ary facts and relies on extraction quality; standard chunk retrieval is inefficient, limiting reasoning depth.

Method: Use self-consistency prompting to stabilize LLM extractions of facts; represent knowledge as a hypergraph and apply Personalized PageRank to retrieve relevant chunks.

Result: Aims to improve accuracy and retrieval efficiency by mitigating extraction errors and retrieval bottlenecks; the abstract does not provide quantitative metrics.

Conclusion: Integrates hypergraph-based knowledge representation with improved extraction and retrieval strategies to enhance reasoning capabilities in RAG systems.

Abstract: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

</details>


### [279] [MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20507)
*Jingquan Chen,Jinghua Piao,Jie Feng,Shaogang Hu,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MiniCache is a reusable program caching framework that caches PoT programs as parameterized cache objects, enabling cross-request reuse and reducing LLM invocations, with small models handling semantic extraction and drafting, achieving lower latency and higher throughput.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce inference cost and latency of LLM-based program-aided reasoning and agentic tasks by reusing computation across structurally similar requests.

Method: Transform Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, reuse the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests, and perform speculative drafting during target-LLM generation to reduce costly invocations while preserving task quality; evaluate on shopping-style datasets (WebShop), Formula, and CodeTAT-QA to analyze latency, cache reuse, and accuracy.

Result: Up to 3.1x latency reduction and 2.8x throughput improvement under parallel serving; improved trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy; demonstrates that small models function effectively as lightweight interface models enabling reliable reusable program caching.

Conclusion: Small models are most effective not as direct replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

</details>


### [280] [Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20510)
*Dmitrii Khizbullin,Zaid Alyafeai,Abdelrahman Eldesokey,Nourah AlSultan,Raghad Alshalan,David R. Pugh,Bernard Ghanem*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on real telecom operator data, with 100 English/Arabic tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning across HTML/static docs, a synthetic SQL DB, and external web archives; evaluated in a sandboxed Docker environment with normalized exact string matching; strongest models solve up to 71%, about 40% under a budget, with visually grounded tasks being the weakest; offers a rigorous, reproducible enterprise testbed and a template for closed-domain benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To create a rigorous, reproducible, closed-domain benchmark that stresses multi-modal reasoning and tool usage for enterprise-grade agents operating on real-world telecom data.

Method: Construct 100 tasks (English and Arabic) demanding multi-hop reasoning (average 4.2 hops) over three heterogeneous sources: static website snapshot (HTML, images, PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives. Delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment; scoring via normalized exact string matching; evaluation across twelve commercial and open LLMs to gauge performance.

Result: Telco-GAIA is challenging: the best model solves 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, performance drops to ~40%. Visually grounded categories are the weakest, with backend scores below 30%, indicating room for improvement in document and image understanding.

Conclusion: Provides a rigorous, reproducible enterprise testbed and serves as a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

Abstract: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

</details>


### [281] [SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20511)
*Keonhee Park,Gunhee Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SiGMA introduces sign-guided adaptive tuning and sign-guided merging to mitigate negative interference in Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT). It reduces forgetting during training and preserves useful knowledge during inference, outperforming state-of-the-art MCIT on UCIT and DCL benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem: MCIT models suffer from negative interference (forgetting and interference from new tasks) and degradation at inference when updates overwrite prior knowledge. Existing MCIT approaches (e.g., Mixture of Experts, expansion merging) do not adequately address inference-time negative interference.

Method: Two components: (1) Sign-guided adaptive tuning: during training, steer updates to reduce collisions with past knowledge and minimize task drift; (2) Sign-guided merging: during inference, selectively scale salient parameters to preserve/amplify useful task-specific knowledge, improving consolidation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on UCIT and DCL benchmarks shows SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state-of-the-art MCIT methods. Code is publicly available.

Conclusion: SiGMA provides a simple, effective framework for MCIT, combining sign-guided training and merging to balance plasticity and stability, achieving superior continual learning performance on multimodal tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

</details>


### [282] [Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20515)
*Jingyi Huang,Ruohan Zong,Yujun Feng,Liran Ma,Lanyu Shang,Yang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO) enhances RLHF by modeling annotator reliability and inferring latent ground-truth labels from noisy feedback, plus a reliability-aware consistency objective that emphasizes high-consensus annotations; it outperforms standard RLHF baselines on LLM alignment benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Human feedback is inherently inconsistent and subjective, causing RLHF to overfit to noisy signals if treated uniformly; existing methods like DPO do not account for annotator reliability or consensus levels.

Method: Estimate annotator reliability; infer latent ground-truth preferences from noisy annotations; develop a reliability-aware consistency optimization that scales the training loss by annotation consensus to prioritize high-consensus signals.

Result: RGPO reduces the impact of inconsistent/noisy data and achieves superior performance compared to widely used RLHF baselines on LLM alignment benchmarks.

Conclusion: Incorporating annotator reliability and consensus-aware optimization yields more robust RLHF, improving alignment quality; code and configs are released for reproducibility.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

</details>


### [283] [CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20518)
*Xue-Jian Gao,Deng Pan,Yueming Su,Jiasheng Li,Bin Du,Fengming Zhu,Chengdi Ma,Junyi Fan,Qichen Liao,Chengqiu Hu,Xinxian Chen,Lingchao Zheng,Jun Li,Jiwei Yang,Yuwei Fan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CANN Bench is an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei Ascend NPU, covering 53 operators across four difficulty tiers, with a 3D weighted score evaluating compilation, correctness, and performance, anchored to real hardware and baseline PyTorch-on-Ascend, designed for community maintenance within the official CANN repo.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the lack of standardized benchmarks for non-CUDA/Triton hardware ecosystems, enabling reproducible, hardware-relevant evaluation of AI-generated operator kernels and promoting ecosystem growth.

Method: A benchmark suite of 53 operators with 1060 test cases across four difficulty tiers (elementwise to MoE/FlashAttention), evaluating FP16, BF16, FP32, INT8. Uses a three-dimensional weighted composite score (compilation, functional correctness, performance). Performance is measured against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and a Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real Ascend hardware. Includes a reward-hacking resistant evaluation harness and versioning within the official CANN repository for long-term community maintenance.

Result: The framework enables principled scoring that reflects genuine optimization headroom, differentiates kernel-generation agents, and provides a reproducible yardstick for Ascend operator authoring.

Conclusion: CANN Bench offers a reproducible, community-driven benchmark for AI operator development on Ascend, aligning with the Ascend ecosystem’s goals and ensuring sustainable evaluation of AI-generated kernels beyond CUDA-focused benchmarks.

Abstract: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

</details>


### [284] [Representation Robustness Under Executable Reasoning Constraints in Large Language Models for Mathematical Problem Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20520)
*Sagnik Nath,Edith Aurora Graf,Liang Zhang,Diego Zapata-Rivera*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs show representational brittleness in math problem solving: equivalent formulations change correctness; code-based reasoning reveals latent capabilities but doesn't fix robustness; representation should be a core interface variable in evaluation/deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To evaluate whether LLMs' math problem-solving performance is robust to surface representations, separating reasoning errors from interface failures and highlighting how reformulations affect outcomes.

Method: Curate a dataset of mathematically equivalent problems across surface forms (story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, isomorphic paraphrases). Evaluate five contemporary LLMs under direct answer generation and a code-augmented setting where reasoning is externalized as Python code executed locally. Assess correctness, robustness across representations, and failure modes.

Result: Models exhibit substantial representational sensitivity: correctness flips across equivalent formulations; isomorphic paraphrases degrade performance; code-augmented reasoning uncovers latent capabilities in some models but introduces new failure modes (protocol violations, execution errors) and does not fully eradicate brittleness; robustness tradeoffs persist (latency, cost, reliability).

Conclusion: Representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment for AI-assisted problem solving; while reasoning scaffolds can reveal latent capabilities, they do not eliminate brittleness and introduce new design tradeoffs.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated on mathematical problem solving, yet prior work often treats representationally equivalent formulations as interchangeable and conflates reasoning errors with interface failures. This paper investigates representation robustness in LLM-based mathematical problem solving by systematically varying surface representations of the same underlying problems, including story problems, word-equations, symbolic equations, and isomorphic paraphrases. Using a curated dataset of mathematically equivalent problems, we evaluate five contemporary LLMs under a direct answer generation condition. We find substantial representational sensitivity: models frequently change correctness across equivalent formulations, with nontrivial flip rates across story, symbolic, and word-equation variants. We also observe systematic regressions under isomorphic reformulations, showing that even subtle paraphrase-level changes can degrade performance despite preserved mathematical structure. We then evaluate a code-augmented condition in which models externalize reasoning as executable Python code that is run locally for validation. This interface reveals strong latent reasoning capability in some models that perform poorly under direct prompting, but it does not uniformly improve robustness. Instead, failures shift across interaction layers, from opaque reasoning errors to protocol violations and execution failures. Even when executable reasoning succeeds, representation sensitivity often persists. Overall, our results show that reasoning scaffolds do not eliminate representational brittleness, but expose new tradeoffs among correctness, reliability, latency, and cost. We argue that representation should be treated as a first-class interface design variable in LLM evaluation and deployment, especially for AI-assisted problem-solving systems.

</details>


### [285] [Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20524)
*Sagar Dangal,Manoj Shakya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper questions whether mean cross-positional attention degradation in transformers causally limits contextual retrieval. Through six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2, it characterizes early attention degradation, explores function-token anchoring, and tests causality via Relay-Aware Attention (RAA). It finds universal degradation patterns but shows that increasing attention to function tokens yields mixed, often null, retrieval effects. The main takeaway is that degradation is largely descriptive: hidden states, not attention receipts, drive function tokens’ contributions, with implications for interpretability methods and KV-cache optimizations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish whether mean cross-positional attention degradation causally limits contextual retrieval and to assess the interpretability implications of attention-based diagnostics across diverse transformer architectures.

Method: Six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. Characterization of short-term attention degradation (5–100 tokens) revealing a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern, analysis of function-token anchoring across architectures, strategic comma insertion to test syntactic boundary effects, Relay-Aware Attention (RAA) to bias attention toward function tokens, and multi-fact retrieval probes to relate degradation rate to retrieval accuracy.

Result: Found a universal exponential-then-plateau degradation pattern whose rate decreases with depth; architecture-specific function-token anchoring (OPT with absolute positional encoding showing distance-dependent specificity; GPT-2 uniform non-specific; LLaMA RoPE showing long-distance reversal). Comma insertion reduces degradation in 40–80 tokens when aligned with syntactic boundaries. RAA increases attention mass by 16–24% but shows mixed to null effects on predictive degradation across models (null for GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm for LLaMA-3B, ~zero for OPT-1.3B). Degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy in multi-fact probes. 

Conclusion: Mean attention degradation appears largely descriptive rather than prescriptive; function tokens influence predictions through their hidden states rather than delivered attention. This challenges attention-score-based interpretability inferences and suggests limited utility of degrading-attention as a causal lever; implications for interpretability methods and KV-cache eviction strategies.

Abstract: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

</details>


### [286] [Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20525)
*Yichen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An autonomous GPT-5.5 Pro agent produced seven correct disproofs of the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over R in eight trials (one trial with an unresolved gap); demonstrates a three-stage prompting pipeline for autonomous proofs, with reproducible code and outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess AI capabilities in autonomous mathematical proof construction and verification, and contribute to the literature on the sum-product phenomenon over the real numbers by providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study.

Method: A problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline: proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review. The agent iteratively generated proofs, some mirroring unit-based constructions and others using L^p-type regions of algebraic integers. It averaged 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial and released code, intermediate outputs, and proofs for reproducibility.

Result: The agent discredited the conjecture over R in 7 of 8 independent trials; one trial identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs varied in approach, with some close to unit-based constructions and others avoiding units via L^p regions; all proofs were produced autonomously.

Conclusion: This work illustrates the potential of AI agents to autonomously generate mathematical proofs and to provide reproducible case studies, while also acknowledging that human verification remains essential due to occasional gaps.

Abstract: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

</details>


### [287] [ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20526)
*Matthew ffrench-Constant,Daniel Yang,Xinmeng Huang,Sanyam Kapoor*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConfidenceBench assesses LLM confidence calibration via verbalized probabilities (Brier score) across 15 models on 200 private MCQs; top performers achieve 0.103, beating the calibrated-random baseline (0.1875). Calibration diverges from accuracy, indicating confidence calibration is a distinct axis of reliability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In high-stakes settings, correct answers alone are insufficient; models must indicate when they are likely to err. Verbalized confidence offers a practical calibration signal, and the Brier score incentivizes truthful probability reporting, enabling fair comparison across closed- and open-source systems without access to logits.

Method: Prompt-based elicitation of confidence (no logits required) for 200 private MCQs spanning spatial reasoning, high-precision math, word lookup, and unknowable questions, evaluated across 15 frontier LLMs in three runs. Brier score is used as the evaluation metric; calibrated-random baseline is 0.1875.

Result: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores (0.103). Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367. Calibrated-random baseline is 0.1875; several models fall below it, indicating miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge across model families; the most accurate model is not necessarily the best calibrated.

Conclusion: Verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct, practically important axis of LLM reliability that complements accuracy-based evaluation. The findings underscore the need to assess both correctness and calibrated confidence, and they highlight variability in calibration across model families that is not explained by accuracy alone.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

</details>


### [288] [Evaluating and Guarding Citation Faithfulness in Agentic Scientific Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20527)
*Taewan Goo,Junsik Kim,Kyulhee Han,GwonYul Jo,Jong-Soo Kim,Tae-Hyung Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Shows variability and unreliability in verifier checks of citations in agentic LLMs; proposes a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and conformal guard; validates across multiple models and benchmarks; enables bounded, reproducible measurement with an open-kit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current citation checks in agentic LLMs are not reliably calibrated; different verifiers produce different flag sets and disagree on which citations to flag, undermining cross-paper comparisons and trust in claimed factuality.

Method: Introduce a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard. Use a swappable verifier calibrated to human gold, deterministic BM25-based re-attribution, and a split-conformal layer to produce distribution-free, finite-sample bounds on truly unsupported citations. Calibrate via a concrete recalibration recipe; validate across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA; provide an open single-GPU kit.

Result: Found that identical agent outputs yield 3%–18% unsupported citations depending on verifier strictness; verifiers agree on which citations are supported but disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27–0.30). The guard yields a bound on true unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flag, calibrated to human gold, and transferrable under certain conditions. Re-attribution is deterministic via BM25. Protocol and guard validated with confidence intervals on headline numbers.

Conclusion: The proposed gold-anchored protocol and conformal guard enable measurable, bounded auditing of citation-checking in agentic LLMs. Cross-paper comparisons require a named verifier and protocol; the approach is open and deployable, but transferability depends on calibration conditions and task/domain. Open-kit facilitates replication.

Abstract: Agentic LLM systems such as OpenScholar and PaperQA2 read the scientific literature and return cited answers, and both they and their benchmarks already check whether those citations hold, with a fixed attribution model or human graders. Neither audits the reliability of that check itself. We show it is not reliable, and that this matters. On identical agent outputs the measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to about 18% depending only on the verifier's strictness, and although verifiers agree on which citations are supported, they disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27 to 0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy and cross-paper comparison is invalid without a named verifier and protocol.
  We present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that make this behavior measurable and bounded. The protocol validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates a guarantee against human gold rather than another model's verdict; the verifier is a swappable instrument chosen on cost (recall 0.94 on the supported class, held out), and re-attribution is a commodity step where a deterministic BM25 matches the best open generator. The guard adds a split-conformal layer placing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flagging rule, a guarantee on catch rate rather than conclusion correctness. The bound holds on held-out gold, and we identify and quantify the condition governing its transfer to deployment, calibration-negative difficulty, with a concrete recalibration recipe, left untested by prior conformal-factuality work.
  Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on public benchmarks (SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA), with confidence intervals on every headline number, the protocol and guard ship as an open single-GPU kit.

</details>


### [289] [PromptPack: Scaling LLM Annotation Agents for Online Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20528)
*Sebastian Koralewski,Merwan Barlier,Yulia Stolin,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Batch-based LLM annotation (PromptPack) reduces per-request cost by 89% and doubles throughput (2.5x) while preserving AUC, via shared prompts, XML envelope, and output correction for multi-creatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Per-creative prompting is costly; redundant system instructions constitute ~94% of tokens; a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation solution is needed for ad creatives in production.

Method: In-context batching with a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives; evaluation via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker; introduction of Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL) as a signal quality metric; batch size of 20.

Result: Cost reduced by 89%, throughput increased by 2.5x, and AUC preserved versus unbatched production baseline; VWAL introduced to quantify feature signal quality; evaluation on an offline benchmark with a downstream LR ranker.

Conclusion: PromptPack demonstrates scalable, accurate LLM-based feature extraction for ads, achieving substantial cost and latency benefits without sacrificing predictive quality; the design—shared prompts, strict structure, and correction layer—enables deterministic, multi-creatives processing; future work may explore broader evaluation, robustness, and generalization across contexts.

Abstract: Online recommendation platforms increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract structured features from ad creatives. While deploying a single-call LLM annotation agent yields significant Click-Through Rate (CTR) improvements in our live production environment, per-creative prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale. The redundant system instructions sent in every request account for 94% of billed input tokens. To break this cost bottleneck, we introduce PromptPack, a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation agent. PromptPack achieves this scale via in-context batching, combining a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives simultaneously. We evaluate PromptPack via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker. To deeply profile the agent's behavior, we measure AUC and introduce Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), a novel metric capturing the signal quality of the generated features. Compared to our live, unbatched production baseline, PromptPack at batch size 20 cuts our LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x while fully preserving AUC.

</details>


### [290] [DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20531)
*Jerzy Kamiński,Ilya Galyukshev,Artem Kuznetsov,Sergey Chuprin,Kirill Redko,Aidar Shumbalov,Anna Kalyuzhnaya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DynamicMCPBench is a reusable framework that evaluates LLM agents on live MCP servers by recording autonomous task trajectories and checking whether agents reproduce the effects of those trajectories, rather than judging final answers. It exposes generalization across servers/models and reveals substantial shortfall in handling long, multi-step tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Benchmarking LLM agents in live, stateful settings is fragile if based on final answers or fixed tool lists. A reusable, server-agnostic framework is needed to measure genuine agentic capabilities through effect reproduction.

Method: Generate realistic goals, execute them live on MCP servers, record successful trajectories, distill into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and score reproduction of these effects (pass^3: three independent attempts must succeed). Run across many models/servers/tasks and validate automatic scoring with human judgment.

Result: Across 24 models, 121 servers, and 750 tasks across 15 categories, strongest agents solve ~50% of tasks; 31% unsolved by any model; task success declines with longer tool chains (39% for shortest, 13% for longest). Human validation yields chance-corrected agreement of 0.76, indicating reliable automatic scoring.

Conclusion: DynamicMCPBench enables practitioners to benchmark on their own servers and models while exposing current limitations of agents in long, multi-step, tool-use tasks, highlighting the need for more robust long-horizon reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed "ground-truth" list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3: it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

</details>


### [291] [AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20536)
*Junzhi Chen,Harsh Trivedi,Jane Pan,Michael JQ Zhang,Tejas Srinivasan,Niranjan Balasubramanian,Ashish Sabharwal*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AppWorld-UL is a user-in-the-loop benchmark with 516 tasks across 9 simulated apps (e.g., Amazon, Spotify) designed to evaluate diverse agent-user interactions, revealing that state-of-the-art LLMs struggle with such interactions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap where existing benchmarks fail to capture the diversity of agent-user interactions and their limited, non-state-changing APIs by introducing realistic, interactive tasks requiring clarifications and user constraints.

Method: Extend the AppWorld framework to 516 tasks with ambiguities and constraints requiring agent-user interaction; simulate users via a controlled LLM with designed knowledge boundaries; evaluate on Claude Opus 4.7 across overall, compositional, and scenario-level metrics.

Result: Claude Opus 4.7 achieves 48.6% overall success, 35.7% on the compositional subset, and 21.3% on scenario-level tasks, highlighting the critical role of correct user-interaction in task success.

Conclusion: AppWorld-UL is a challenging, realistic benchmark that can drive research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents and reveal limitations of current LLMs in managing interactive workflows.

Abstract: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a ``user-in-the-loop'' benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

</details>


### [292] [StrideDiffusion: Accelerating Diffusion Models for Time-series Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20545)
*Du Yin,Estrid He,Julián Jerónimo Bañuelos,Yang Yang,Feng Hu,Yuchen Luo,Hao Xue,Stephan Sigg,Flora Salim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: StrideDiffusion is a training-free, spectral-aware sampler for time-series diffusion that adaptively selects the denoising stride based on band-level activity, enabling large speedups with preserved or improved quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion models for time-series demand many sequential denoising steps. Fixed or generic timesteps fail to exploit that different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process.

Method: At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to decide whether to take fine steps (active high-frequency bands) or larger jumps (dominant low-frequency structure). The approach is training-free. A bandwise stability analysis shows inactive bands change linearly with jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, supporting spectral activity as a step-size indicator.

Result: Across six unconditional time-series benchmarks, it uses 14–66 function evaluations instead of 500–1000 steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it delivers 5–14x average acceleration with similar predictive accuracy.

Conclusion: Spectral evolution provides a practical, principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling; the method is training-free and scalable across tasks; code is released.

Abstract: Diffusion models have become competitive generators for time series, but their practical use is limited by the large number of sequential denoising steps required at inference time. Existing fast samplers typically use fixed or generic timestep schedules, overlooking a distinctive property of time-series diffusion: different spectral bands evolve at different rates during the reverse process. We introduce StrideDiffusion, a training-free spectral-aware sampler that adaptively selects the denoising stride from band-level activity. At each step, StrideDiffusion monitors relative band energy, log-power drift, and phase velocity to identify whether high- frequency dynamics remain active or whether the trajectory is dominated by stable low-frequency structure. It then takes fine steps when rapidly varying bands are active and larger jumps once only coarse components remain. A bandwise stability analysis shows that inactive frequency bands change only linearly with the jump size under deterministic affine reverse updates, providing a local justification for spectral activity as a step-size indicator. Across six unconditional time-series generation benchmarks, StrideDiffusion uses only 14-66 function evaluations instead of 500/1000 denoising steps, achieving up to 18.9x wall-clock speedup while preserving or improving generation quality. On conditional imputation and forecasting, it further delivers 5-14x average acceleration with comparable predictive accuracy. These results show that spectral evolution provides a practical and principled signal for fast time-series diffusion sampling. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/stridediff-ts.

</details>


### [293] [CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20553)
*Yubo Wang,Qiuyu Zhao,Zenghui Sun,Shichao Dong,Jinsong Lan,Xiaoyong Zhu,Haoyang Li,Bo Zheng,Lei Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes CMI-Mem, an RL-based lightweight memory manager that uses a hybrid reward (downstream QA correctness + intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information) to assess the contribution of new inputs to memory, independent of sampled QA queries, complementing QA grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing memory managers rely on LLM-judged synthetic QA pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. The authors aim to provide a query-agnostic information contribution signal via intrinsic CMI to complement QA grounding.

Method: Train a lightweight memory manager with reinforcement learning using a hybrid reward: downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by a new conversational input relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thus offering a query-agnostic valuation of memory updates.

Result: The abstract does not report empirical results. It presents the proposed approach and provides code availability (GitHub) and a 4B model checkpoint.

Conclusion: CMI-Mem introduces a complementary signal to QA grounding by using intrinsic CMI as part of a hybrid RL reward to guide memory updates, potentially improving memory valuation beyond QA-grounded signals; code and model weights are publicly available.

Abstract: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

</details>


### [294] [AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20554)
*Giambattista Amati,Federica Mangiatordi,Simone Angelini,Emiliano Pallotti,Pierpaolo Salvo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A real-time, graph-based Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework using a GINE network for NR-V2X multi-hop relay selection, supervised by an offline MILP oracle, achieving MILP-like connectivity with orders-of-magnitude lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome limited RSU density, frequent NLOS, and dynamic vehicular topologies that hinder stable single-hop connectivity; MILP gives optimal decisions but is impractical in real time due to high complexity.

Method: Model CAVs and RSUs as attributed graphs with candidate links as edges; use propagation-aware edge features; train an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) to mimic MILP oracle decisions; offline MILP provides supervision; deployment yields near-constant, real-time inference.

Result: On large-scale SUMO-GEMV2 urban datasets, the L2O approach achieves connectivity comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude, enabling scalable NR-V2X operation.

Conclusion: The framework enables cost-effective, real-time enhancement of urban V2X connectivity using existing vehicular assets, supporting scalable NR-V2X relay selection in smart city environments.

Abstract: Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude. The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

</details>


### [295] [KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20556)
*Yan Zhu,Y. Chen,Rebecca Faust*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KeySI introduces a keyword-centric interaction for tuning pre-trained embeddings via concept groups, translating keyword-level feedback into document-level supervision, reducing labeling burden and improving domain adaptation; evaluated through user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale text embeddings often miss domain-specific semantics and require labeled data and complex pipelines to adapt. By enabling keyword-based feedback, KeySI lowers the barrier to aligning embeddings with user intent without extensive document labeling.

Method: Prototype that curates representative keywords from a corpus, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, lets users form keyword groups representing concepts, and translates these groups into document-level supervision for subsequent fine-tuning of embeddings. The process supports iterative refinement with system feedback.

Result: Empirical evaluation (user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments) demonstrates that the keyword-based supervision can capture user intent and improve embedding alignment.

Conclusion: Keyword-based interaction through keyword groups is an effective and low-barrier approach to domain adaptation of text embeddings, with KeySI providing a practical prototype and positive initial evidence.

Abstract: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

</details>


### [296] [WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20638)
*Yichuan Liu,Daniel Cummings,Nick Vadlamudi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WaveformQA is an open-source benchmark to test LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms, featuring 360 questions across 8 categories, programmatically generated ground truths from real hardware, and an event-time JSON representation that improves accuracy over VCD; the framework is extensible for future research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks emphasize HDL code generation and treat waveforms merely as context, leaving a gap in evaluating LLMs' temporal reasoning over waveform data and grounding benchmarks in real hardware behavior; addressing context window and multi-signal reasoning challenges.

Method: Construct 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight temporal categories (including multi-signal correlation and event ordering); generate waveforms from open-source designs to ensure realism; compare representations by evaluating LLMs on VCD vs an event-time JSON format; provide an open-source framework for extending questions and waveform sources.

Result: Frontier LLMs show reasonable accuracy on simple queries but degrade on complex temporal and multi-step questions due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulty; event-time JSON representation improves LLM reasoning accuracy over VCD; the framework enables rapid, reproducible temporal reasoning experiments and easy extension to new sources/categories.

Conclusion: WaveformQA offers a reproducible, extensible benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning in hardware design, grounded in real waveform sources and supporting improved representations to boost reasoning.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

</details>


### [297] [NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20709)
*Paul Furgale,Severin Klingler,James Nolan,Matt Staats,Gaia Di Lorenzo,Elisa Martinez Abad,Christian Schüller,Razvan Dinu,Alessio Devoto,Pascal Berard,Gal Kaplun,Elad Sarafian,Riccardo Roveri,Leon Derczynski,Ricardo Silveira Cabral*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NOOA offers a model-agnostic Python framework where agents are Python objects; methods with '...' are completed by an LLM-driven loop at runtime, unifying agent development with standard software engineering practices.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional agent development is fragmented into prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs, hindering testability and reliability; NOOA aims to simplify and unify agent development via a Python-native interface with shared abstractions.

Method: Agent-as-a-Python-object: an agent is a Python class; methods are actions; fields are state; docstrings encode prompts; type annotations specify contracts. A method with body '...' triggers a runtime LLM-driven action loop; normal bodies are deterministic Python. Exposes context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops through Pythonic APIs; supports pass-by-reference on live objects, code-as-action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context/events.

Result: Empirical validation on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 as well as ARC-AGI-3; NOOA demonstrates effective use by current models in targeted capability tests and agentic/reasoning benchmarks.

Conclusion: The approach provides a unified, testable, and refactor-friendly interface that aligns agent development with standard Python software practices, potentially accelerating adoption by leveraging familiar abstractions.

Abstract: Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python. This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events.
