We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

</details>


### [298] [ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20764)
*Pavel Golikov,Evgenii Opryshko,Gennady Pekhimenko,Mark C. Jeffrey*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark suite ARBIGRAPH that models tasks as natural-language problems with executable Python solvers and typed intermediate states to form controllable task graphs, revealing failures in long-horizon, tool-assisted reasoning not seen in isolated tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-task benchmarks miss failure modes in extended reasoning with tool use; a controllable, verifiable benchmark is needed to evaluate retention, update, composition, and discard of task-relevant context across chains and branches.

Method: Construct ARBIGRAPH as natural-language problems each paired with an executable Python solver; compose tasks via typed intermediate states (scalar/list) to create graphs with adjustable length, dependencies, distractor counts, and value types; instantiate categories (math, GSM-style word problems, Python-tracing) and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies.

Result: High accuracy on isolated tasks; substantial degradation on complex dependent tasks, with up to 33.3% accuracy drop on branching chains of dependent math tasks; demonstrates that ARBIGRAPH uncovers failures not evident from single-task evaluation.

Conclusion: ARBI GRAPH exposes failure modes overlooked by single-task tests; provides code, datasets, and evaluation results at the linked GitHub repository for reproducibility and broader benchmarking.

Abstract: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

</details>


### [299] [The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20781)
*Bonny Banerjee,Shreya Singh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Analytical HAT model for human–AI task allocation in hierarchical organizations, deriving a substitution principle and conditions for AI-driven workforce transformation, including abrupt transitions, hybrid structures, and implications for organizational design and governance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the core economic and organizational question of when AI replaces human labor; formalize asymmetry between human skill growth and AI scaling; unify automation economics with organizational design.

Method: Develop a theoretical analytical model of HAT in hierarchical organizations, encoding asymmetry; derive risk-adjusted cost conditions, depth, deployment scale, and risk differentials; establish the Human–AI Substitution Principle; analyze transitions, hybrid forms, and structural vulnerability across layers.

Result: Derives precise condition for AI substituting for human labor; identifies abrupt transitions, hybrid organizations, and absence of minimum-human-fraction constraints; shows middle-management vulnerability and skill-threshold effects; predicts flatter hierarchies under AI adoption; connects automation economics, organizational design, governance, and workforce planning.

Conclusion: Offers a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation, providing criteria for adoption and governance that integrate economics, structure, and workforce planning.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

</details>


### [300] [Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20791)
*Phillip Howard,Xin Su,Allen Roush,Manikandan Ravikiran,Amir Abdullah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper addresses preserving refusal behavior in high-temperature, high-entropy LLM sampling by proposing an efficient sequential decoding method that maintains most of the greedy-decoding refusals (91-99%) with minimal latency, without sacrificing safe-prompts performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: High-temperature sampling increases diversity but weakens model safety/refusal behavior. There is a lack of methods that preserve refusals under high entropy, creating a gap for safe and diverse generation.

Method: An efficient sequential decoding approach designed to preserve a model's greedy decoding refusal responses at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency during decoding.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows the proposed method preserves 91-99% of greedy-decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets, with no degradation to the model's high-temperature performance on safe prompts.

Conclusion: Refusal behavior can be maintained efficiently under high-temperature sampling, enabling diverse outputs without compromising safety guarantees on prompts.

Abstract: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

</details>


### [301] [Can an AI System Be Creative? A Critical Perspective from Art and Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20796)
*Ivan Magrin-Chagnolleau*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Using Boden's framework, the paper argues AI cannot achieve creativity in its strongest sense; AI displays combinatorial creativity but is limited in exploratory and transformational creativity due to lack of serendipity and subject-position; advocates realistic human–AI collaboration; demonstrates thesis via a self-referential human–AI composition and related experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ground AI creativity claims within a well-established theoretical framework (Margaret Boden), and reconcile technical capability with lived practice in arts, philosophy, and cognitive science; argue for a realistic, collaborative model.

Method: Theoretical analysis applying Boden's three properties (novelty, surprise, value) and three processes (combinatorial, exploratory, transformational); integrates cross-disciplinary experience (engineering, arts, philosophy); includes empirical demonstrations via concrete experiments and a methodological note describing the human–AI collaborative process used to compose the paper.

Result: AI systems exhibit genuine combinatorial creativity; significant limitations in exploratory creativity and are fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity; serendipity/accident and a subject-position to recognize chance events are missing; the paper itself demonstrates a human–AI collaborative process.

Conclusion: AI creativity is real but bounded; proposes a realistic, generative model of human–AI collaboration; encourages leveraging collaboration to produce novel outputs while acknowledging core theoretical limits; the paper doubles as a demonstration of its thesis.

Abstract: This paper examines the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems can be creative, approached from the dual perspective of a researcher trained in electrical engineering, pattern recognition, machine learning, and neural networks, who has also spent most of his life engaged in the arts as actor, stage and film director, writer, composer, and visual artist, and in philosophy. Drawing on Margaret Boden's foundational framework, both her three properties of creativity (novelty, surprise, and value) and her three types of creative processes (combinatorial, exploratory, and transformational), the paper argues that AI systems are structurally incapable of creativity in its strongest sense. While they exhibit genuine capability in the domain of combinatorial creativity, they are significantly bounded in exploratory creativity, and fundamentally incapable of transformational creativity. The paper further argues that the most important limitation of current AI systems is not the absence of novelty per se, but the absence of any mechanism for serendipity, accident, or the unexpected, all of which play a central role in the phenomenology of creativity, and the absence of any subject position from which to recognize and welcome such chance events. The paper concludes by proposing a model of human, AI creative collaboration that is both realistic and generative, illustrated by several concrete experiments. The paper is itself a demonstration of the thesis it advances: it was composed through a deliberate human AI collaborative process, which is described in the methodological note that opens it.

</details>


### [302] [Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20806)
*Tomohiro Harada,Enrique Alba,Gabriel Luque*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PTME-based framework for precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLMs on edge devices; reveals that traditional proxies miss precision; Pareto-frontier analysis identifies non-dominated configurations for deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing efficiency evals rely on proxy descriptors (e.g., parameter count, FLOPs) that decouple cost from task precision. A precision-aware, hardware-measured profiling is needed to guide deployment under resource constraints.

Method: PTME framework: measure Precision, Time, peak Memory, and Energy via direct hardware-level measurements. Apply to lightweight LLMs running locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, with benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding.

Result: Static proxies approximate inference cost but do not predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without improving precision; increases in execution time exceed energy changes; larger models are penalized more. No single model dominates across all PTME metrics; Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations, informing deployment under different resource envelopes.

Conclusion: PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost. Relying on size/FLOPs/latency/accuracy alone can mislead model selection; PTME-guided profiling reveals trade-offs and better deployment options.

Abstract: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

</details>


### [303] [Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20814)
*Hai-Nam Duy Vuong,Duy-Anh Bui,Trong-Nghia Nguyen,Kim-Ngan Thi Nguyen,Trang Mai Xuan,Tien-Cuong Nguyen,Van-Dem Pham,Thien Van Luong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A guide-grounded multimodal ECG report system integrates a CNN+Grad-CAM with a fixed, distilled ECG Interpretation Guide to anchor LLM-generated reports to clinical criteria, improving semantic quality and consistency while preserving classification performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs for medical report generation risk hallucinations and weak grounding in diagnostic criteria. There is a need to align LLM outputs with established guidelines to improve trust and reproducibility.

Method: A CNN+Grad-CAM extracts class probabilities and heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. An offline-distilled ECG Interpretation Guide (from textbooks/guidelines) is injected as a fixed knowledge block. An LLM, conditioned on the image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN fact pack, and the guide, generates structured, guideline-consistent diagnostic reports.

Result: Grounding with the interpretation guide improves semantic quality and consistency (higher BERTScore: 0.953 vs 0.818) while maintaining competitive classification performance on PTB-XL. Reports align more closely with reference interpretations.

Conclusion: Injecting a distilled interpretation guide into multimodal prompting reduces hallucinations and enhances clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, enabling more trustworthy deployment.

Abstract: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

</details>


### [304] [Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20820)
*Christian Arzate Cruz,Stefanos Gkikas,Houshyar Asadi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can be a computationally efficient and interpretable alternative to graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition, achieving near-state performance on DIEM-A with substantially fewer parameters and lower latency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce computational cost and enhance interpretability in body-based emotion recognition by replacing or augmenting expensive graph-based skeleton models with lightweight TCNs.

Method: Evaluate a family of TCN models on the DIEM-A dataset and compare them to a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Conduct region-focused analyses via region-specific TCNs, zero-based occlusion, and gradient saliency on G-TSG.

Result: G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, while TCN-Base remains within 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points of G-TSG. TCN-Base uses 79.18% fewer parameters and reduces classifier latency by ~12.5x. Upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone cue; usefulness of regions varies by emotion; interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior.

Conclusion: Lightweight TCNs can deliver efficient body-based emotion recognition with competitive accuracy and offer practical insights into motion cue contributions, supporting real-time deployment and interpretability.

Abstract: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

</details>


### [305] [Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20827)
*Junchi Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Target-specific authorization auditing reveals that LLM agents are influenced by both trusted and untrusted context. In 450 controlled tasks, differences between trusted vs untrusted evidence appear in 5.4% of cases where competition matters and 1.7% where the proposition is supported; with degradation, unauthorized competition persists in 2.4% of comparisons (95% CI 2.1–3.0). Models respond to source-authority cues but untrusted evidence still affects actions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how mixed-context information (including untrusted text) affects LLM decision-making and to develop an auditable mechanism that labels context factors per tool/argument target, enabling detection and localization of authorization failures.

Method: Introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Conduct 450 controlled next-action tasks using multiple open-weight LLM families, holding task elements (task, proposition, position, policy) fixed while only varying the proposition source authority. Include adversarial degradation by weakening valid evidence and use context-subset interactions as a diagnostic. Measure rate of unauthorized actions under trusted vs untrusted evidence and report confidence intervals.

Result: Trusted and untrusted variants produced different actions in 5.4% of competing cases versus 1.7% of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition persisted in 2.4% of comparisons (95% CI 2.1–3.0). These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. Models respond to textual source-authority cues, but untrusted evidence can still influence actions.

Conclusion: Per-tool/argument-level source-authority signals influence LLM behavior, but untrusted evidence can override or bias decisions. The audit provides a diagnostic framework for detecting and localizing authorization gaps, highlighting residual risk and the need for stronger safeguards.

Abstract: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

</details>


### [306] [Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20848)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A behavioral audit of medical LLMs evaluates evidence-use in diagnosis by decomposing patient information into evidence units, exploring candidate diagnoses under evidence subsets, and analyzing interactions to separate plausible evidence use from failures. Five open-weight LLMs evaluated on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase show that most interactions reflect plausible differential diagnoses or robust reasoning, not errors; a blinded review links many invalid/shortcut-like cases to negated/absent findings and local evidence; conclusion: accuracy alone can mask evidence-use failures and role-aware audits are warranted for medical LLM evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To move beyond diagnostic accuracy as the sole metric and assess whether medical LLMs use evidence appropriately, by auditing evidence use, isolating interaction discovery from failure assignment, and identifying robust checks through controlled experiments and blinded reviews.

Method: Decompose patient information into discrete evidence units; evaluate candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets; mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins; evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase; perform a blinded, enriched review (130 items) in a DDXPlus-focused sample to inspect validity of interactions and the presence of shortcut-like reasoning.

Result: Most interaction strength arises from faithful support or plausible differential constraints; many interactions are clinically plausible rather than errors. In a blinded review, invalid or shortcut-like cases cluster around negated/absent findings and local clinical evidence, suggesting some deficiencies are associated with missing or negated data rather than systematic misreasoning.

Conclusion: Diagnostic accuracy can conceal evidence-use failures; role-aware audits are necessary for robust evaluation of medical LLMs.

Abstract: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

</details>


### [307] [Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20852)
*Junchi Liao,Jiawen Deng,Fuji Ren*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Weak verifiers with scaffolding can catch some residual bugs after public-test success, but many hidden bugs remain; adversarial pressure and evidence limits reduce detection; partial recovery exists with GLM-5.1, highlighting need for stronger signals or inference auditing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Public tests do not guarantee correct specification; a deployment-like monitor is needed to detect hidden bugs in generated code after pass of public checks.

Method: Code Monitor Red Teaming protocol instantiated as CodeMonitorBench, across function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Evaluates 71,000 generated candidates; varies generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and model capability; measures public-test pass vs hidden-test failure; introduces adversarial public-test-overfit pressure; tests GLM-5.1 verifier; performs an inferability audit.

Result: Of 71,000 candidates, 43,677 pass public tests; 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family but miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and increases low-FPR miss rates. GLM-5.1 recovers part of the gap under the same boundary. Inferability audit shows misses arise from both verifier failure and limits in M1 evidence.

Conclusion: Public/test-based verification remains an incomplete gate for deployment; stronger or additional evidence signals and auditing of inference limits are needed to reduce residual hidden-bug risk in LLM-generated code.

Abstract: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

</details>


### [308] [Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20891)
*Pengyu Zhu,Lijun Li,Longju Yang,Sen Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MisKnow-Agent framework introduces controlled misleading knowledge into Deep Research workflows to test reliability; findings show susceptibility to false conclusions despite focused verification; defenses help but do not fully prevent misinference; implications call for end-to-end verification and correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess the reliability of Deep Research agents in open information environments and how misleading knowledge can propagate into final reports.

Method: Generate 5,933 quality-controlled misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles; apply to DeepResearch Benchmark tasks; evaluate open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents; analyze the gap between corpus-level verification and workflow-level evidence use; assess pre-, post-, and combined defenses.

Result: Exposure to misleading knowledge can cause false-conclusion adoption in final reports; corpus-validated verifiers flag the misleading instances, but adoption persists during long-horizon tasks; defenses mitigate but do not fully prevent false conclusions.

Conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction at both model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, or report-generation.

Abstract: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

</details>


### [309] [Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20913)
*Yi Xiong,Yuan-Yuan Cheng,Xiao-Ming Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a source-prior–driven selective adaptation for diffusion models, using a static parameter mask and structured updates to improve adaptation while preserving broad generative capability, outperforming strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fine-tuning large diffusion models often sacrifices general generative ability for target-specific performance. Existing full- and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods handle this trade-off only implicitly. A principled, explicit selection of adaptable parameters is needed, guided by source priors and parameter behavior.

Method: 1) Learn a static mask that identifies parameters better suited for downstream adaptation. 2) Construct structured update strategies for the selected subset, based on two observations: (a) the loss in general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (b) parameters with small impact on general capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. 3) Apply the masked, structured updates during fine-tuning.

Result: Experiments show that the proposed method achieves a better adaptation–retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

Conclusion: Source-prior–driven selective adaptation enables efficient and effective fine-tuning of diffusion models by targeting a principled subset of parameters with tailored update strategies, yielding superior preservation of general generation while achieving target-specific improvements.

Abstract: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

</details>


### [310] [Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20916)
*Deyu Jing*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Traceable Scholarship for AI-assisted humanities, embedding source traceability into generation via page anchors, citations-first modes, and a three-layer AIH-Infra, demonstrated on a Kant knowledge base to preserve verifiability and refutability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generative AI can produce fluent text that looks scholarly but lacks verifiable sources; without clear anchors, page numbers, or evidence, readers may misperceive confidence as truth. The paper argues for a normative condition—traceability—that enables public, refutable scholarship across print, digital, and AI-enabled knowledge infrastructures.

Method: Proposes design elements: page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract. Builds AIH-Infra as Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). Validates via a Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base (29 volumes) to show retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading.

Result: Demonstrates that traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Argues traceability is a normative condition—not merely a software feature—necessary to keep scholarship public and refutable in the AI era; provides a concrete architectural blueprint and a case study.

Conclusion: Traceability is the essential condition for public, refutable AI-assisted humanistic scholarship in the generative era. It is not just software but a governance/architecture standard that upholds scholarly integrity.

Abstract: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

</details>


### [311] [OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20918)
*Tong Zhao,Yuyang Hu,Reed Li,Yu Lu,Haibo Shi,Yutao Zhu,Zhicheng Dou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPOD is an on-policy distillation method that routes student outputs to modality-specific teachers (text, image, audio), gating feedback by teacher superiority and per-modality weights, to train a balanced, high-performing omni-modal model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Joint omni-modal training on pooled data often underperforms modality-specialized models and suffers from conflicting guidance; a mechanism is needed to coordinate modality-specific teachers without sacrificing cross-modal balance.

Method: For each student response, route tokens to the corresponding text/image/audio teacher. Only apply teacher feedback when the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student. Independently adjust each modality teacher’s influence during training. Have the routed teacher assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct outcome. After training, discard the modality specialists, yielding a deployable single omni-modal model.

Result: OPOD achieves the best average across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, with scores of 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2, surpassing the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On a 30B model, it outperforms the base model and a pooled multimodal post-training approach on all twelve benchmarks, ranking first or second on eleven. The modality specialists are discarded after training.

Conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers via OPOD effectively improves a shared omni-modal model while preserving cross-modal balance, with a deployable single model emerging after training.

Abstract: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

</details>


### [312] [Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20925)
*Shen Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a two-dimensional, interpretable representation of entity importance: audience evaluation and structural authority. Finds these signals are only weakly correlated and non-redundant, advocating task-aware retention of both signals rather than collapsing to a single score.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single scalar importance often masks meaningful distinctions between entities across tasks. A minimal, interpretable, multi-signal representation can preserve distinctions needed for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and reasoning.

Method: Define two signals per entity: audience-evaluation (e.g., IMDb ratings/ rankings) and structural-authority (e.g., PageRank on a knowledge graph built from Wikidata/Wikipedia links). Use 482 entities and 13,690 directed edges in a movie domain. Align entities across sources (IMDb, Wikidata, Wikipedia). Quantify association with Spearman correlation and overlap of top-K lists (Top 10, Top 100).

Result: Found a significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Overlap of top-K is small (10% for top 10, 34% for top 100); divergences occur in both directions, indicating non-redundant signals.

Conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority are complementary, not redundant. The paper offers a minimal representation framework and empirical evidence supporting task-aware systems that preserve distinct importance signals before task-specific selection/aggregation.

Abstract: AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

</details>


### [313] [SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20926)
*Yinhao Tang,Youqing Fang,Yanan Sun,Wenran Liu,Weiming Zhang,Bin Liu,Kuikun Liu,Wenwei Zhang,Kai Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SciExplore is a new benchmark for scientific information-seeking and reasoning, with 103 tasks across 10+ disciplines, evaluating LLMs and agents on progressively harder tasks from entity-level to domain-level synthesis, revealing significant performance gaps especially in structured knowledge synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific QA. There is a need to evaluate realistic scientific workflows that involve cross-source navigation, ambiguous retrieval, missing references, and evidence-grounded synthesis.

Method: Four task types (scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, cross-source structured knowledge synthesis) across 103 expert-curated tasks and 10+ disciplines; benchmarks evaluated with 10+ state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents.

Result: Models show substantial performance gaps; accuracy drops as task complexity increases; extremely low accuracy on structured synthesis tasks indicating difficulty in evidence-grounded, domain-level synthesis.

Conclusion: Current LLMs and agents are limited for realistic scientific information-seeking; SciExplore provides a diagnostic benchmark to drive progress toward better cross-source reasoning and knowledge synthesis in scientific contexts.

Abstract: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

</details>


### [314] [Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20937)
*Chinmaya Kumar Dehury,Boris Sedlak,Alaa Saleh,Ilir Murturi,Lauri Loven,Satish Narayana Srirama,Praveen Kumar Donta*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CEI proposes a three-layer architecture that makes intelligence a first-class, shareable entity across the edge–cloud continuum, enabling inventories, semantic representation, discovery, observability, marketplaces, and standardization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the shift from data to derived intelligence and the shortcomings of current edge AI research, which focuses on edge resource management and lightweight models, by providing an intelligence-centric framework where intelligence can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications.

Method: Proposes Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI) as a conceptual framework with a three-layer architecture and identifies enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

Result: A conceptual framework and architectural blueprint for CEI, outlining enabling technologies and research dimensions. No empirical results are presented; the work establishes the design space and guidelines for future development.

Conclusion: CEI aims to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across distributed edge and cloud resources, facilitating interoperable and standardized intelligence ecosystems.

Abstract: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

</details>


### [315] [From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20970)
*Weihan Zhang,Xuan Zhao,Yenwen Peng,Yuqi Chen,Jun Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reformulate INR training for time-varying fields by using spatially indexed time series with sequence-level supervision, removing dense spatiotemporal sampling; yields better reconstruction and lower training cost, and MoE can further improve performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense spatiotemporal sampling in implicit neural representations is computationally expensive and does not exploit temporal structure; there is a need to leverage full temporal evolution at each spatial location.

Method: Represent data as spatially indexed time series and supervise INRs at the sequence level per location; compatible with existing INR architectures; enable mixture-of-experts to allocate capacity for heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

Result: Consistent improvements in reconstruction quality and significant training cost reduction; MoE instantiation further enhances quality over both the base reformulation and existing MoE INR methods.

Conclusion: A per-location sequence-level INR training paradigm efficiently learns time-varying fields, reduces sampling requirements, and benefits from MoE for heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

</details>


### [316] [Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20972)
*Swapnanil Saha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Two-tier memory architecture for coding agents with a harness-controlled cue-anchored memory; deterministic, persisted recall via injected content outperforms voluntary memory use; delivery is the reliable memory channel.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current agents rely on writable documents for memory; crucial situational knowledge remains tacit, not written, and must be harnessed rather than chosen by the agent; a durable offloaded memory supports long-running autonomy.

Method: Grounded in cognitive memory literature; proposes a two-tier design; develops a cue-anchored memory model with trigger conditions across vocabularies (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal) evaluated by the harness; conducts a controlled evaluation on a real coding task with pre-seeded stores; uses a repeated-compaction decay probe to compare harness-owned vs external store injections.

Result: Voluntary memory usage is near zero (0 ops in 114 turns); deterministic injection from harness yields zero false alarms; 39% of intra-session re-reads re-use pre-seeded content memorized earlier; ten facts stored in conversation vanish after first summary and remain absent through 106 of 108 compactions, while facts injected from a harness-owned store survive through all 138 compaction resumes; final summaries do not carry these injected facts.

Conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is the product. A reliable memory channel is the one the agent never has to think about; harness-managed memory provides the load-bearing, durable memory for long-running agents.

Abstract: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

</details>


### [317] [Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20981)
*Jay Gor,Karm Dave,Akshita Abrol,Rajesh Gupta,Sudeep Tanwar,Zhengkui Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey of efficient vision-language and multimodal LLMs, showing that token compression, routing, KV-cache, quantization, and hardware must be co-optimized. It introduces Temporal Routing Consistency for video MoEs and outlines design trade-offs and open directions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient multimodal inference is constrained not only by model quality and FLOPs but also by latency, memory, and energy costs of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations. The interactions among techniques can dramatically alter downstream behavior.

Method: Literature review and synthesis that organizes existing work around the interactions between compression, routing, caching, quantization, and hardware constraints; introduces a diagnostic (Temporal Routing Consistency) and discusses trade-offs and open directions.

Result: A taxonomy and synthesis of design trade-offs (accuracy vs token budget, static vs adaptive compression, sparse routing vs expert collapse, low-bit inference vs modality degradation) and a set of open research directions, including routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking.

Conclusion: Efficient multimodal systems require holistic co-design across compression, routing, caching, quantization, and hardware; advocate for routing-aware methods, cross-modal cache policies, and unified benchmarks for edge multimodal intelligence.

Abstract: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

</details>


### [318] [GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20982)
*Vishal Ishwar Naik,Chenyu Xu,Donna Dong,Hussein Hassan,Abhishek Pradhan,Ofer Mendelevitch,Tallat Shafat,Humayun Irshad*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GuardianAgentBench (GABench) benchmarks safety and reliability of autonomous LLM agents with tool use, revealing two failure regimes and showing execution-time guardrails outperform system prompts by recovering 19.9% of failures at a 0.5% FPR.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLM agents autonomously interact with tools and environments, there is a critical need for rigorous benchmarks and defenses to ensure safe, reliable behavior under adversarial conditions.

Method: Constructed GuardianAgentBench with 580 scenarios across six domains, evaluated on LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. Includes multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Tested six state-of-the-art models, analyzing tool-use patterns and comparing guardrail interventions to system prompts.

Result: Best-performing configuration achieves 74.8% overall accuracy. Identified two failure regimes: stronger models under-call tools and weaker models mis-select/over-call tools. Performance degrades with larger tool sets and deeper turn sequences; long-horizon planning is especially bottlenecked. Guardrail interventions outperform system-prompt defenses, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of 0.5%.

Conclusion: Execution-time structural intervention improves safety without materially impacting correct agent behavior and offers a more reliable defense than system prompts.

Abstract: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

</details>


### [319] [Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.20999)
*Zibin Lin,Shengli Zhang,Taotao Wang,Yihan Xia,Deen Ma,Guofu Liao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML) to diagnose and localize failures in skill-based agent workflows and to reuse third-party knowledge via a six-module optimization loop (WGSO); achieves strong benchmark performance and transfer with efficient compiled execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current optimizers cannot jointly pinpoint failure location, the causal mechanism, and how to reuse external Skills; need provenance- and scope-aware mechanisms for robust repair and reuse.

Method: 1) Node–Mechanism Attribution to identify failed node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit; route defects to L3 (single-mechanism) or L2 (cross-mechanism) paths. 2) Six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop to select provenance- and scope-aware external knowledge, apply bounded patches, evaluate candidates, and store verified outcomes in optimizer memory.

Result: On SpreadsheetBench: 90.33±1.53 (DeepSeek) and 74.67±3.51 (Qwen3.6-Flash) Hard Accuracy. Without optimization, learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00±2.00 (Denotation) and 83.00±2.00. On Compiler-Supported50: highest hard-PASS rate and lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution reduces tokens/calls vs direct SkillAgent while preserving most tasks.

Conclusion: WML enhances failure localization and controlled knowledge reuse, yielding higher accuracy and efficiency; source code and artifacts are available at the provided GitHub link.

Abstract: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

</details>


### [320] [Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21000)
*Hyuk Lim,Seunghyun Yoon*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Decoupling retention and write in a discrete-time recurrent unit (Naju) yields both near-perfect long-range retention and rapid overwriting, addressing a key limitation in coupled designs and outperforming Mamba baselines while scaling linearly.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-sequence memory tracking requires sustaining stored bindings over long horizons while still allowing overwriting of stale information. Continuous-time SSMs rely on discretization and coupled recurrent gates, which may constrain memory performance. The paper argues that disentangling memory retention from write dynamics can overcome a fundamental trade-off.

Method: Introduce Naju: x_n = f_n ⊙ x_{n-1} + i_n ⊙ (B_n u_n), with an explicit discrete pole f_n (0 < f_n < 1) and an independent write gain i_n, decoupled from the input map. Provide Schur-stability of frozen coordinates and a fading-memory/BIBO bound without extra regularizers. Argue that in coupled designs, |r|+w ≤ 1 links retention r and write w; decoupling removes this constraint. Evaluate on a diagnostic suite (long-range memory tracking) and standard benchmarks (WikiText-103, Long Range Arena, multi-query associative recall).

Result: Naju demonstrates strong long-range memory while maintaining effective overwriting, outperforming Mamba baselines in principal comparisons and remaining competitive with Transformers, all with linear-time and linear-memory scaling. It remains robust when evaluated at 4× the training length and across diverse tasks.

Conclusion: Decoupling memory retention from write dynamics yields a practical, scalable recurrent unit that simultaneously supports durable retention and flexible overwriting. Naju offers a compelling alternative to existing SSMs and Transformer baselines for long-sequence processing and related memory-heavy tasks.

Abstract: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

</details>


### [321] [Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21010)
*Vasudha Bhatnagar,Purnima Bindal,Vikas Kumar,Raj Kumari Bahl*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes a two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM-generated summarizers based on stability, using document-level analyses and a stratified corpus-wide stability index; empirical study shows variability across models and genres, highlighting a stability/trustworthiness issue in zero-shot summarization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs introduce stochasticity in zero-shot summarization, raising concerns about stability and trustworthiness, especially in educational contexts where accurate summaries are essential.

Method: Level 1: perform multiple LLM-generated summaries per document under controlled conditions and compute a stability coefficient; score each summary for semantic and factual alignment with the source to assess multi-dimensional stability. Level 2: aggregate observations from a stratified sample to estimate an overall stability index for the LLM-summarizer across the corpus.

Result: Empirical study across three LLM-summarizers and three document genres reveals statistically significant differences in generation-level variability across metrics, indicating non-uniform stability across models and metrics.

Conclusion: Highlights the stability problem in LLM-generated summaries and motivates further research toward robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM-based summarizers.

Abstract: Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

</details>


### [322] [EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21013)
*Lihuang Fang,Yuchen Zou,kebin Jin,Jinghui Qin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RL-based dynamic agent specialization (EmoAgent-R1) for MLLMs in multimodal emotion recognition, featuring a cold-start bootstrap with synthetic data, a two-step agent workflow (selection, specialization), and Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to turn sparse rewards into fine-grained signals; shows superior emotion reasoning and training stability on MER benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLM-based MER is hindered by fixed prompts and static perception, which fail to capture the dynamic, multimodal nature of emotional cues. A dynamic, agent-based RL framework is proposed to improve emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization.

Method: 1) Cold-start strategy: bootstrap preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing via synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. 2) RL training with a two-step workflow: agent selection and agent specialization. 3) Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO): combines group-relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to convert sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals and mitigate coarse credit assignment in GRPO.

Result: Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability for EmoAgent-R1 compared to baselines.

Conclusion: Dynamic agent specialization via P-GRPO is effective for enhancing MER in MLLMs, improving emotion understanding and generalization, and offering a transferable framework for complex multimodal reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description.
