However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

</details>


### [323] [HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21019)
*Wei Liu,Siya Qi,Linhai Zhang,Lorainne Tudor Car,Yulan He*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HiMe is a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform for real-time personal health analytics from wearables, aiming for Pareto-optimal tradeoffs and treating the database as a first-class citizen to enable continuous, personalised health monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses limitations of traditional wearable health signal analysis (rigid frameworks, limited personalization) and privacy concerns; fills the gap of an open-source, locally deployable platform capable of real-time processing with long-term user modeling to enable Personal Health Agentic Analysis.

Method: Proposes design principles for HiMe: (1) treat the database as a first-class component, (2) jointly optimize effectiveness and efficiency to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance, (3) real-time processing with long-term user modeling; platform claims to be privacy-first, locally deployable, and compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across various wearables.

Result: Conceptual/design presentation describing HiMe; no empirical results or evaluations are provided in the abstract; emphasizes feasibility and architectural choices to support real-time, personalized health monitoring.

Conclusion: HiMe aims to operationalize Personal Health Agents by providing a privacy-preserving, real-time, locally deployable platform with a database-centric architecture and Pareto-efficient design to enable continuous, personalized wellbeing monitoring.

Abstract: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

</details>


### [324] [Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21042)
*Muyang Du,Shuang Yu,Junjie Lai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates all components of IndexTTS-2 on GPUs (TensorRT) to enable streaming and batched inference, achieving up to 5x GPT speedup and 3.6x end-to-end with minimal quality loss.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autoregressive TTS models offer high naturalness but incur slow sequential inference; production deployment requires low latency, streaming, and efficient GPU utilization.

Method: Optimize and accelerate GPT, flow-matching diffusion transformer, and vocoder using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM; enable streaming synthesis and batched inference; evaluate on Seed-TTS English/Chinese.

Result: End-to-end speedup up to 3.6×; autoregressive GPT speedup up to 5.0×; minimal degradation in WER, speaker similarity, and naturalness.

Conclusion: Provides a practical blueprint for deploying fast autoregressive TTS on GPUs and for streaming/batched inference in production environments.

Abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

</details>


### [325] [Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21101)
*Jie Peng,Yanping Zheng,Zhewei Zhe,Bin Tong,Guan Wang,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SID-based generative recommender is compositional and can reach some future items via observed tokens, but fails for unseen tokens/pathways; hierarchical semantic bucketing explains the boundary; future work includes independent SID spaces, scoring interfaces, and dynamic context.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess open-endedness of SID-based generation under an absolute-time protocol by separating seen and unseen targets and diagnosing token-level cold-start reachability.

Method: Absolute-time temporal protocol; seen/unseen-hit analysis; coldness taxonomy; oracle-prefix probing; interpret SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing (coarse early tokens, fine-grained late tokens).

Result: Current SID models can reach future items supported by observed tokens/prefixes but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths; boundary explained by hierarchical bucketing; SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended.

Conclusion: SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended; future directions include more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual contexts.

Abstract: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

</details>


### [326] [AttriMem: Attribution-Guided Process Feedback for Agent Memory Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21106)
*Qinfeng Li,Yuntai Bao,Xinyan Yu,Hongze Chen,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AttriMem introduces an attribution-guided RL framework for memory-construction policies in long-horizon LLM tasks. It supplements the global task outcome with token-level contribution rewards to address credit-assignment bottlenecks and improves performance, generalization, and training stability over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Effective memory construction remains difficult: heuristic methods misalign with downstream goals; RL with coarse rewards fails to identify which intermediate memories drive final answers, and designing process-level feedback is hard due to lack of ground-truth targets and uncertain reasoning trajectories.

Method: AttriMem augments the overall task reward with local, token-level attribution rewards that quantify each memory decision's contribution to the final answer. This attribution-guided process-feedback is used to train memory-construction policies via reinforcement learning, evaluated on long-horizon dialogue QA.

Result: AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines; demonstrates generalization across benchmarks and models; stabilizes RL optimization in memory construction.

Conclusion: Fine-grained, attribution-based feedback aligns memory construction with downstream objectives, enabling better performance and robustness in RL-for-memory policies, with stronger generalization across tasks and agents.

Abstract: Effective memory is crucial for LLM agents, yet constructing it effectively remains challenging. A memory-construction policy decides what information to extract, store, update, compress, or discard as interactions accumulate. Heuristic memory methods rely on subjective, task-specific rules, which can misalign with downstream objectives and limit cross-task adaptability. RL-based methods, by contrast, learn from task feedback but mainly use outcome- or module-level rewards. These coarse signals indicate task success but cannot identify which intermediate memory contents support the final answer, creating a fine-grained credit-assignment bottleneck. However, constructing such process feedback is prohibitively difficult because intermediate memory decisions lack unique ground-truth targets, while the appropriate credit varies with the agent's uncertain reasoning trajectory and therefore cannot be specified in advance. We propose AttriMem, an attribution-guided process-feedback framework for learning memory-construction policies with RL. AttriMem augments the global outcome reward with local rewards derived from token-level contributions to the final answer. Experiments on long-horizon dialogue question answering show that AttriMem outperforms retrieval-based, heuristic, and RL-based baselines, generalizes across benchmarks and answer models, stabilizes RL optimization.

</details>


### [327] [V-DEAL: Diagnosing Video Safety De-Calibration as an Understanding-Refusal Coupling Failure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21151)
*Zhetong Zhang,Honghao Fu,Miao Xu,Yiwei Wang,Yujun Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A three-level diagnostic framework (V-DEAL) reveals that harmful videos paired with benign queries yield high attack success on Video LLMs; a prompt-injection defense substantially mitigates this risk.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand and mitigate safety vulnerabilities in Video LLMs where query content interacts with video content to enable attacks.

Method: Three-level diagnostic framework evaluating model behavior, understanding, and internal representations; empirical study across six Video LLMs and three benchmarks; hidden-state analysis; development of a prompt-injection intervention; comparison with finetuning-based defenses.

Result: Harmful videos with benign queries achieve 48.33% attack success (despite >81% harm recognition accuracy); visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding; prompt injection reduces attack success by 48.24 percentage points, comparable to finetuning-based methods.

Conclusion: V-DEAL offers a diagnostic lens to analyze the observed vulnerability in Video LLMs, and prompt injection provides a practical, effective defense against such safety risks.

Abstract: As Video Large Language Models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, ensuring their safety alignment has become critical. Counterintuitively, we find that harmful videos paired with benign queries achieve higher attack success rates than the same videos paired with explicitly harmful queries. To understand the underlying mechanism of this vulnerability, we present V-DEAL, a three-level diagnostic framework that jointly analyzes this failure across model behaviour, understanding, and internal representations. By progressively ruling out perception failure and quantifying the model's internal refusal tendency, V-DEAL provides a new diagnostic perspective for analyzing the underlying mechanism of the observed vulnerability. We tested six Video LLMs on three public benchmarks and observed that models correctly recognize harmful video content with over 81\% accuracy, yet the average attack success rate still reaches 48.33\% under the condition pairing harmful videos with benign queries. Hidden-state analysis further shows that visual understanding activates a weaker refusal tendency than textual understanding. Furthermore, we introduce a prompt injection intervention method that reduces attack success rates by an average of 48.24 percentage points and achieves performance comparable to prior fine-tuning-based methods, providing an effective and practical means to address such safety risks in Video LLMs.

</details>


### [328] [SafeStep: AI-powered Travel Assistance for Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21156)
*Elderly People with Frailty or Dementia Azul Debenedetti,David Gamez,Franco Such,Nik Kairinos*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SafeStep is an AI-driven travel assistant for elderly/frail/dementia patients that uses a novel travel-graph to integrate route planning with predictive modeling; it generates failure scenarios with LLMs and Anticip8, proposes interventions, and estimates their impact to maximize the chance of reaching the destination; field study (26 journeys) shows Anticip8+GPT evaluation yields best reliability; user feedback improves confidence but usability needs work; potential broad applications and future release planned.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address mobility constraints and safety concerns of over a million elderly individuals in the UK who suffer from frailty or dementia, aiming to enable safer, more confident urban travel.

Method: Develop a travel graph that combines planning with predictive modeling. For each journey stage, generate personalized failure scenarios using a combination of large language models (LLMs) and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine; propose targeted interventions; estimate how interventions affect outcome probabilities; select interventions that maximize likelihood of reaching the destination. Evaluate via travel-graph generation experiments and a field study of 26 real-world journeys.

Result: The combination of Anticip8 for failure prediction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yielded the most reliable performance. User feedback indicated increased confidence and perceived safety, though interface usability requires improvement.

Conclusion: SafeStep demonstrates a viable AI-assisted travel solution for frail elderly users, with potential applicability to other domains (e.g., mental health, career coaching, addiction treatment); future work includes release and broader deployment, with ongoing improvements to usability.

Abstract: More than a million people in the UK suffer from frailty or dementia, which severely compromise their ability to travel in urban environments. This paper presents SafeStep, an AI-driven travel system that assists elderly users with their journeys. At the core of SafeStep is a novel travel graph representation, which integrates route planning with predictive modelling. For each stage of a journey, the system (i) generates personalized failure scenarios using a combi-nation of LLMs and the Anticip8 behavioral prediction engine, (ii) proposes targeted interventions, and (iii) estimates the impact of interventions on out-come probabilities. This enables SafeStep to select interventions that maximize the likelihood of the person reaching their destination. SafeStep was evaluated through experiments on travel graph generation and a field study involving 26 real-world journeys. Results showed that combining Anticip8 for failure pre-diction with GPT-based models for intervention evaluation yields the most re-liable performance. User feedback indicated that SafeStep improves confidence and perceived safety during travel, although interface usability needs to be im-proved for the target demographic. In the future, we would like to improve and release SafeStep. The AI system that was developed for SafeStep could be ap-plied in other areas, such as mental health, career coaching and addiction treatment.

</details>


### [329] [Safeguards for Speech2Speech LLM-Assistants: A Case Study in Automotive Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21180)
*Gregor Endler,Sebastian Kraus,Lukas Stappen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: End-to-end S2S guardrails in automotive face latency and determinism issues; transcript- and tool-based guards insufficient for industrial deployment; need open challenges and future work.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automotive S2S assistants aim for natural, humanlike dialogue but require safeguards; end-to-end models constrain modular guardrail integration.

Method: Empirical evaluation of two guardrail strategies: transcript-based and tool-based; measure latency and tool-call behavior; analyze feasibility for industrial deployment.

Result: Both strategies show prohibitive latency (0–1.4 s per answer even for cheap checks) and issues like non-deterministic tool calls; thus not suitable in many cases.

Conclusion: Open challenges for S2S guardrails in automotive; need improved architectures, safeguards, deterministic tool behavior, and latency reduction; more research required.

Abstract: Recent advances have introduced speech-to-speech (S2S) conversational assistants capable of producing natural-sounding interactions, including non-verbal cues like tonality and mood. In the automotive domain, this enables intuitive and humanlike in-car dialogue experiences. However, integrating these end-to-end assistants limits architectural options for programmable domain-specific safeguards. This paper discusses two implementation approaches for S2S guardrails: transcript-based and tool-based. Through an empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that both strategies are insufficient for industrial deployment in most cases due to prohibitive latency (delaying each answer by 0 to 1.4 seconds even for computationally cheap checks) and technical impediments (like potentially non-deterministic tool call behavior). Finally, we outline open challenges for S2S guardrails in the automotive context.

</details>


### [330] [Explaining Weather Bulletins via ILP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21184)
*Enrico Santi,Alessandro Dal Palù,Agostino Dovier,Talissa Dreossi,Andrea Formisano*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ILP-based pipeline using ASP facts and FastLAS2 to learn interpretable explanations of weather bulletin symbols; generalizable across regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide transparent, explainable reasoning for meteorological bulletins and the symbol choices in forecast pictograms, bridging symbolic learning with expert knowledge.

Method: Convert simulated meteorological data and bulletins into ASP facts; generate ILP examples; apply FastLAS2 to induce an explanatory hypothesis; translate the hypothesis into natural language; validate that it explains the expert forecast decisions and symbol choices.

Result: Demonstrates feasibility of learning an explanatory hypothesis that aligns with expert weather forecasts and symbol rationale; the approach is generalizable and not tied to a specific region.

Conclusion: ILP with FastLAS2 can yield simple, interpretable explanations for complex domain knowledge in meteorology; the pipeline can be applied to other bulletins and regions.

Abstract: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) originated within the Logic Programming community in the Nineties as a framework for combining symbolic learning with declarative knowledge representation. Nowadays, mature ILP frameworks exist and they are capable of learning complex, non-monotonic hypotheses, thus broadening both the modeling capabilities and the scope of real-world applications of ILP. This work is primarily based on the FastLAS2 framework and aims to generate simple, interpretable hypotheses to help clarify the weather bulletins issued by OSMER FVG, the Regional Meteorological Observatory of the Italian region of Friuli Venezia-Giulia. In this paper we present a pipeline that, starting from simulated meteorological raw data and from OSMERs' bulletins (used as ground truth), extracts data as ASP facts and generates ILP examples. From such examples an explanatory hypothesis is then inferred via FastLAS2. Such a hypothesis (translated into natural language) explains the weather forecast issued by human experts, and in particular the rationale behind experts' choices of specific symbols in the bulletin pictogram (the symbol-annotated meteorological map of the forecast). The proposed approach is general, not specific to any particular region and it can equally be applied to bulletins from other sources and to different regions.

</details>


### [331] [Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21185)
*Akihiro Takemura,Katsumi Inoue*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Matrix-based differentiable logic programming reduces reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems by unifying rules and constraints, analyzing t-norms, and showing that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms lowers both constraint and cognition shortcuts; architecture of symbol-learner coupling is critical.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neurosymbolic models exhibit shortcut reasoning that harms generalization and interpretability. Soft probabilistic grounding can allow constraints to be satisfied without genuine task understanding; a unified, differentiable logic framework may mitigate such shortcuts.

Method: Build on matrix-based logic programming semantics to unify rules and constraints in a single matrix. Explore connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and compare gradient flow properties. Conduct MNIST-variant experiments using one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms, contrasting with soft-probability baselines. Assess how coupling architecture affects shortcut mitigation.

Result: One-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both constraint-satisfaction shortcuts and cognition shortcuts compared to methods relying on soft probability distributions. Gradient-flow characteristics vary with the chosen t-norms, informing design choices. Architectural coupling between symbolic knowledge and neural learning plays a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

Conclusion: Architectural choices in neurosymbolic systems are crucial for mitigating shortcut behaviors. A unified matrix-based logic encoding that tightly binds rules and constraints, together with careful grounding, improves robustness against shortcuts.

Abstract: Neurosymbolic (NeSy) systems integrate neural networks with logical reasoning to achieve both generalization and interpretability, but recent work has shown they are susceptible to shortcut reasoning behaviors.  We propose a novel method using matrix-based differentiable logic programming to mitigate reasoning shortcuts in two phenomena: constraint satisfaction shortcuts, where constraints are satisfied without achieving the intended task, and cognition shortcuts, where biased data leads to semantically incorrect concept mappings despite logically sound inference. Building on recent matrix-based logic programming semantics, we introduce design elements to mitigate shortcuts, including a unified encoding of rules and constraints in a single matrix.  We also identify connections to fuzzy logic t-norms and empirically compare their gradient flow properties. Through carefully designed experiments on MNIST variants, we show that one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms significantly reduces both shortcut types compared to previous methods that rely on soft probability distributions.  We then confirm that architectural choices in coupling symbolic knowledge with neural learning play a critical role in shortcut mitigation.

</details>


### [332] [Identifying Good Rules for Efficient SAT Encodings of Single-Constant Multiplication Using Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21188)
*Chufeng Jiang,Neng-Fa Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A neuro-symbolic SCM method leverages a graph neural network to guide operator selection, substantially speeding up encoding and reducing memory usage while maintaining near-optimal additions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SCM is NP-hard and existing dynamic-programming/SAT encodings become costly for large constants; fast, scalable encodings are needed in hardware design to reduce area/latency and design time.

Method: Train a graph neural network to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions. Use GNN-derived confidence scores to prune no-good choices during the symbolic search for SCM encoding, effectively guiding the SAT encoding process.

Result: On unseen 17–32 bit constants, encoding time is reduced by 1–2 orders of magnitude; memory usage drops by over 97%; branching is reduced by about an order of magnitude; encoding quality (additions) is preserved near-optimally.

Conclusion: Learning-guided symbolic strategies can substantially improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encodings; code and data are publicly available at the provided GitHub repository.

Abstract: The Single Constant Multiplication problem is a fundamental NP-hard optimization task in hardware design, which seeks to decompose a fixed constant using only additions, subtractions, and bit-shifts. Although dynamic programming methods can produce near-optimal SAT encodings for SCM, their encoding cost remains high for large constants. We propose a neuro-symbolic framework that accelerates SCM SAT encoding by identifying good rules for guiding operator selection during decomposition. Our approach employs a graph neural network model to predict promising operator types from constant decompositions, and exploits the resulting confidence scores to prune no-good choices in the symbolic search. Experimental results on unseen 17-32 bit constants demonstrate one to two orders of magnitude reductions in encoding time, over 97% reduction in memory usage, and an order-of-magnitude decrease in branching, while preserving near-optimal encoding quality in terms of additions. These results show that learning-guided symbolic strategies can significantly improve the scalability and efficiency of SCM encoding. Our code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/Chufeng-Jiang/SCM_MLDP

</details>


### [333] [Bound-Founded Semantics for Answer Set Programming with Difference Constraints: Preliminary Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21201)
*Pedro Cabalar,Jorge Fandinno,Nicolas Rühling,Torsten Schaub,Sebastian Schellhorn,Philipp Wanko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A many-sorted Bound-founded HT logic (HTb) is proposed to unify equilibrium semantics for ASP with linear constraints, enabling a single framework to characterize difference-constraint hybrid systems (e.g., clingo[DL], clingcon, flingo) and analyze constraint atoms and foundedness of numeric variables.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hybrid ASP solvers that integrate linear constraints use diverse semantic foundations, hindering cross-system reasoning and formal guarantees. A unified logical basis is needed to compare, reason about foundedness, and support future integration.

Method: Introduce a many-sorted extension of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb). Use this framework to characterize equilibrium models across alternative semantics for ASP with linear constraints, with a focus on difference constraints. Formalize foundedness for numeric variables and analyze how clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo justify constraint atoms within this framework.

Result: A single, consistent formal framework that captures the foundations of current systems (e.g., clingo[DL]) and supports rigorous analysis of program simplifications and future integration of diverse semantic principles across ASP with linear constraints.

Conclusion: The HTb-based, many-sorted framework provides a unified theoretical grounding for ASP with linear constraints, clarifying semantic roots of different hybrid approaches and facilitating cross-system reasoning and extensions.

Abstract: While the integration of linear constraints has significantly expanded the reach of Answer Set Programming (ASP), existing hybrid solvers often rely on disparate semantic underpinnings that lack a unified logical foundation. We address this gap by introducing a many-sorted variant of the Bound-founded Logic of Here-and-There (HTb), providing a versatile framework capable of characterizing equilibrium models across a wide spectrum of alternative semantics for extensions of ASP with linear constraints. We apply this framework to the setting of difference constraints, focusing on the semantic characterization of clingo[DL]. Central to our approach is the formalization of foundedness for numeric variables. By investigating how different hybrid systems - such as clingo[DL], clingcon, and flingo - justify constraint atoms, we uncover the semantic roots of their varying behaviors. This investigation results in a single, consistent framework that not only formalizes the foundations of current systems like clingo[DL] but also facilitates the rigorous study of program simplifications and the future integration of diverse semantic principles.

</details>


### [334] [A New Well-Supported Semantics for Description Logic Programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21203)
*Spencer Killen,Jia-Huai You*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a stricter well-supported semantics for description logic programs that preserves NP-complete consistency and provides a reduct-based characterization, along with a fixpoint operator; equivalent to current semantics on a syntactic class; strictly contained within the existing well-supported semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current well-supported semantics exhibit (i) higher complexity for the consistency problem (potentially reaching the second level of the polynomial hierarchy) and (ii) lack of a reduct-based characterization. The work aims to tighten the evaluation of ontological atoms to retain NP-complete consistency while enabling a reduct-based analysis and to identify syntactic fragments where this new semantics coincides with the existing one.

Method: Propose a new semantics that evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the existing well-supported semantics. Develop a fixpoint operator to characterize the semantics and introduce a reduct-based transformation. Prove that the new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics. Identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which the two semantics are equivalent.

Result: NP-completeness of the consistency problem is preserved (not raised to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy). The semantics is characterized by a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. The new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, maintaining the prior notion of well-supportedness while imposing stricter criteria. Equivalence with the current semantics holds for a identified syntactic class.

Conclusion: The proposed semantics preserves the intuitive notion of well-supportedness from logic programming while enforcing a stricter evaluation of ontological atoms. It offers a reduct-based formalization and a fixpoint characterization, enabling clearer analysis and potential practical benefits due to retained NP-complete reasoning and closer alignment with standard logic programming semantics.

Abstract: Description logic programs are a powerful formalism for combining rules with ontologies. The well-supported semantics for description logic programs ensures that no answer sets rely on cyclic dependencies. Most popular semantics for logic programming have this property of well-supportedness. We recognize two limitations of the current well-supported semantics for DL programs: its increased computational complexity for the consistency problem and its lack of a reduct transformation characterization.  In this work, we present a new semantics which evaluates ontological atoms more strictly than the current semantics. This keeps the complexity of its consistency problem NP-complete, rather than increasing it to the second level of the polynomial hierarchy. Additionally, we identify a syntactic class of description logic programs for which our new semantics is equivalent to the current semantics. We characterize our semantics using a fixpoint operator and a reduct-based transformation. Our new semantics is a strict subset of the current well-supported semantics, so it maintains the prior notion  of well-supportedness while inducing its own stricter notion. We prefer our new notion of well-supportedness due to its similarities with logic programming.

</details>


### [335] [How Rules Represent Causal Knowledge: Causal Modeling with Probabilistic Logic Programming](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21208)
*Kilian Rueckschloss,Felix Weitkaemper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Extends Pearl's causal reasoning to probabilistic logic programming (PLP) by defining a formal causal semantics with interventions; shows equivalence with P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog, with potential divergences in non-stratified cases and other PLP formalisms.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To transfer causal reasoning from Pearl's Bayesian-network framework to PLP, overcoming acyclicity limitations and aligning with philosophical foundations that do not rely on temporal notions.

Method: Introduce a formal causal semantics for PLP, define interventions within this semantics, propose an implementation, and compare the resulting semantics with existing P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog.

Result: The proposed causal semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog; differences may occur in non-stratified cases and for other PLP formalisms; an implementation of the approach is presented.

Conclusion: Pearl's causal ideas can be instantiated within PLP under the proposed semantics; the correspondence with stratified ProbLog shows consistency, while non-stratified PLP and alternative formalisms require careful handling.

Abstract: Pearl famously argues that causal knowledge enables the prediction of intervention effects. By contrast, purely descriptive knowledge supports only conclusions drawn from observations. His theory of causality, however, is developed exclusively within Bayesian networks and causal models. Consequently, it is largely restricted to acyclic causal relationships, and transferring its ideas to other formalisms risks misinterpretation or inconsistency.
  This paper brings Pearl's approach to causality into probabilistic logic programming (PLP). To this end, such programs are aligned with philosophical foundations established in prior work that do not rely on temporal notions; that is, all relevant events are assumed to occur simultaneously. A formal causal semantics for these programs, together with a notion of intervention and an implementation, is proposed. It is shown that this semantics coincides with the P-log semantics for stratified ProbLog programs, while the two may differ in the non-stratified case and for other PLP formalisms.

</details>


### [336] [ICAE-Bench: Evaluating Coding Agents as Interactive Project Builders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21217)
*Zhongyuan Peng,Dan Huang,Chuyu Zhang,Caijun Xu,Changyi Xiao,Shibo Hong,David Lo,Lin Qiu,Xuezhi Cao,Jiyuan He,Yixin Cao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ICAE-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating coding agents in interactive project-building tasks, using fuzzy requirements derived from real repositories, with standardized user simulations and multi-dimensional evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the shift from static, fully specified coding tasks to vibe-coding workflows, where agents must plan, clarify requirements, and construct repository-level software in collaboration with a user. Existing benchmarks fail to capture this interactivity and ambiguity.

Method: Three designs: (1) derive ambiguity from precise open-source repositories with executable behavior to ground fuzziness; (2) ground interaction via User Agent Data to ensure reproducible user simulations and prevent inventing new requirements or leaking impl artifacts; (3) evaluate open-ended repositories with standardized black-box tests and multi-dimensional diagnostics (functional correctness, semantic/API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, interaction quality).

Result: A realistic, evaluable framework for interactive code-building agents, enabling fair assessment across open-ended repositories and multiple objectives, aligning benchmarks with real-world coding workflows.

Conclusion: ICAE-Bench fills a critical gap by enabling evaluation of coding agents under interactive project-building with fuzzy requirements, providing reproducible user simulations and multi-faceted evaluation to assess both technical and interaction aspects.

Abstract: The recent emergence of vibe-coding workflows is changing what coding agents are expected to do. Instead of merely completing code under fully specified instructions, agents are increasingly expected to transform incomplete product intent into working software by combining various abilities including planning, requirement clarification, tool use, debugging, and repository-level construction. Yet existing benchmarks have not fully caught up with this shift, evaluating agents on static, fully specified tasks.
  In this paper, we introduce ICAE-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under interactive project-building settings. The basic idea is to start from a fuzzy product requirement, simulating the dynamic paradigm with an automated User Agent. To make this setting both realistic and evaluable, ICAE-Bench introduces three key designs. First, to avoid the ambiguity of unconstrained fuzzy requirements, each task derives ambiguity from a precise real open-source repository with executable behavior. Second, to ensure high-quality and reproducible user simulation, ICAE-Bench grounds interaction through User Agent Data, allowing the User Agent to reveal hidden constraints without inventing new requirements or leaking implementation artifacts. Third, to evaluate open-ended repositories fairly, ICAE-Bench uses standardized black-box tests together with multi-dimensional diagnostics, including functional correctness, semantic and API similarity, structural fidelity, design quality, and interaction quality.

</details>


### [337] [Logic Programming Semantics for Causal Processes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21233)
*Felix Weitkämper*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Links logic-programming semantics (stable and supported models) to causal process states; stable models map to eventual states from a neutral, undisturbed start, while supported models map to eventual states from arbitrary starting points, adding a temporal causal interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by modelling challenges in life sciences, the work aims to align logic-programming semantics with causal/explanatory reasoning and to introduce temporal dimensions into the interpretation of stable and supported models.

Method: Theoretical analysis establishing precise correspondences between semantic notions (stable and supported models) and the evolution of causal processes; distinguishes positive programs and starting-point conditions (neutral vs arbitrary); discusses semantics as a temporal causal rule language.

Result: Formal correspondences: stable models ↔ eventual states from neutral starting point; supported models ↔ eventual states from arbitrary starting points; adds temporal perspective to the causal interpretation of logic-programming semantics.

Conclusion: Provides a temporal causal interpretation of logic-programming semantics, enriching the use of stable and supported models as causal rule semantics in life-science modelling.

Abstract: Motivated by challenging modelling issues in the life sciences, we investigate the relationship between logic programming semantics and the eventual states of causal processes compatible with those logic programs. More precisely, we show that while stable models of positive logic programs correspond to the eventual states of processes commencing from a neutral state and continuing undisturbed indefinitely, supported models describe the eventual states reachable from arbitrary starting points. This also contributes to the discussion of the appropriate semantics for logic programming as a causal rule language, adding a temporal perspective to recent interpretations of the stable and supported model semantics from an explanatory viewpoint of causality.

</details>


### [338] [BasketEvent: Understanding Who Did What and When in Basketball Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21267)
*Yu Zhang,Jiayuan Rao,Haoning Wu,Weidi Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: BasketEvent grounds basketball events to responsible players and provides a subset with precise intervals for temporal localization; PlayNet is a player-centric reasoning framework that integrates player identity tracking, player-player and player-ball interactions, and global court context with gated pooling to predict player-level events and temporal evidence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video understanding methods treat perception and recognition separately and fail to ground events to specific players or temporally localize evidence in complex team sports. A dataset and model that ground events to players and provide temporal evidence is needed.

Method: Introduce BasketEvent dataset with player-grounded event labels and a subset of 1,000 samples with precise temporal intervals for evaluating temporal localization. Propose PlayNet, a framework that tracks entities, associates identities, and reason about events via player-player, player-ball, and global court interactions, using gated pooling to aggregate sparse temporal evidence.

Result: Experiments show PlayNet outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, validating the effectiveness of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding.

Conclusion: The dataset and model establish a compelling direction for player-centric sports video analysis; the authors will release data, code, and models to enable further research and benchmarking.

Abstract: Comprehensive basketball video understanding requires resolving not only what event occurs, but also who is responsible and when the key evidence appears. However, exist- ing methods typically treat spatial perception and semantic recognition as isolated tasks, failing to ground events to individual players or pinpoint their temporal boundaries within complex collective dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce BasketEvent, a player- centric basketball event understanding dataset curated from real NBA broadcasts. In BasketEvent, event labels are grounded to the responsible players, and a manually an- notated subset of 1,000 samples with precise event intervals is provided to evaluate tem- poral evidence localization. Based on this data, we propose PlayNet, a player-centric reasoning framework that maps basketball videos to player-level event predictions with temporal evidence. Concretely, PlayNet tracks key entities, associates player identities, and reasons about events by modeling player-player, player-ball, and global court inter- actions, while aggregating sparse temporal evidence via gated pooling. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that PlayNet significantly outperforms representative video-level and crop-based baselines, proving the superiority of player-centric modeling for fine-grained sports video understanding. Our data, code, and models will be made publicly available.

</details>


### [339] [An LLM-Driven Workflow for Automated Process Control Strategy Generation and Tuning from Dynamic Process Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21292)
*Ari Luna Rueda,Eike Cramer,Klaus Hellgardt,Mehmet Mercangöz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An LLM-driven, structured workflow for automated multi-variable control design using constrained, code-generated steps; demonstrates PI-based decentralized control and BO-based tuning on a nonlinear gas-preheater, achieving ~26.5% improvement over initial workflow controller; highlights feasibility and need for broader validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce manual control-design effort, increase reproducibility, and enable executable, validated control-design workflows directly from dynamic process models; address multi-variable control complexity via MV-CV pairing and constrained code generation.

Method: Decompose the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and Bayesian-optimization-based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated; failed artifacts repaired using validation feedback. Demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. Yields a decentralized PI controller with feedforward and an executable tuning environment.

Result: Bayesian optimization reduces the closed-loop performance objective by ~26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly via improved pressure-loop transient performance. This gain pertains to the tuning stage, not a comparison with manually designed controllers.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured LLM-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plant-wide benchmarks.

Abstract: We present a structured large-language-model-driven workflow for automated multi-variable control design from dynamic process models. The workflow decomposes the design task into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, manipulated-variable controlled-variable (MV-CV) pairing, controller specification, closed loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation and Bayesian-optimization (BO) based tuning. Generated artifacts are executed and validated before downstream tasks proceed, and failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The proposed approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics. The generated workflow produces a physically consistent decentralized PI (proportional-integral) feedback-feedforward control structure and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed loop performance objective, which aggregates set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors for the controlled variables, by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller generated by the workflow, mainly through improved pressure-loop transient performance. This figure quantifies the automated tuning stage rather than a comparison against a manually designed controller. The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

</details>


### [340] [Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21302)
*Gong Gao,Weidong Zhao,Xianhui Liu,Ning Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper proposes Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) for online RL, using Q-CVAE to generate expert priors from the replay buffer, plus Expert Policy Guidance and Policy Gradient Correction to combine Q-guidance with supervision; yields improved sample efficiency and stability on robotics and industrial benchmarks without offline pre-training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline datasets used for policy priors in BPRL suffer from limited diversity and quality; need dynamic priors derived from online data to improve exploration and stability.

Method: Train a Q-guided CVAE to model expert action distribution from online replay; generate high-value actions to guide policy updates; employ EPG to select expert actions from a generative support set; incorporate PGC to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision.

Result: Experimental results show state-of-the-art improvements in sample efficiency and stable convergence across Gym, PyBullet, and DMControl benchmarks.

Conclusion: EBP introduces a viable, online-prior-based BPRL paradigm, reducing dependence on pre-collected offline demonstrations and improving robustness and efficiency.

Abstract: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

</details>


### [341] [Regulating autonomous and agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21345)
*Chris Reed,Alex Austria,Anmol Bharuka,Pragnitha Mandava,Khushiya Mujawar,Luka Shakhkulashvili*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Regulating autonomous and agentic AI requires new, active governance beyond traditional models; a cross-system analysis identifies how existing frameworks fail and outlines proactive, supply-chain-aware solutions across four regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI autonomy and the distributed nature of the AI supply chain undermine assumptions of regulator control; existing governance models risk systemic failure without reform.

Method: Comparative regulatory analysis of four regimes (UK platform regulation, data protection, UK financial services, EU AI Act cross-sectoral) to identify challenges and propose proactive regulatory approaches.

Result: Identifies that knowledge and control assumptions no longer hold, governance cannot duplicate old models, retrospective oversight is ineffective, and AI autonomy creates systemic risks. Proposes regulatory enhancements such as supply-chain coverage, proactive risk management, adaptive governance, and cross-sectoral coordination to shift regulation from reactive to active.

Conclusion: A fresh, proactive regulatory paradigm is needed to manage AI autonomy, requiring cross-regime coordination, supply-chain accountability, and ongoing adaptation to evolving AI capabilities.

Abstract: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act\'92s cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

</details>


### [342] [SPORD: A Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose Approach for Supply Chain Planning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21354)
*Jiayin He,Yutong Pan,Sen Yang,Ningxuan Kang,Yongzhi Qi,Jianshen Zhang,Wei Qi,Zuo-Jun Max Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The SPORD framework decouples simulation from optimization to tackle large-scale, complex supply chain planning in e-commerce. It enables rapid, end-to-end planning via NetSim, delivering substantial computational speedups and operational improvements, while improving executive trust through transparent, configurable outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address three core barriers: (1) proliferation of bespoke models (operational fragmentation), (2) combinatorial intractability at scale (millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, intricate routing), and (3) implementation gap due to lack of executive trust in model outputs.

Method: Simulation–Propose–then–OR–Dispose (SPORD) decouples the pipeline: (a) simulation generates and evaluates the full set of operationally valid candidate paths with full business logic; (b) an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset; (c) matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU-accelerated simulation; (d) list scheduling to reduce coupled-order processing from hours to minutes; (e) intelligent diagnosis engine for closed-loop feedback; (f) deployed on JD.com’s NetSim platform to optimize end-to-end services.

Result: Computational: 10–100x speedup over serial methods; operational: list scheduling reduces processing time from hours to minutes. Real-world impact: NetSim optimized end-to-end services for >20,000 suppliers; cross-regional fulfillment rate reported as dropping from 6.1% to 4.9%; average monthly carbon reduction ~5,745 tCO2e.

Conclusion: SPORD shifts simulation from passive monitoring to active planning, producing transparent outputs that bolster executive trust and enabling configuration-based planning for future iterations; the modular design supports rapid scalability and reuse.

Abstract: For years, supply chain planning at e-commerce firms has operated as a collection of isolated projects. Each planning task from static network planning to dynamic warehouse assortment planning requires analysts to spend weeks building models from scratch, calibrating and persuading executives to act on outputs they cannot verify. Three barriers drive this: bespoke models proliferate because standardization is difficult (operational fragmentation); once unified, the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and intricate routing logic exceeds what solvers can handle within a tight window (computational intractability); and a mathematically optimal solution still fails to be implemented if the executives do not trust it (implementation hurdle). To bridge this gap, we propose and implement the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose method, deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform. The central insight is decoupling: simulation proposes by generating and evaluating the full set of operationally valid candidate paths-absorbing all idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computationally, matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation achieves a 10-100 times speedup over serial methods, and a list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Operationally, we establish a closed loop via an intelligent diagnosis engine. Since 2025, NetSim has optimized end to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers, the cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and the average monthly carbon reduction is approximately 5,745 tCO2e. SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning. The transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures that the next planning requires just configuration, not reconstruction.

</details>


### [343] [Towards Faithful Graph Explanations with Synergistic Edge Effects via Granular Balls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21381)
*Jiancu Chen,Shuyin Xia,Guan Wang,Degang Chen,Fan Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A parameter-free GNN explainer SeeExplainer uses a granular-ball graph to capture edge synergistic effects and explains by perturbing nodes/edges on the structural graph, achieving state-of-the-art performance on graph classification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Edge-wise perturbation methods often ignore interactions among edges (edge synergy), leading to inaccurate explanations; a synergy-aware, instance-level explanation is needed for GNNs.

Method: Refine the original graph into a disjoint granular-ball graph with variable sizes and treat these granular-balls as nodes to build a structural graph. Then perturb nodes and edges on this structural graph to derive explanatory subgraphs based on their contributions; the approach is parameter-free.

Result: Experiments on several graph classification datasets across different networks show SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

Conclusion: A synergy-aware, parameter-free explainer that uses granular-ball graph refinement better captures edge interactions, yielding superior explanations for GNNs.

Abstract: Instance-level explanations aim to reveal the rationale behind a model's decisions for a specific graph. Previous methods explain graph neural networks (GNNs) by selecting important edges to induce subgraphs, where edge importance is assessed by perturbing each edge and observing changes in the model predictions. However, they often neglect the synergistic effects among edges, which are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance. To address this issue, we propose SeeExplainer, a parameter-free explainer to interpret GNNs. Specifically, we first introduce a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into several disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size, and utilize them as nodes to construct a structural graph. This process can better capture the synergistic effects among edges. Then, we perturb nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

</details>


### [344] [Multimodal Pretraining for Generalizable EEG Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21384)
*Targol Bakhtiarvand,Jugal Kalita,Adham Atyabi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multimodal foundation model for EEG combines raw signals, time-frequency data, and text encodings, trained with self-supervised objectives, achieving state-of-the-art seizure detection on CHB-MIT and robust LOSO performance across datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG models are often dataset- and task-specific; foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest adaptable, cross-dataset representations for EEG tasks.

Method: A multimodal backbone comprising a raw-signal encoder (Mamba), a ViT-style time-frequency encoder, and a lightweight text encoder, all projected into a shared embedding space. Pretraining uses masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses to learn seizure-relevant representations without labels; fine-tuned on CHB-MIT and additional seizure datasets; evaluated under standard splits and LOSO.

Result: Best single AUROC on CHB-MIT: 0.874; ensemble AUROC: 0.878 (state-of-the-art). LOSO mean balanced accuracy: 0.558 across 19 subjects. Demonstrates robust, adaptable seizure detection and interpretable localization across datasets.

Conclusion: The multimodal EEG foundation model enables robust, cross-dataset seizure detection with straightforward adaptation to new scenarios and supports interpretable seizure localization.

Abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) models used for epilepsy are often limited to specific datasets and tasks. This limited approach can make it challenging to apply these models across different datasets or in various situations. However, recent studies in foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest that an adaptable EEG backbone could support a range of EEG related tasks. In this study, we have developed a multimodal EEG foundation model that combines a raw signal encoder based on the Mamba architecture, a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and a lightweight encoder for text, all within a shared embedding space. The pretraining process relies on several innovative techniques, such as masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. These methods are designed to create rich, seizure-relevant representations without requiring labeled data. To assess the efficacy and generalization of our pretrained model, we fine-tuned it on the canonical CHB-MIT seizure detection benchmark and additional seizure detection datasets, and conducted extensive experiments comparing different model variants. On the standard CHB-MIT split, our best single model achieved an AUROC of 0.874, and an ensemble variant reached 0.878 AUROC, representing state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark. In addition to standard train-test splits, we evaluated performance under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, which is rarely reported in prior EEG seizure modeling work and highlights the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection, with a mean LOSO balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects. Across datasets and evaluation settings, our multimodal foundation model enabled robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

</details>


### [345] [MSBraM: A Multi-scale Self-supervised Brain Foundation Model for Hierarchical EEG Dynamics Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21402)
*Tao Zhou,Jing Han,Lingyu Shu,Zixing Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MSBraM introduces a multi-scale self-supervised framework for EEG foundation models, combining a multi-scale neural tokenizer with vector-quantized reconstruction and curriculum masking, achieving state-of-the-art transfer performance across 12 EEG datasets and 10 downstream tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EEG signals exhibit hierarchical, multi-scale temporal structures with local patterns and long-range dependencies. Existing self-supervised methods struggle to capture cross-scale representations, hindering generalization across diverse tasks.

Method: A two-stage pretraining: (1) a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG into semantic codes at multiple temporal resolutions via vector quantized reconstruction; (2) pretraining to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy that gradually integrates fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context.

Result: Pretrained on ~2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluated on 10 downstream tasks across 12 public datasets, MSBraM outperforms state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability.

Conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is beneficial for EEG foundation models, with MSBraM showing improved cross-task generalization and transfer performance.

Abstract: Self-supervised foundation models have recently shown strong potential for electroencephalogram (EEG)-based analysis. However, existing approaches struggle to capture the inherently multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals, where local neural patterns and long-range dependencies jointly encode task-relevant information. This limitation hampers cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose MSBraM, a Multi-Scale self-supervised Brain foundation Model designed to learn hierarchical EEG representations. MSBraM follows a two-stage pretraining framework. First, a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG signals into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Second, the model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. We pretrain MSBraM on over 2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluate it across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets. Extensive experiments show that MSBraM achieves superior performance on other state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability. These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for effective EEG foundation models.

</details>


### [346] [Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21412)
*Bartolomeo Bogliolo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Euclid-MCP is an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic Horn-clause reasoning via SWI-Prolog using Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation. It offers a translate-run-inspect-repair loop for tool-augmented agents, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full proof traces. Empirically, it delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs than LLMs alone on larger knowledge bases, arguing semantic RAG is unsuitable for rule enforcement and that Euclid-MCP can be a shared reasoning substrate for RAG and agentic systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs are unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Neuro-symbolic approaches exist but lack a standardized, engine-agnostic interface for tool-augmented agents, hindering reuse and verification.

Method: Introduce Euclid-MCP: an open-source MCP server backed by SWI-Prolog, featuring Euclid-IR—an engine-agnostic, human-readable Horn-clause intermediate representation that can be compiled to Prolog or other backends. Provide a compact translate-run-inspect-repair tool interface enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while exposing proof traces and derivation logs.

Result: Evaluation on a realistic IT security and compliance use case shows LLMs hallucinate on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP yields exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs.

Conclusion: Semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for enforcing rules; Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.

</details>


### [347] [Logical Regression for Planning with Axioms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21414)
*Connor Little,Christian Muise*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an approximation method for logical regression in planning domains with axioms, focusing on producing minimal partial states to enable efficient, robust execution monitoring.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Logical regression with axioms is computationally hard and can hinder plan execution and robust policy generation. The work seeks scalable, generalizable regression that avoids frequent axiom recomputation and yields compact representations.

Method: Introduce an approximation that confines regression results to partial states, producing minimal partial states and avoiding axiom re-evaluation; integrate this regression into an execution-monitoring framework.

Result: In execution monitoring, the approach reduces the number of variables needed by up to 70% and demonstrates robustness, with recovery in over 50% of trials in environments with unexpected changes across multiple domains.

Conclusion: Partial-state regression in the presence of axioms can be effectively approximated to yield compact, generalizable execution-monitoring policies, offering efficiency gains and robust recovery.

Abstract: In automated planning, logical regression is an operation that returns the most general condition necessary for an action to achieve a particular formula. It has many applications, such as allowing for more robust plan execution and providing compact policies for non-deterministic planning. Although relatively simple to calculate in basic planning settings, logical regression becomes significantly more complex when additional factors, such as axioms, are present. We introduce a methodology for approximating the logical regression of an action in a domain that includes axioms; an approximation that limits conditions to partial states. Our method produces minimal partial states while avoiding the recalculation of axioms. To demonstrate the impact of our methods, we embed our form of regression in an execution monitoring context, a well-established setting that can benefit greatly from logical regression. Our results show that this form of regression can dramatically generalize partial states across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70%, and demonstrate that the resulting execution monitor is robust enough to recover frequently in an environment with unexpected changes: several domains recover over 50% of the time in our tests.

</details>


### [348] [PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21419)
*Yipeng Shi,Zhipeng Ma,Yue Wang,Qitai Tan,Yang Li,Peng Chen,Zhengzhou Zhu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Policy-centric training Pats reframes skill usage as a dynamic training scaffold to guide long-horizon LLM agent RL, enabling adaptive context and efficient prompting; shows improved task performance and reduced prompt tokens, with scaffold discarded at deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weak policies in long-horizon LLM agents recurrently fail and produce uninformative rollouts. Existing skill-centric approaches focus on skills themselves rather than adaptive training-time support for evolving policies.

Method: Turn rollout groups from the current policy into evidence cards, use task-specific evaluation to adjust the context for subsequent rollouts, provide concrete guidance to complete tasks, and revise/remove redundant context as policy improves. The policy is trained with environmental rewards via standard RLVR, and the scaffold is discarded at deployment.

Result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

Conclusion: A policy-centric training scaffold can adaptively guide learning, reduce dependence on explicit guidance as the policy matures, and maintain deployment-time performance, with demonstrated gains in long-horizon RL tasks and prompt efficiency.

Abstract: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts. Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

</details>


### [349] [Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21421)
*Michael Romei de Socio,Gian Luca Pozzato,Alessio Merlo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Post-sampling symbolic constraints improve structural admissibility of generative graph trajectories without sacrificing much sample efficiency; hard filtering is effective especially as graph complexity grows.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the gap between statistical plausibility and structural feasibility in generative models for dynamic graphs by applying symbolic constraints after sampling.

Method: Use a conditional diffusion model to generate future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, with an external symbolic layer implementing hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair.

Result: In a compact graph regime, invalid mass is ~0.003; in a medium-complexity regime, invalid mass is ~0.156. Hard filtering removes all invalid trajectories while preserving ~84% of samples; soft weighting preserves effective sample size but offers limited validity gains. Dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility.

Conclusion: Statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties; the value of symbolic constraint handling grows with graph-structural complexity; post-sampling symbolic constraints can substantially improve admissibility.

Abstract: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime.
